title: chore: Add CRAN submission and release workflows
description:
This PR adds RSQLite's CRAN release tooling, copied from duckdb/duckdb-r at commit 86ac17f6b (the commit for its 2.0.0 release) and then adapted to RSQLite. Once it's merged into `main`, the release workflows can be started with `workflow_dispatch`.

## What it adds

- **`.github/workflows/cran-submission.yaml`**, with the local actions `.github/actions/cran-tag/` (`cran-tag.sh`, which drafts the release and tags the commit, and its offline test) and `.github/actions/cran-submit/` (`cran-submit.sh` and its offline test).
  - You dispatch it by hand on a ref, with the inputs `dry-run`, `allow-dev-version` and `retag`; one run goes at a time, and on a fork every job is skipped.
  - It stops if DESCRIPTION carries a development version.
  - It drafts the GitHub release `RSQLite <version>` from that version's NEWS.md section, with the marker `<!-- cran-submission: RSQLite <version> -->`, and tags `v<version>`. It writes nothing when the tag exists (without `retag`), when the tags on GitHub cannot be read, or when a published release or more than one draft carries the tag. When it updates an existing draft, it first removes the tarball an earlier attempt attached.
  - It builds the package with `R CMD build`, recompresses it with zopfli (`pigz -11`), verifies it and keeps it as an artifact.
  - It uploads the tarball through CRAN's form, the way `devtools:::upload_cran()` does, with the one-line comment `RSQLite <version>`.
  - It attaches the submitted tarball to the draft release, after checking its sha256 and that the draft is the only release with the tag.
- **`.github/workflows/cran-release.yaml`**, with the local action `.github/actions/cran-release/` (`cran-release.sh` and its offline test).
  - It runs nightly. It publishes the marked draft as the latest release, by its id, once P3M's source index lists the version, the draft carries the submitted tarball and is the only marked draft for its tag, and the tag points at the draft's commit.
  - It reports to the release's checklist issue: the open issue whose body carries `<!-- release-checklist: RSQLite <version> -->` and that an owner, member or collaborator of the repository opened. An issue opened by anyone else, a workflow or a bot included, is ignored with a warning.
  - It closes that issue once the release is published.
- **`.github/workflows/release-gate.yaml` and `.github/workflows/winbuilder.yaml`**, both dispatch-only.
- **`.github/actions/release-report/`**, which posts a workflow's result as one comment and updates it in place on later runs, and whose `close-checklist.sh` closes the checklist issue once the release is published.
  - Submission, release gate and win-builder post it on the open release PR whose head is the branch they were dispatched on.
  - `cran-release.yaml` posts it on the checklist issue instead, because the release PR is merged right after the submission.
- **`.github/actions/cran-lib/`**, the log and summary helpers the scripts share.
- **The release process**, written into the header of `cran-submission.yaml`, since RSQLite has no handbook. It covers seven steps: pre-cut review, cut, check, dry run, submit, merge back and publish. It is adapted from duckdb's `handbook/operations/releases/cran/README.md` and `process/README.md`.

## Commits

1. Three verbatim copies. Each file's first line names its source and commit; in scripts it is the second line, after the shebang. These lines keep duckdb's original paths.
2. Adaptation to RSQLite:
   - drop duckdb's vendored-engine check;
   - install the package dependencies before `R CMD build`, because the vignette needs them;
   - update the repository names and test fixtures;
   - fix one shellcheck finding.
3. The tag job never moves an existing `v<version>` tag.
   - If the tag exists, the job prints the tag and its commit and stops before drafting, tagging or uploading.
   - The `retag` input is only for a submission CRAN never received: it prints the old commit, then moves the tag.
   - A resubmission after a rejection uses a new patch version instead.
4. An `attach-tarball` job with `contents: write` runs after the upload. It checks the sha256 and attaches the submitted tarball to the draft release, so the record of what went to CRAN outlives the run's artifact.
5. The scripts move from `scripts/` into local actions under `.github/actions/`, and `^scripts$` leaves `.Rbuildignore`.
6. The `cran-*` push triggers go, so every release run is dispatched by hand, and the result-reporting comments are added.
7. The process text no longer uses `cran-comments.md` or `fledge::bump_version()`.
   - fledge's marker line is removed from NEWS.md by hand.
   - The NEWS heading is exactly `# RSQLite <version>`, with no date.
   - A full dry run comes before the real run.
   - Nothing is submitted while any check on that commit is still running or red.
   - After the merge back, `main` gets a development version and a compare link.
8. `cran-release.yaml` reports to the checklist issue and closes it once the release is published, using the new `published` step output.
9. Review fixes:
   - the tag job and the issue-closing loop move into scripts with offline tests;
   - the tag check fails closed when the tags on GitHub cannot be read;
   - NEWS code fences no longer cut the section, following CommonMark's fence rules;
   - only a member's or collaborator's issue is the checklist, and a rejected one raises a warning;
   - the docs job reports its real result;
   - a draft is published only with the submitted tarball, and a retargeted draft loses the earlier attempt's tarball;
   - submissions run one at a time and drafts are addressed by id;
   - every job is skipped on forks;
   - the reports state only what happened, and a cancelled win-builder run says its upload state is unknown.

The template workflows (R-CMD-check, rhub, pkgdown, revdep) are unchanged.

## Validation

- Offline tests:
  - `cran-submit-test.sh`: 94 passed, including the real `R CMD build` and `pigz` path.
  - `cran-release-test.sh`: 53 passed.
  - `cran-tag-test.sh`: 94 passed. It runs the tag job's script against a local bare remote and a stubbed `gh`, and covers a fresh tag, an existing draft (including the removal of an earlier tarball), several drafts, an existing tag (real run, dry run, `retag` dry and real), an origin that cannot be read, a published release, a missing NEWS section, and each code-fence rule.
  - `release-report-test.sh`: 27 passed.
  - The regression tests for the review findings fail against the scripts before the fixes.
- shellcheck is clean on `.github/actions/*/*.sh`.
- actionlint is clean on the four workflows. Two warnings are ignored because the existing workflows trigger them too: the `ubuntu-26.04` runner label and the missing `description` in the existing custom actions.
- No workflow has been dispatched, so the GitHub-side behaviour is verified by the offline tests and by reading only.

## Review

Two clean-context reviews: the first found two Medium and eight Low issues, the second confirmed the fixes and found four more Low ones, also fixed. What remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/820#issuecomment-6771408287).

title: docs: clarify remote SQLite connection entry points
description:
## Summary
Document both supported entry points for remote read-only SQLite databases using the optional HTTP VFS.

## Thanks to maintainers
Thanks for adding the HTTP VFS in #680 and for maintaining RSQLite.

## Issue or motivation
Addresses #505. Remote access is available, but the package documentation did not show users how to open a remote database.

## Root cause
The `dbConnect()` documentation covered local and in-memory files, and the README listed the HTTP VFS helpers without showing a connection example.

## Change
- Document the optional HTTP VFS under `dbname`, including the required read-only flag for an explicit SQLite URI.
- Add examples for `sqliteRemote()` and the explicit `file:https://...` URI form.
- Regenerate `man/SQLite.Rd`, `README.md`, and `index.md` from their source files.

## Tests
- `tools::checkRd("man/SQLite.Rd")`: passed.
- Rendered `README.Rmd`; the generated `README.md` matches the render output and `index.md` was regenerated.
- `NOT_CRAN=false devtools::test(reporter = "summary")`: passed; 19 tests were skipped for CRAN or platform conditions.
- `R CMD check --no-manual --as-cran --no-multiarch` with force-suggests and remote incoming checks disabled: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 NOTE for the development version number.
- Ran the repository's `clang-format` 21.1.8 source-file command: no changes.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- With `NOT_CRAN=true`, three local HTTP VFS integration tests fail to open the test database; those tests are marked `skip_on_cran()` and were skipped in the passing as-cran check.

## Scope
This change documents the existing read-only HTTP VFS. It does not change VFS behavior or add a new API.

feat: Request R types for result columns with `ptype`
description:
Stacked on #801 (base branch `claude/elegant-tesla-mja103-schema`), which is stacked on #800, #796 and #795.

`dbSendQuery()`, `dbGetQuery()` and `dbReadTable()` gain a `ptype` argument for connections opened with `arrow = TRUE`, the data frame counterpart of the `schema` argument of #801:

```r
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), arrow = TRUE)
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM t", ptype = list(id = bit64::integer64(), when = as.POSIXct(character(), tz = "UTC")))
```

- `ptype` is a data frame or a named list of vectors whose values are ignored, so a zero-row data frame and a list of zero-length vectors describe the same thing. Entries are matched to the result columns by name, exactly: a name not in the result, one the result carries twice, an unnamed entry, a duplicate name, a data frame column, a raw vector (the message points to `blob::blob()`), and a nanoarrow schema (the message points to lists and data frames) are errors raised when the query is sent, with no result left open. Without `arrow = TRUE` the argument is an error too.
- Each named column is requested from SQLite as the Arrow type `nanoarrow::infer_nanoarrow_schema()` gives for the prototype, through the machinery of #801, and converted back to the prototype's type: `integer` as `int32` (values outside the range become `NA` with the warning of #800), `integer64` as `int64` and it stays an `integer64` whatever the values and whatever `bigint` says, `logical` as `bool`, `Date` as `date32`, `blob` as `binary`. `POSIXct` (and `POSIXlt`) and `hms` are requested as `timestamp[us]` in the prototype's time zone and `time64[us]`, which fixes their type, but data frame fetches read them like the times and timestamps decided from `extended_types`: as doubles in seconds with the default path's precision and range (fractions below a microsecond, times outside a day), whatever the declared type, with the prototype's class and time zone (the session's for an empty one); an Arrow stream of the result has them in microseconds. A factor is read as text and converted to its levels, values outside them becoming `NA` as with `factor()`, or to the levels found in the values of each fetch when it has none; an ordered factor stays ordered. A prototype nanoarrow finds no Arrow type for (a complex vector, `NULL`), one of a type RSQLite cannot fill (`difftime`, which nanoarrow maps to `duration`), and one nanoarrow cannot convert back to (an `AsIs` vector, a list) are rejected with the column name before the query is sent, so that an open result is left alone.
- A column with a prototype keeps its type in every fetch, whatever the values. The other columns are typed for each fetch like on the default path (#796), and `bigint` applies only to them. The prototype is stored on the result, so it holds across chunked fetches including `n = 0`, across `dbBind()` and `dbBindArrow()`, for empty results, and for the rows kept when an Arrow schema was requested first.
- The error messages of the shared schema request now name the argument they check (`schema` or `ptype`), and `result_set_arrow_schema()` takes a logical `seconds` per requested column for the times and timestamps that data frame fetches store in seconds.

Tests in `test-arrow-ptype.R` cover the type table, data frame and list prototypes, matching, validation, chunking, binding, empty results, rows kept for a schema, coercion, `bigint`, factors and `dbReadTable()`, compare the columns without a prototype with the default path over sequences of `dbFetch(n)`, and compare `POSIXct` and `hms` prototypes with the default path for fractions below a microsecond and times beyond a day. The Arrow tests (with and without the arrow package), DBItest and DBItest-arrow pass on the branch.

## Review

A clean-context review (2026-09-27) had no findings of its own; it noted that finding 1 of the review on #796 (a small first fetch fixing NULL-first columns) applied to `ptype` fetches too, which holds after merging the reworked layers below and is tested. Problems found while checking every promise above against the merged code are fixed (an ordered prototype without levels came back unordered; prototypes that cannot be requested or converted back failed late or without naming the column; `POSIXct` and `hms` prototypes lost precision below a microsecond and times outside a day). #801 is merged up to 4614fa23; the remaining limitations will be listed in an "Accepted limitations" comment after a final clean review of the whole stack.

Since the integration review: `dbSendQueryArrow()` and `dbGetQueryArrow()` refuse `ptype` together with `schema` (9f385a37), and with `arrow = TRUE`, `dbColumnInfo()` reports the class each prototype produces, as `dbFetch(rs, n = 0)` does (96cc3282); a `blob` or `integer64` prototype is named by its class, while the same types without a prototype keep the default path's names (`list`, `double`).

What remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/802#issuecomment-6778102903).

title: feat: Request Arrow types for result columns with `schema`
description:
Stacked on #800 (base branch `claude/elegant-tesla-mja103-warnings`), which is stacked on #796 and #795.

`dbSendQueryArrow()`, `dbGetQueryArrow()` and `dbReadTableArrow()` gain a `schema` argument that fixes the Arrow types of some or all result columns before the first row is read:

```r
dbGetQueryArrow(con, "SELECT * FROM t", schema = list(id = na_int32(), when = na_timestamp("ms", "UTC")))
```

- `schema` is a struct `nanoarrow_schema`, an arrow `Schema`, or a named list of column types. Entries are matched to the result columns by name, exactly: a name that is not in the result, a name the result carries twice, an unnamed entry, and a data frame (use `nanoarrow::infer_nanoarrow_schema()`, or the upcoming `ptype`) are errors. The form of `schema` is evaluated and checked before the query is sent, the names and types once it has been sent, so a statement with side effects has run when they fail; no result is left open either way.
- A column with a requested type is typed without looking at its values: no widening, no dependence on `chunk_size` or on NULL first rows, and its declared type and `extended_types` play no part. The other columns are typed as before. The request outlives `dbBind()`, so a query executed several times keeps its types. When every column has a requested type, `get_schema()` no longer reads the first chunk, so the warning for the first chunk comes with its array.
- With `dbConnect(arrow = TRUE)`, `dbFetch()` of a result sent with `schema` keeps the requested types: they take precedence over the seconds in which a data frame fetch holds decided times and timestamps, so a requested time or timestamp has its unit, time zone and time of day, and over the types carried over to a new binding after `dbBind()`. Every requested format is converted to R by nanoarrow's prototypes, `uint64` like `int64`.
- The column builder now fills every scalar type of Arrow that SQLite values can be read into: `null`, `bool`, `int8` to `int64`, `uint8` to `uint64`, `float`, `double`, `utf8`, `large_utf8`, `binary`, `large_binary`, `date32`, `date64`, `time32` and `time64` in any unit, `timestamp` in any unit and time zone (read as UTC, labelled with the zone). Dictionary, decimal, nested and extension types are rejected with the column name. The large types never end a chunk at #795's byte limits, since their 64-bit offsets cannot overflow; the rows kept for a schema are split correctly for every requested type. A number in a date column is a count of days, truncated; in a time or timestamp column it is a count of seconds. Times and timestamps are rounded to the nearest tick of their unit, a time to the last tick of the day at most: exactly for integers and for text, which is read to the microsecond, and in double precision for reals. Every array the tests build passes arrow's `ValidateFull()` where arrow is installed.
- Values of another storage class follow one set of rules, for requested and decided types alike, documented in `?"sqlite-arrow"`: integers into floating point and text types, reals into text types and text into binary types are silent; text and blobs into numeric types, reals into integer types (truncated) and into `bool` (true unless zero) are converted with the warning from #800; text or a blob that is not valid UTF-8 without NUL bytes becomes `NULL` in a stream (in a data frame, text ends at its first NUL, as on the default path), and a number outside the range of an integer type (including a real or text beyond 64 bits, which SQLite would saturate), a finite number beyond `float`, a date outside its type, a time outside a day (0 up to 24 hours excluded), a timestamp outside the range of its unit, an unparsable date or time, and any value in a null column become `NULL` with the warning (`invalid_utf8`, `out_of_range`, `null_type`). `uint64` reads reals and text up to 2^64 − 1. Three tests of the layers below relied on these warnings and were updated: two of #800 on an integer-into-text warning, and the comparison of the data frame path with the default path, which now puts a number rather than text into a blob column. Unlike the default path, data frame fetches through Arrow don't warn for these exact conversions, as `?"sqlite-arrow"` now says.
- `dbGetQueryArrow()` and `dbReadTableArrow()` get explicit methods, since DBI's defaults would pass `schema` on to `dbFetchArrow()` or drop it; `dbReadTableArrow()` takes any name that `dbQuoteIdentifier()` takes, such as a string, `SQL()` or `Id()`.
- `dbColumnInfo()` is not touched; a new internal `result_column_names()` reads the names from the prepared statement without stepping it.

The `ptype` counterpart for data frames fetched with `dbConnect(arrow = TRUE)` follows in the next PR of the stack.

## Review

Two clean-context reviews: the first (2026-09-27) found one Low issue and two nits; the second confirmed those fixes and three bugs found on the way, and found three Medium issues (reals and text beyond 64 bits saturating in `int64`/`uint64`, numbers beyond 32 bits wrapping into wrong dates, `time32`/`time64` arrays that Arrow rejects for values outside a day) and four Low ones. All are fixed. #800 is merged up to dc4776ef; the remaining limitations will be listed in an "Accepted limitations" comment after a final clean review of the whole stack.

Since the integration review: a requested `uint64` makes a data frame column a `double` once a value is beyond 2^63 - 1, instead of wrapping it to a negative number (bed25276; the stream keeps the exact value); `dbColumnInfo()` names, for every format a schema can request, the R type that `dbFetch()` returns (9789588b, 221b2f3d); and a number of days beyond 32 bits in a `DATE` column, `NA` with a warning here and a wrapped date on the default path, is listed among the documented differences (4293d3fe, 91b31f75).

What remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/801#issuecomment-6772524830).

The test fixtures this pull request adds live in `tests/testthat/helper-arrow.R`, so every `test_that()` block runs on its own right after `load_all()`. The wrappers that validate every Arrow result in `test-arrow-schema.R` are named `validated_dbGetQueryArrow()`, `validated_dbReadTableArrow()` and `validated_dbFetchArrowChunk()`, so that they do not mask DBI's functions in other test files.

title: feat: Report coerced values once per chunk or `dbFetch()`, with their rows
description:
Stacked on #796 (base branch `claude/elegant-tesla-mja103-arrow-option`), which is stacked on #795. Applies to the native Arrow path, and through #796 to data frames fetched with `dbConnect(arrow = TRUE)`.

Values that are not of their column's Arrow type were reported with one warning per column, raised in the middle of reading a row and naming only the first offending storage class. They are now logged per column with their 1-based row numbers in the result, and reported by one warning that lists every affected column: once per chunk for an Arrow stream and `dbFetchArrowChunk()`, and once per `dbFetch()` for a data frame through Arrow, after its arrays have been conformed to the final types (a column logged as `int64` that became `double` later in the fetch is named `double`). The `dbFetch()` warning is raised from R once the data frame is built, outside #795's busy guard, so a handler can use the result; the warning of a chunk or schema request is raised inside the fetch, where a handler that uses that result gets #795's error.

```
Warning message:
Mixed types in 2 columns, values converted to the column types:
• Column `x` (double): 1 string value converted (row 3)
• Column `y` (utf8): 1 integer value converted (row 3); 1 blob value not valid UTF-8, NA (row 4)
```

- The warning has class `RSQLite_warning_coercion` and carries the structured details in its `coercions` field (column, type, and per storage class and reason the count and rows), so consumer packages and tests can inspect it without parsing the message.
- Long row lists are truncated the way cli does it: the first rows, an ellipsis, and the last two, for example `rows 2, 3, …, 19, …, 30, and 31`. The C++ log keeps only the first 20 and the last 2 row numbers per column and reason, so memory stays bounded, also across the arrays of a data frame fetch. Row numbers are printed in full (`row 100000`, not `1e+05`); the `coercions` field keeps them numeric; they restart with each execution after `dbBind()`.
- cli is used when it is installed, checked once per session: rlang formats the bullets through cli (`local_use_cli(format = TRUE, inline = FALSE)`, so column names with braces are safe), and `cli::ansi_collapse()` joins the rows. Without cli, rlang's own bullets and a plain join give the same text. cli was already in Suggests, so no new dependency.
- The date, time and timestamp parsers no longer raise one warning per value: failures are dropped to `NULL` and listed in the same warning with reason `unparsable`. The default data frame path keeps its per-value warnings, untouched.
- The values that #795 makes NULL (times outside a day, times and timestamps beyond the int64 microseconds, text that is not valid UTF-8 without NUL bytes) are logged too, with reasons `out_of_range` and `invalid_utf8`, instead of one warning per column.
- Text and blobs in a `utf8` column that are not valid UTF-8 without NUL bytes become NULL (since #795) and are logged with reason `invalid_utf8`; on the data frame path text is cut at its first NUL and not checked, as on the default path, while blobs are checked as in a stream. This is the Arrow-path counterpart of #799, sharing the same `src/utf8.h` validator; with #799 merged, both data frame paths return the same values.
- Values in a column of the null type (a first chunk of only `NULL` without a declared type, in a stream or in data frame fetches after a stream or chunk fixed the types) are dropped and listed with reason `null_type`, "dropped by the null type, NA".
- For a lazy stream the warning surfaces when the chunk is fetched from the result: when the array is requested, or for the first chunk when the schema is requested before it. Documented in `?"sqlite-arrow"`, together with how the data frame path differs from the default path, which warns on the same fetches but once per column.
- A coercion warning that an exiting handler or `options(warn = 2)` turns into an exit leaves the result usable: a data frame fetch through Arrow reopens its columns before warning, and the schema request of a stream keeps the first chunk before warning, so a retry returns the schema and every row.
- Each fetch starts with an empty coercion log, so values logged by a fetch that failed (an error of the statement or an interrupt) are not reported by the next one.
- On the data frame path, a string or blob converted to an integer that needs 64 bits keeps the column `integer64` (following `bigint`) in later fetches too, as an integer of that size does; the default path truncates such a value to `integer`, which `?"sqlite-arrow"` lists among the differences.
- A fetch of no rows never warns through Arrow, since it returns no value; the default path warns there about the next row. Documented, and the comparison of both paths in `test-arrow-df.R` spells this exception out.
- The Arrow test helpers, including #796's, moved to `tests/testthat/helper-arrow.R` so the new `test-arrow-coercion.R` can use them. The comparison of both data frame paths in `test-arrow-df.R` now also checks that they warn on the same fetches.

## Review

Two clean-context reviews: the first (2026-09-27) found two Low issues, the second confirmed those fixes and found two Medium issues (a warning that exits a fetch left a NULL-only column null-typed, and a warning that exits a stream's schema request lost the first chunk) and four Low ones; all are fixed or documented. #796 is merged up to cbac340b; the remaining limitations will be listed in an "Accepted limitations" comment after a final clean review of the whole stack.

On a worker thread, where R can't be called (arrow's scanner, Acero, `write_dataset()`), the coercion warning becomes the error of the stream, with the warning's text as R shows it without cli followed by "(an error instead of a warning, …)", like the other warnings of #795 (c7327bec); on R's main thread nothing changes.

What remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/800#issuecomment-6778101427).

title: feat: Add `arrow` argument to `dbConnect()` to route data frames through Arrow
description:
Stacked on #795 (base branch `claude/elegant-tesla-mja103`; retarget to `main` once #795 is merged). Adds `dbConnect(..., arrow = FALSE)`: with `arrow = TRUE`, data frames travel through the native Arrow interface introduced in #795.

- `dbFetch()` fetches its rows as Arrow arrays typed for that fetch, the way the default path types it, and converts them with one set of rules, in `R/arrow-df.R`: nanoarrow's conversions, except that `int64` columns become `integer` when every value fits and follow the `bigint` argument otherwise, also in later fetches once a value needed 64 bits, and `null` columns become `logical`. A column that sees only NULL stays open until its first value, integers widen to double, a column without a value takes its declared type or `logical`, and the next fetch starts from these types, also after `dbBind()`. Times and timestamps travel as doubles in seconds, so they keep the default path's precision and range, times outside a day included, and text ends at its first NUL and is not checked for UTF-8, as on the default path; streams have microseconds, only times of day, and only text that is valid UTF-8 without NUL bytes, and make other values NULL with a warning. Three differences are documented: a real number after an integer too large for an `integer` makes the column a double, which rounds integers beyond 2^53, where the default path truncates the real; `-2147483648` is a value here and `NA` on the default path; and a blob in a text column is text only if it is valid UTF-8 without NUL bytes, as in a stream, NA with a warning otherwise, where the default path cuts it at its first NUL (until #799). Once `dbFetchArrow()` or `dbFetchArrowChunk()` has fixed a result's types, data frame fetches keep them and the rules of a stream (microseconds; times outside a day, timestamps beyond the microseconds and invalid text become NULL), and hand out the rows kept for a schema or held back by the byte limits. `dbFetch(n)` gathers arrays until it has `n` rows, since #795 can end an array early. `Date`, `hms`, `POSIXct` (UTC) and `blob` columns come out as on the default path; fetching from a statement returns an empty data frame with the same warning as the default path. With `arrow = TRUE`, `dbColumnInfo()` answers from the Arrow columns: it names the types that a fetch of no rows returns and, like the default path, decides them for the next fetch, without converting the values of the next row.
- `dbAppendTable()` writes the data frame as an Arrow stream through `dbAppendTableArrow()`, after the same preparation as the default path (factors to strings, lists of raw vectors to blobs, `POSIXlt` to `POSIXct`, which the default path can't write, and `difftime`, `POSIXct` and `Date` to their numbers in their own units). `dbGetQuery()`, `dbReadTable()` and `dbWriteTable()` follow, since they are built on these two.
- The option is stored on the connection and propagated when a connection is cloned, together with `bigint` and `extended_types`, which a clone dropped before. It is documented in `?SQLite` and in the "Data frames" section of `?"sqlite-arrow"`. Experimental, the default stays `FALSE`.
- A data frame fetch through Arrow is covered by #795's guard against re-entry: a warning handler of the fetch that uses the same result gets an error instead of using freed memory.

**Memory.** A benchmark of this path (below) found three problems, fixed in 75ea617:

- A fetch of `n` rows kept every chunk alive behind its data frame: nanoarrow's character vectors read from the Arrow array until they are touched. The strings are now copied out and the array released right away.
- A fetch of all rows held the result twice, as Arrow arrays and as the data frame, because `nanoarrow::convert_array_stream()` collects every array of a stream of unknown size before it converts. Every `dbFetch()` now goes through `result_fetch_arrow_df()`, which hands it the arrays as a list with their lengths and formats: a single array is converted directly with its strings copied, and several are copied into columns allocated once with the row count known, each array released as soon as it has been copied.
- A loop over `dbFetchArrowChunk()` that discards its chunks piled them up as garbage the collector does not see. `dbFetchArrowChunk()` now triggers a collection of the young generation after every 64 MB of arrays handed out; the "Chunking" section of `?"sqlite-arrow"` says so and points to `nanoarrow::nanoarrow_pointer_release()` for tighter loops.
- The check whether 64-bit integers fit into an integer vector moved to C++ (`integer64_to_integer()`), which spares the temporary vectors it needed in R.

**Benchmark.** `experiments/2026-09-26-arrow-df-fetch/` records it in the shape of the shared experiments convention: `bench.R` fetches a synthetic table of one and five million rows (integers, reals, two text columns, NULLs) per strategy in fresh subprocesses and records wall time and peak RSS; the four CSV files hold the runs before (`83bb24e`) and after (`75ea617`) the fixes, and the README carries the tables and the findings. On five million rows: a full fetch through Arrow takes about a third less time than on the default path on every query (12.1 against 17.8 s for all columns), at 823 against 679 MB above the 100 MB floor (1,081 MB before the fixes); a chunked fetch of 10,000 rows runs at 7.1 s and 131 MB against 9.5 s and 99 MB on the default path (230 MB and growing before); a `dbFetchArrowChunk()` loop that discards its chunks stays at 113 MB (366 MB before). Re-measured at one million rows on d2013e38: full and chunked fetches are within noise of the record. Small fetches cost more than on the default path: 20,000 calls of `dbFetch(rs, 1)` take 2.3 s against 0.66 s. `experiments/` is in `.Rbuildignore`, and the `arrow` argument's source carries a plain comment pointing at the record.

DBItest: `tests/testthat/test-DBItest-arrow.R` runs the whole suite a second time with `arrow = TRUE` through a second, non-default context, with the same skips as the default run. Both runs pass locally, as do the unit tests in `tests/testthat/test-arrow-df.R`, which compare both paths with `expect_identical()` on mixed, NULL-first, declared, blob and 64-bit columns over several sequences of small `n` and several bindings, and cover results larger than one chunk, arrays cut short by the byte limits, fractional times and timestamps, times outside a day, text that is not UTF-8, and the ownership of strings fetched in chunks. Random comparisons over thousands of tables found no differences beyond the documented ones. The tests pass with and without the arrow package installed (CI's smoke job does not install it; `arrow` is in Suggests since #795). The full suite has four errors here that need a local HTTP server or an installed RSQLite (`test-httpvfs.R`, the `callr` test in `test-dbConnect.R`).

## Review

Two clean-context reviews: the first (2026-09-27) found one High finding (a small first fetch fixed the column types before a value was seen, and data was lost) and three Low ones; the second confirmed those fixes and found two Medium issues (sub-microsecond precision lost on times and timestamps, types reset by `dbBind()`) and five Low ones. All are fixed or documented, except the mixed-type warning once per result, which #800 replaces. #795 is merged up to 68a1cbc5; the remaining limitations will be listed in an "Accepted limitations" comment after a final clean review of the whole stack.

title: feat: Implement the DBI Arrow interface natively
description:
Query results are written from the SQLite statement straight into nanoarrow arrays, and Arrow arrays are bound straight to statement parameters, without passing through R vectors.

- `dbSendQueryArrow()` returns the new `SQLiteResultArrow` class. `dbFetchArrow()` returns a lazy `nanoarrow_array_stream` that fetches one chunk per `get_next()`, and `dbFetchArrowChunk()` returns one such array per call. A result set is never materialized as a whole on the Arrow path.
- A chunk holds at most `chunk_size` rows (default 65536; it must be finite and is capped at 2^53), and it ends early before any text or blob column would pass the 2^31 - 1 bytes its 32-bit offsets can address. Rows read ahead to determine the schema are kept and handed out by later fetches, also smaller ones; `dbHasCompleted()` and `dbGetRowCount()` count them only once they are handed out, and a data-frame `dbFetch()` fails while such rows, or a row held back by the byte limit, wait. Fetched rows are counted in 64 bits, so a stream can read past `INT_MAX` rows; `dbGetRowCount()` returns the count as an integer while it fits, as before, and as a double beyond.
- The stream shares ownership of the C++ result, so it stays readable after `dbClearResult()` (which is what `dbGetQueryArrow()` needs), while other queries run, and after `dbDisconnect()`; until it is read to the end or released, it keeps the statement, a read transaction and the database file open. It fails once its result is bound to new parameters with `dbBind()` or `dbBindArrow()`. After `dbDisconnect()`, an SQLite error raised through it carries only SQLite's generic message for the error code.
- `dbBindArrow()` binds Arrow streams batch by batch, executing the statement once per row; `dbAppendTableArrow()`, `dbWriteTableArrow()` and `dbCreateTableArrow()` build on it. Named placeholders are matched to column names like `dbBind()` does it. Binding a result to a stream of its own rows is rejected; a parameter row that fails to bind ends the execution, and a failed first row requires a new bind. The indices of a dictionary column are checked against the dictionary, and text and blobs are bound with 64-bit sizes, so a value beyond SQLite's length limit gives its "string or blob too big" error.
- A result refuses to be fetched from, bound, inspected or cleared while one of its own fetches or binds is running, as from a handler of a warning that the fetch raised; before, such re-entry could use freed memory. The mark is reset through `R_ExecWithCleanup()`, so also when an R error leaves the fetch by a longjmp instead of through cpp11 (a raw allocation that fails, an ALTREP parameter, a parameter stream of another package that calls R); such a longjmp still skips the C++ destructors of the frames it leaves.
- Result columns keep the SQLite values intact: integers are always `int64`, reals `double`, text `utf8`, blobs `binary`, and with `extended_types = TRUE` the declared `DATE`, `TIME` and `DATETIME`/`TIMESTAMP` columns become `date32`, `time64[us]` and `timestamp[us, UTC]`. SQLite is dynamically typed, so the first chunk decides the types (the first non-NULL value, widening `int64` to `double` if a real turns up, the declared type for columns that only held NULL). Values an Arrow array cannot hold become `NULL` with a warning, so every array passes Arrow's full validation: text or blobs in a `utf8` column that are not valid UTF-8 without NUL bytes, times outside a day, and timestamps beyond the int64 microseconds. Text in a `binary` column is its UTF-8 bytes, also in a UTF-16 database, as on the data frame path. A blob in a `utf8` column keeps its bytes for the UTF-8 check, also in a UTF-16 database, where SQLite would otherwise transcode it. See `?"sqlite-arrow"` for the full mapping, the parameter mapping, and the chunking rules.
- The nanoarrow C library 0.9.0 is vendored in `src/vendor/nanoarrow` (with `NANOARROW_NAMESPACE` set to `RSQLite`, documented in the README there), and the nanoarrow package is a new dependency; `arrow` is suggested, for a test that runs Arrow's full validation where it is installed. The result external pointer now owns a shared pointer, the same idiom the connections use.
- SQLite errors raised while fetching are C++ exceptions rather than R errors, so that they can cross the Arrow stream callbacks (nothing may longjmp through the consumer's C frames); cpp11 turns them into the same R errors at the entry points. The stream callbacks continue a `cpp11::unwind_exception` with `R_ContinueUnwind()`, as cpp11's own wrapper does, except when RSQLite binds one of its own streams, where they rethrow it through C++ so that RSQLite's frames unwind.
- `src/Makevars.deps` now drops system headers on every line of the generated `.dd` files, including gcc's one-space continuation lines; before, CI's auto-update could commit absolute runner paths into them, which breaks a source install anywhere else.
- Arrow streams can be read on any thread, one call at a time, as the C stream interface allows: arrow's scanner, Acero (behind its dplyr verbs) and `arrow::write_dataset()` call `get_next()` on worker threads, and the scanner and Acero read ahead in the background while R goes on. On a thread other than R's main thread, RSQLite calls no R API: values that would be converted with a warning fail the stream with the warning's message instead. A result is used by one thread at a time, under an atomic busy mark that records whether R's main thread or another thread holds it; while another thread reads, fetching from, binding or describing the result on R's main thread fails with a message that says so, while `dbClearResult()`, `dbGetRowCount()`, `dbHasCompleted()` and the next query on the connection keep working and the stream reads on. A result that a stream lets go of on another thread has its statement finalized at once if nothing else holds it, and is otherwise destroyed on R's main thread when its result object is cleared or at the next result operation there.
- The tests with real column sizes (chunks of 1 GiB and 2 GiB blobs, a parameter of 2^31 bytes) peak at about 2.5 GB each and release their memory before the next test (the test process peaks at about 3.3 GB), and run only with `RSQLITE_TEST_LARGE_ARROW=true`, which the `custom/after-install` hook sets for the GitHub Actions checks; CRAN, the R-hub containers and users running the tests skip them.
- On the default path, `dbBind()` of an unnamed list to a query without placeholders now says "Query does not require parameters." where `main` said "Named parameters not used in query: ".

DBItest: the whole suite passes. Twelve Arrow round trip specs are skipped and explained in `tests/testthat/helper-DBItest.R` (`arrow_read_table_arrow`, `arrow_read_table_arrow_empty`, and the `roundtrip_integer`, `_logical`, `_character`, `_blob` and `_mixed` variants of `arrow_write_table_arrow` and `arrow_append_table_arrow`), and only when RSQLite with its own `dbFetchArrow()` method is installed, so the copies of the helper in DBItest and DBI skip nothing. SQLite integers are 64-bit, so an R integer column comes back as `int64`, which nanoarrow converts to `double` by default, and the specs compare against R `integer` columns with `expect_identical()`. This is a property of SQLite rather than of the implementation (DuckDB and ADBC map SQLite integers to 64 bits too); the alternative, reading declared `INTEGER` columns as `int32`, would fail on values above 2^31 that turn up after the first chunk. A DBItest tweak that relaxes the comparison for 64-bit backends would let the specs run. #831, on top of the stack, declares the DBItest version in the helper.

## Review

Three clean-context reviews: the first (2026-09-27) found one High, four Medium and two Low issues; the second confirmed those fixes and found one Medium (the per-row size check slowed text columns by about 30 %, now about 6 %) and six Low ones; the third confirmed those and found one Medium (a heap use after free from a warning handler that re-enters its own result, found with AddressSanitizer) and three Low ones. Reviews of the pull requests above and the integration review found more issues located here (out-of-range times and timestamps, times outside a day, text that is not valid UTF-8, `arrow` missing from Suggests, unchecked dictionary indices and 32-bit sizes of parameters, the 32-bit row counter, UTF-16 bytes for text in a binary column), and the busy mark could stay set after an R error that bypassed cpp11. All High and Medium findings are fixed, AddressSanitizer is clean on the reviewers' reproducers and on `test-arrow.R`, and CI is green on c7ab2b63. The review of the fixes up to c7ab2b63 found that Arrow's Acero engine and `write_dataset()` read the stream on a worker thread, where its callbacks called R; that is fixed in 033dded7. The [second integration review of the stack](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6776830099) found the date and time parsers still calling R's `ISNAN()` there, arrow's read-ahead running into the busy mark, and a stream released on a worker thread keeping its statement open; all three are fixed up to 68a05750, where an interposer counts no R call off R's main thread. That was the last review round for the stack. What remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/795#issuecomment-6801022224). #830, from `main`, fixes the restart of a result after an SQLite error and the state after a failed bind, and merges in here. title: fix: Validate blobs that are read into a text column
description:
When a column is typed as text from its first values and a blob turns up later, the blob was read with `sqlite3_column_text()` as a C string: it was silently cut at the first NUL byte, and bytes that are not UTF-8 were handed to R as a string marked UTF-8. A blob `X'00ff'` came back as `""`.

A blob in a text column is now read with `sqlite3_column_blob()` and `sqlite3_column_bytes()` and validated in `fetch_string()`. A blob that is well-formed UTF-8 without NUL bytes becomes the full string, an empty blob becomes `""`, and anything else becomes `NA`, with one warning per column and fetch that counts the replaced values, next to the existing mixed-type warning:

    Column `x`: 2 blob values are not valid UTF-8 text, NA is returned
    Column `x`: mixed type, first seen values of type string, coercing other values of type blob

Because `sqlite3_column_text()` is never called on a blob, the value keeps its storage class. A peek with `dbFetch(res, n = 0)` or `dbColumnInfo(res)` therefore no longer switches the check off for the next fetch of the same row, and in a UTF-16 database the blob is no longer transcoded before the check (`X'6162'` used to come back as `"扡"`). The peek itself does not warn about invalid blobs; the fetch that returns the row does, so each value is reported once. Both column warnings now pass their message as an argument rather than as a format, so a column name containing `%` is printed as is; on `main`, a column name containing `%n` aborted R (`*** %n in writable segment detected ***`).

Behavior change: a blob holding a NUL byte, such as a NUL-terminated C string stored with its terminator, now becomes `NA` with a warning, where `main` returned the string up to the NUL.

Text values are not checked and are read as before: text with an embedded NUL is still cut silently, and text that is not valid UTF-8 is still returned marked as UTF-8. The warning text for a non-ASCII column name is not marked as UTF-8, as in the existing mixed-type warning, and a peek still emits the mixed-type warning, so it appears twice for the same row, as on `main`. The validator lives in a new header `src/utf8.h`, shared with the Arrow path of #795; whether it moves into a `.cpp` file is an open question on #829.

The tests in `tests/testthat/test-blob.R` cover the malformed UTF-8 forms (overlong, surrogate, beyond U+10FFFF, truncated), a NUL-terminated C string, an empty blob, a fetch in chunks where a later chunk holds only blobs, a peek between two chunks, a UTF-16 database, and a column name containing `%s%d`.

No open issue covers this. The closed #439 is the related case of text coerced to 0 in numeric columns.

A clean review of 867813e8 found one Medium and six Low issues. The Medium and four of the Low ones are fixed in d26413c3, which a [second clean review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/799#issuecomment-6772799501) confirmed without High or Medium findings; what remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/799#issuecomment-6798327460).

title: ci: Document with a patched roxygen2 that keeps the sentence gap
description:
Stacked on #788, which this pull request targets. It does not depend on it, and can be retargeted to `main` so that it is decided on its own and CI runs on it.

## The problem

commonmark discards the whitespace a line break stands for. roxygen2 turns every softbreak into a bare newline, so the `.Rd` carries a line break with nothing after it and `Rd2txt()` renders it as a single space. Prose written one sentence per line therefore comes out single-spaced, while the same words wrapped to a fixed width with two spaces after the period keep the gap.

That makes the two styles mutually exclusive: splitting a sentence pair separated by two spaces silently drops one of them. That is what forced the very long single roxygen lines this package used to carry, because joining was the only way to keep the gap.

Only the text renderer is affected. `Rd2HTML()` and `Rd2latex()` differ by whitespace that HTML and TeX collapse, and LaTeX applies its own sentence spacing regardless. But text is what `?topic` shows, so it is the version most people read.

## The change

A new composite action, `.github/workflows/roxygen2-fork`, installs roxygen2 from upstream with the `R/` part of the fork branch `krlmlr/roxygen2@f-sentence-spacing` applied on top. The repository's own hook, `.github/workflows/custom/after-install`, runs it in the `rcc-smoke` job only, before the Roxygenize step; the other jobs do not document and skip it. The step runs with `continue-on-error`: if the install fails, `R-CMD-check.yaml` skips Roxygenize and lists the failure in the check summary, so the other checks still run.

The action fetches upstream and the fork by pinned full commit SHAs (`upstream-sha` and `fork-sha`, which move together in a reviewed commit), with history but without file contents, and retries the fetches. It computes the diff against their merge base restricted to `R/`, and applies it with `git apply --3way`. Restricting to `R/` means an unrelated upstream change to a test fixture cannot fail the documentation step. It aborts if the patch is empty or does not apply, rather than silently installing an unpatched build, and afterwards asserts that what it installed really carries the patch.

`Config/roxygen2/version` becomes `8.1.1.9100`: upstream's 8.1.1.9000 with the `.9100` suffix, which distinguishes a patched build from upstream's own `.9000` development builds. The suffix is stamped with a single-line edit of roxygen2's `Version:` field. `DESCRIPTION` is DCF and cannot carry a comment line, since `read.dcf()` rejects one as malformed, so the explanation lives in a `Config/cynkra/roxygen2` field.

## Why it is a separate pull request

Taking it changes rendered help across the package; leaving it means the reformatting renders exactly as the package renders today, with one space between sentences. Neither half needs the other to be correct, so they should be able to be decided separately.

`man/` is not edited by hand here. The `.Rd` files are generated output, so CI roxygenises and commits them itself; 16 regenerated `.Rd` files are part of this pull request's diff as an automated commit, and the hand-written half stays reviewable on its own.

## Upstream

The roxygen2 side is `krlmlr/roxygen2#8`, on the fork, not yet filed with r-lib. It is deliberately narrow: mid-sentence breaks are untouched, links are unaffected, and two guards keep it from firing wrongly: an abbreviation list so a line ending in `e.g.` or `et al.` does not gain a mid-sentence gap, and a fix for a determinism bug where a line starting with `\doi{}` or `\code{}` gained or lost its gap at random, because the test was reading roxygen2's own random placeholder for protected Rd tags.

## Review

A clean-context review found one High and four Medium issues, all fixed; what remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/791#issuecomment-6764413966), most importantly that nothing of the new setup has run in CI yet.

title: feat: Deprecate setting the `row.names` default via pkgconfig, and move pkgconfig to Suggests
description:
RSQLite 2.0 changed the default of `row.names` to `FALSE` (#210) and offered `pkgconfig::set_config("RSQLite::row.names.query" = NA)` (and `"RSQLite::row.names.table"`) as a temporary, per-package way to restore the old default. This PR starts retiring that setting, and with it the hard dependency on pkgconfig.

## Changes

- The `row.names` arguments of `dbFetch()`, `dbReadTable()`, `dbWriteTable()`, `sqlData()`, and `sqliteBuildTableDefinition()` now default to a plain `FALSE`. The man pages show that instead of the `pkgconfig::get_config(...)` expression.
- If `row.names` is not passed, the new internal `row_names_default()` (in `R/pkgconfig.R`, replacing the `pkgconfig_dummy()` stub) consults pkgconfig, but only if its namespace is already loaded. Anyone who called `pkgconfig::set_config()` has it loaded, so nothing is loaded otherwise. The per-calling-package lookup works as before.
- A value found there is still honored, with a deprecation warning once per key and value. The warning says the setting may come from a package in use, and asks to remove the `pkgconfig::set_config()` call and pass `row.names` explicitly. An explicit `row.names` argument always wins. The `row.names` documentation of `dbReadTable()` and `dbWriteTable()` says the same.
- Internal metadata queries (`dbListTables()`, `dbExistsTable()`, and the schema lookup behind them) now pass `row.names = FALSE`. Before, they read the setting too, so the deprecation warning fired even when all user-facing calls were explicit, and a value of `TRUE` made them fail with "Column row_names not present in output" (also on `main`).
- pkgconfig moves from Imports to Suggests. No other hard dependency of RSQLite pulls it in, so it drops out of the install tree.
- The documented default for `row.names` in `sqliteBuildTableDefinition()` is corrected from `TRUE` to `FALSE`.
- New tests in `tests/testthat/test-row-names-default.R` cover the plain default, the warn-and-honor path for both keys, the per-package lookup (a setting registered for another package applies only to calls from that package), and the internal queries. They use `expect_no_warning()`, so the testthat requirement is now 3.1.5.

## Review

A clean-context review found no High or Medium issues; its Low findings are fixed or listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/805#issuecomment-6764344519).

## Follow-up

Removing the setting entirely after this is released is tracked in #803.

## Checks

The new tests pass, and the new internal-query test fails without the fix. The full local test suite has errors only in `test-httpvfs.R` ("unable to open database file" when connecting to a local HTTP server) and in the `callr` test of `test-dbConnect.R` (no installed RSQLite in the subprocess); `origin/main` fails the `test-httpvfs.R` tests the same way in the same container, so they are unrelated to this change.

description:
Rendering `README.Rmd` on a clean machine does not reproduce the committed `README.md`.

The example prints `mtcars` through `dbReadTable()`, and whether that output is truncated is decided by `max.print`, which this file never sets and which no `.Rprofile` in the repository sets either. R's default is 99999, so a clean render prints all 32 rows. The committed `README.md` instead shows the 9-row form ending in `[ reached 'max' / getOption("max.print") -- omitted 23 rows ]`, which means it was rendered under a personal `options(max.print = 99)`. Anyone who re-renders without that setting produces a 23-row diff they did not intend.

Pinning the option in the setup chunk, next to the existing `pkgload::load_all()`, makes the truncation a property of the file rather than of whoever renders it. Verified against the current CRAN toolchain (knitr 1.52, rmarkdown 2.32, downlit 0.4.5, commonmark 2.0.0): with this change a clean render reproduces the committed `README.md` byte for byte, which is why `README.md` is not touched here and the diff is a single file.

Found while checking README rendering stability across the package fleet. Of the repositories that render a README, most are already reproducible; this one and DBI shared this `max.print` dependency, fixed the same way in r-dbi/DBI#759.

Two related observations, deliberately left out of this PR. Rendering rewrites `index.md`, because the cynkratemplate version installed here (0.0.2.9028) does not emit the `<!-- Generated by cynkratemplate: do not edit by hand -->` banner that the committed `index.md` carries — a cynkratemplate version skew rather than anything wrong in this repository. Rendering also touches `src/cpp11.dd`, which is a `load_all()` build artifact. Both are left untouched.

title: docs: State the goals and non-goals
description:
A reader landing on this README should be able to tell in a few seconds whether RSQLite is what they want, and which parts of their question belong to DBI instead.

Evidence behind each claim:

- **"will never use a system SQLite"**: the sources and extensions ship in `src/` and are compiled into the package; nothing looks for a SQLite on the host.
- **"you should always start by loading DBI, not RSQLite"**: verbatim from `vignettes/RSQLite.Rmd`, which is the basis for the non-goal about not defining the interface.
- **"conforms to the specification"**: the full DBItest suite runs in `tests/testthat/test-DBItest.R`.
- **"exposes SQLite-specific features"**: the bundled extension functions enabled by `initExtension()`, and read-only remote access when `configure` finds libcurl.
- **"does not keep the pre-DBI API alive"**: `R/deprecated.R` plus the NEWS entries deprecating `dbGetPreparedQuery()`, `sqliteBuildTableDefinition()` and `make.db.names()`.

**Why the consistency bullet is narrow.** It promises the same SQLite engine, with the same build options, on every installation, and nothing more. `configure` probes for libcurl with pkg-config or curl-config, and on a host that has it the build links `-lcurl` and compiles in the HTTP VFS, which the next bullet advertises; so the build is not free of system libraries, but the SQLite engine is always the one included here, and libcurl is the one system library `configure` looks for.

**Worth knowing, not changed here:** the sentence the bullet was paraphrasing is in `DESCRIPTION` itself ("System libraries will never be consulted because this package relies on static linking for the plugins it includes"), and it has the same problem, two sentences after it describes the optional libcurl-dependent VFS. Fixing `DESCRIPTION` is a different concern from the README section and is left for a separate change.

**One bullet is softer than the others.** "Make up for what SQLite does not do" is an inference from the README's own description of SQLite as single-user, light-weight and implementing a subset of SQL 92; it is not a written scope statement anywhere. If you read that as overreach, drop that bullet; the rest stand on explicit text.

**One structural change:** the README's install instructions were glued to the intro with no heading, so there was nowhere to put a section between them. An `## Installation` heading now sits above the existing install text. Nothing else moved.

Only `README.Rmd`, `README.md` and `index.md` change; no `R/`, no `man/`. `README.md` and `index.md` are rendered from `README.Rmd` with cynkratemplate's `readme_document` format, the way CI's re-render step does it, and a second render is byte-identical.

A clean-context review found the factual claims sound; its findings on the generated file and the wording are all fixed, so there are no accepted limitations. #791 is stacked on this pull request.

title: docs: Break lines at meaning boundaries
description:
Reformatting only, no wording changes. Prose in `README.Rmd`, `vignettes/RSQLite.Rmd`, and the roxygen and inline comments under `R/` now breaks at sentence and clause boundaries rather than wrapping to a fixed width.

The payoff is sentence-level diffs. A reworded sentence touches one line instead of reflowing the paragraph around it, so review sees the change and not the rewrap.

## `man/` is left to CI

`man/` is not part of this pull request. Every commit in the chain leaves the `.Rd` files byte-identical to `main`, and CI regenerates and commits them after merge, so what is under review here is the sources alone.

## Verification

- Word-level identity for every file touched: comment markers stripped, whitespace collapsed, compared — nothing reworded, added or dropped.
- `render_readme()` run twice — byte-identical output.
- Every `R/*.R` still parses. `src/cpp11.dd` was not touched.

## One consequence, stated plainly

A line break which follows the end of a sentence currently renders as one space, not two, so writing one sentence per line drops the sentence gap from the rendered help. That is why an earlier revision of this branch kept sentence pairs joined on one line in `@param synchronous`, `@param flags`, `@param value`, `@param append` and the `dbWriteTable()` `@details`; those joins are undone here, and `@param flags` now breaks at its semicolons so each item and each sentence starts a line. Restoring the gap needs a patched roxygen2, which is a separate decision: it is #791, stacked on top of this chain, and can be taken or left on its own. Without it, this change renders as the package renders today, minus that gap.

## One block still left as it was

`@param default.extensions` is a sharper case and worth a separate look: the source reads `...on the new connection.Setting this value to \`FALSE\`` — a **missing space** after the period. Any break at that sentence boundary would *insert* a space and so change the rendered help, and every alternative break exceeds 140 columns. It is left exactly as it was; fixing the typo is a content change and does not belong in a reformatting pass.

Generated files are left alone: `R/cpp11.R`, `R/export.R`, `R/import-standalone-*.R`.

Part of a fleet-wide pass. r-lib/here#195 is the reference PR, reviewed by hand before the rest were run.

title: docs: Harmonize README and pkgdown front page rendering
description:
Part of a fleet-wide pkgdown harmonization. Stacked on #783 (the `pak::pak()` README change), which this PR targets, so any conflict surfaces here rather than at merge time. The output format lands in cynkra/cynkratemplate#116, and the CI step that will keep these files current in cynkra/cynkratemplate#118.

## What changes

`README.Rmd` declares `output: cynkratemplate::readme_document` — a `github_document` that also writes the pkgdown front page from the same render, with `-smart` and `--wrap=preserve` so diffs stay sentence-level. Stating the format by name rather than repeating its settings means the settings live in one place instead of thirty.

`index.md` is newly added here: the README's trailing boilerplate belongs on GitHub while pkgdown puts that material in its sidebar, so the two files genuinely differ. It is added to `.Rbuildignore`, since `R CMD check --as-cran` otherwise reports it as a non-standard top-level file.

The `README.md` diff is otherwise the pandoc settings taking effect: `--wrap=preserve` stops lines being rebroken at 72 columns, `-smart` leaves quotes and dashes as written. No prose changes.

## `src/cpp11.dd`, and why it is no longer here

`src/cpp11.dd` is a compiler-generated dependency list, tracked here but rewritten by any build. The render step built the package first and then committed the whole working tree, so 710 lines of absolute include paths from the rendering machine were swept into the render commit. A third commit used to put the file back.

That left the pollution in history and, worse, on the three branches stacked above this one, which branched from the render commit and not from the restore. The render commit no longer touches the file at all, and the restore commit is gone. `git diff main..<branch> -- src/cpp11.dd` is empty on all four branches in the chain.

## The print limit

The rendered example is truncated at `max.print = 100`, pinned by the output format during the render (cynkra/cynkratemplate#124). Without it the front page opened with two complete 32-row `mtcars` dumps, whose length depended on whatever the rendering session had `max.print` set to.

## Reproducing

```r
rmarkdown::render("README.Rmd")   # or devtools::build_readme(), or Knit
```

Two consecutive renders are byte-identical — checked before committing, because cynkra/cynkratemplate#118 re-renders in CI and commits the result.

title: docs: Drop the branch from the coverage badge
description:
Two URLs make up the coverage badge and they had drifted apart: the image is served from the bare `codecov.io` host, the link opens the UI on `app.codecov.io`. Both are brought to their current form.

The branch is dropped from the image URL rather than pinned to `main`. A branch-pinned badge keeps reporting the branch it names, so it goes stale silently the next time a branch is renamed — which is how several badges in this fleet came to report a branch that no longer exists. Without the pin, codecov reports the default branch and the badge follows a rename on its own.

The link moves to `/tree/main`, the address the `?branch=` query redirects to.

```
image  codecov.io/gh/r-dbi/RSQLite/graph/badge.svg
link   app.codecov.io/gh/r-dbi/RSQLite/tree/main
```

The owner and repository are carried over from the URL being rewritten, so this cannot retarget a badge at a different project. The badge block is pass-through markdown, so `README.md` and `index.md` carry the identical edit rather than a re-render; that equivalence was checked against a real render before the change was applied across the fleet.

This is part of a fleet-wide badge harmonization. Stacked on the pkgdown harmonization, which this PR targets, so the diff is the badge change alone.

ci(rcc-dev): install dev package deps from P3M instead of patching `Suggests`
description:
## Problem

The scheduled **`rcc dev`** workflow (`.github/workflows/R-CMD-check-dev.yaml`) fails at the R CMD check step with ~300 test failures:

```
Error in `loadNamespace(x)`: there is no package called 'purrr'
...
[ FAIL 304 | WARN 6 | SKIP 62 | PASS 2750 ]
Error:
! Test failures.
Execution halted
```

## Root cause

The failure was in the workflow, not the package. The "Install dev version" step ran:

```r
remotes::install_runiverse("<pkg>", linux_distro = "noble")
```

`install_runiverse()` installs the **dev package** but does **not** pull the new hard dependencies that dev version may declare. Dev `DBItest` (>= `1.8.2.9020`) moved `purrr` into its **Imports** and calls `purrr::map_lgl()` / `purrr::map()` in its internal `stream_frame()` helper (`DBItest/R/spec-arrow.R`), which backs every Arrow spec test. Since `purrr` was never installed, every Arrow roundtrip spec errored with `there is no package called 'purrr'`, and the ~300 failures pushed the run past testthat's limit and aborted R CMD check.

Adding `purrr` to `Suggests` (the previous version of this PR) only masked this one instance — the next dev dependency a checked package adds would break the run again. The fix belongs in the workflow.

## Fix

Replace the single-line install step with a **three-phase install** that provisions whatever hard dependencies the dev package declares, sourcing them as released binaries from P3M (Posit Package Manager) rather than dragging the whole dev tree from r-universe:

1. **Install the dev package alone** with `dependencies = FALSE`, keeping `linux_distro = "noble"` so we still get the fast r-universe *binary* build instead of compiling from source.
2. **Provision new hard deps from P3M**: read the freshly installed dev package's `Depends` / `Imports` / `LinkingTo`, diff against what's already installed, and `install.packages()` the missing ones from P3M (with `repos` set explicitly, since step 1 may have pointed repos at r-universe). This is what brings in dev `DBItest`'s `purrr`, dev `tidyr`'s `cpp11`, etc. — as released binaries.
3. **Re-install the dev package** with `dependencies = TRUE` to ensure it's in place and fill any residual gaps, now that its hard deps are already satisfied.

The `purrr`-in-`Suggests` workaround has been **reverted** from `DESCRIPTION`.

### `noble` caveat

`linux_distro = "noble"` is retained to preserve fast binary installs, but r-universe has renamed its Linux binary distro from **`noble`** to **`resolute`**. The hardcoded value can therefore start returning **404** for some packages (it already broke a dev `tidyr` install). It's kept for now to keep binary installs working; `linux_distro` should be updated or dropped once it starts 404ing. This is documented inline in the workflow.

## Verification

The `rcc dev` workflow only triggers on schedule / `cran-*` / tags / manual dispatch, not on PR branches. A manual `workflow_dispatch` run has been triggered against this branch to confirm the fix on the CI runner.

title: ci(covr): install xml2 from r-lib/xml2#479 to fix multi-hour coverage runs
description:
## Problem

The coverage job on GitHub Actions takes ~5 hours. The time is spent entirely **after** the last `Moving gcov outputs to covr directory.` message — i.e. in `covr::to_cobertura(cov)`, which the covr action runs after `package_coverage()`.

`to_cobertura()` builds the Cobertura report by appending one `<line>` XML node per covered source line. With released xml2, `xml_add_child()` defaults to `.where = length(xml_children(.x))`, which re-enumerates **all** existing siblings on every append → **O(n²)** per file. For RSQLite's bundled `sqlite3.c` (~67k covered lines under a single `<lines>` node) that is ~4.5 billion operations.

### Evidence

Profiling the real coverage object (74,017 entries; `sqlite3.c` = 67,619) showed everything up to and including `package_coverage()` finishing in ~1.2 min, while `to_cobertura()` dominated, with `Rprof` attributing **94%** of time to `xml_add_child` → `xml_children`/`xml_nodeset`.

## Fix

The root cause is in xml2 and is fixed upstream by **[r-lib/xml2#479](https://github.com/r-lib/xml2/pull/479)**, which makes the default append O(1).

This PR installs xml2 from that PR at the start of the covr action, so the fast path is used **only for coverage runs**:

```yaml
- name: Install xml2 with O(1) xml_add_child() (r-lib/xml2#479)
  run: pak::pak("r-lib/xml2#479")
  shell: Rscript {0}
```

`pak` is already provisioned by `setup-r-dependencies` in this job, so no extra setup is required.

### Verified

With xml2 installed from the PR, the **unmodified, released** `to_cobertura()` processes the full RSQLite coverage data in **~25 seconds** (down from ~5 hours).

> [!NOTE]
> This pins coverage to a PR build of xml2. Once r-lib/xml2#479 is merged and released, this step can be dropped (or switched to `r-lib/xml2` / the released version).

title: Fix: add parameter names to http.c for C17 compatibility (#745)
description:
Hot fix for #745, builds on RHEL 8 and other distros whose system compiler defaults to C17.

## Problem

`src/vendor/extensions/http.c` defines VFS methods with unnamed parameters, e.g. `httpWrite(sqlite3_file*, const void*, int, sqlite3_int64)`. This is valid C23 but rejected by C17 with `error: parameter name omitted`. GCC 8–13 default to `gnu17`, breaking every build on RHEL 8-family distros.

## Fix

Add parameter names to all 21 affected function definitions, following the existing naming conventions in the file (`pFile`, `pVfs`, `zBuf`, `iAmt`, `iOfst`, `flags`, `eLock`, etc.). Unused parameters receive `(void)` casts to match the pattern already used elsewhere.

## CI

CI on `ubuntu-24.04` (GCC 14, default `gnu23`) did not catch this because the compiler silently accepts the C23 syntax. A CI guardrail (e.g. adding `-std=gnu17` to the smoke test) is discussed in the issue but left to the maintainer.

Closes #745

title: ci: pair C standards with older R releases; drop C90
description:
Builds on #751–#753 (all merged). Reorganizes the compile-only C lanes so each older standard runs against a correspondingly older R release, and drops C90.

## Changes

| Lane | `-std` | R release | extra flags |
|---|---|---|---|
| C99 | `gnu99` | **oldrel-4** | — |
| C11 | `gnu11` | **oldrel-3** | `-Werror=c11-c2x-compat` |
| C17 | `gnu17` | **oldrel-2** | `-Werror=c11-c2x-compat` |
| ~~C90~~ | — | — | **dropped** |
| C++23 | `gnu++23` | newest release | — |

- **Drops the C90 lane.**
- Pairs each C standard with an older R release (`oldrel-N`), so the matrix exercises an old standard *together with* an old R C API — the combination that actually occurs on long-lived systems — rather than running every standard on the newest R.
- A per-entry **`r`** column carries the release; C++ continues to build on the newest release.
- C11/C17 keep `-Werror=c11-c2x-compat` (no C23 features).

`matrix.r` flows straight to `r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2`, which accepts the `oldrel-N` selectors.

## Note

The C11 and C17 lanes remain **red until `vendor/extensions/http.c` is fixed** (C23 unnamed parameters) in its separate PR — unchanged from before. C90's removal retires that lane (and its separate for-loop concern) from CI.

title: ci: also reject C23 constructs on the C17 lane
description:
Follow-up to #752 (now merged). Adds `-Werror=c11-c2x-compat` to the **C17** compile-only lane as well, so it rejects C23-only constructs just like the C11 / RHEL 8 lane. One-line change to the `flags` column, rebased onto current main.

## The case (it *is* redundant today — here's why it's still worth it)

C17 added no language features over C11, so the C17 lane catches exactly the same C23 constructs as the RHEL 8 / C11 lane right now. The justification is **intent and lifecycle**, not catching different bugs:

| Lane | Motivation | Lifecycle |
|---|---|---|
| `C11 (RHEL 8 gcc 8)` | **Platform** — gnu11 is gcc 8's default, reproduces what RHEL 8 actually does | Tracks one distro's compiler; may be rebased/retired as platforms move (RHEL 8 EOL, RHEL 9 = gcc 11/C17, …) |
| `C17` | **Standard** — a platform-agnostic contract: "RSQLite's C compiles as C17 with no reliance on C23 features" | Durable; C17 is R's default on 4.4 and the floor of most current toolchains |

Keeping the C23 guard on the standard-defined C17 lane means the protection **survives if the RHEL 8 entry is later changed or removed** — the two lanes answer different questions and have independent lifecycles even though they agree today.

**Cost (honest):** a second CI job that currently always agrees with the RHEL 8 lane, and — like that lane — it's **red until `vendor/extensions/http.c` is fixed** in its separate PR.

title: ci: add RHEL 8 (old gcc) lane that rejects C23 code
description:
Follow-up to #751 (now merged). Adds a compile-only matrix lane that replicates **RHEL 8's system gcc 8** — which defaults to C11 and cannot compile C23 — on a modern compiler, **without installing an old toolchain**.

## The problem

RSQLite's bundled HTTP VFS extension (`vendor/extensions/http.c`) defines functions with **unnamed parameters** (`static int httpWrite(sqlite3_file*, const void*, int, sqlite3_int64){…}`), which is **C23-only** syntax. RHEL 8's gcc 8 rejects it, but the existing `gnu17` matrix lane stays green because **modern gcc accepts C23 constructs as silent extensions even under an old `-std`**.

## The fix

A new `compile-only C11 (RHEL 8 gcc 8)` entry that pins `-std=gnu11` (gcc 8's C default) and promotes the C11→C23 compatibility warnings to errors:

```
-std=gnu11 -Werror=c11-c2x-compat
```

`-Wc11-c2x-compat` is surgical — it flags **only** constructs valid in C23 but not C11, so a modern gcc rejects exactly what RHEL 8 does. It avoids the false positives of `-pedantic-errors` (which would also reject GNU extensions RHEL 8 accepts, plus vendored-code nits). Verified locally: the lane fails with **all errors confined to `http.c`** — the SQLite amalgamation is untouched.

(gcc 14+ spells the flag `-Wc11-c23-compat`; the `c2x` alias still works.)

## Mechanism

- The `c_stds` / `cxx_stds` tables in `versions-matrix/action.R` gain a **`flags`** column for per-entry extra compiler flags.
- The `install` action gains a matching **`flags`** input, appended after `-std` in the generated Makevars (reusing the existing centralized override logic — no duplication).
- `rcc-full` passes `matrix.flags` through.

## ⚠️ Expected red until a follow-up

Like the C90 lane, this entry is **red until `vendor/extensions/http.c` is fixed** (name the parameters) in its dedicated PR. That's the agreed accept-red-until-fixed arrangement.

title: ci: compile-only matrix for non-default C/C++ standards
description:
## Summary

Expands the dynamic version matrix (`.github/workflows/versions-matrix/action.R`) with **compile-only** entries that build the package's native code under a pinned, non-default language standard — *without* running `R CMD check`. The goal is to catch portability problems before R flips its default standard. Entries are added **only when the package ships the relevant sources**:

| Native code present | Compile-only entries added |
|---|---|
| C (`.c`) | `compile-only C90`, `compile-only C99`, `compile-only C17` |
| C++ (`.cc/.cpp/.cxx`) | `compile-only C++23` |

For RSQLite this yields four extra Ubuntu jobs on the newest released R.

## How it works

- A new `std` matrix column marks an entry as compile-only and carries the `-std` value (`gnu90`, `gnu99`, `gnu17`, `gnu++23`); a `lang` column selects `CC` vs `CXX`.
- A new **`compile` composite action** reuses the ccache Makevars from the install step and appends a `-std` override on the relevant default compiler (a later make assignment wins), keeping ccache. It then runs `R CMD INSTALL .` — compile only, no check.
- The override is scoped to the compile step, so **dependency installs stay at the default standard**.
- In `rcc-full`, the `check`/`covr`/snapshot/notes steps are gated off for `matrix.std` entries, and the new compile step is gated on.

## ⚠️ Expected: the C90 entry is red until a follow-up lands

RSQLite is C90-clean *except* for the bundled SQLite HTTP VFS extension (`vendor/extensions/http.c`), which uses C99 for-loop initial declarations. The fix (hoisting six loop variables) is **intentionally not part of this PR** — it will be picked up in a dedicated PR. It is preserved in this branch's history (commit `b863017`) and immediately reverted (commit `908c861`), so this PR's net diff leaves `http.c` untouched.

Until that follow-up merges, the **`compile-only C90`** job will fail (only on the HTTP VFS extension). This is the agreed-upon trade-off. C99, C17 and C++23 all build cleanly today.

## Verified in-session

Built RSQLite locally under each pinned standard (plain `-std`, no `-Wpedantic -Werror`):

| Standard | Result |
|---|---|
| C90 | ❌ fails on `http.c` (fixed by the follow-up PR) |
| C99 | ✅ builds |
| C17 | ✅ builds |
| C++23 | ✅ builds |

(`-Wpedantic -Werror` was evaluated and rejected: it fails on vendored third-party code — SQLite amalgamation, the HTTP VFS extension, boost — producing non-actionable red.)

## Also included

A companion fix to the ccache Makevars generation (`install/action.yml`): skip undefined compiler switches by **exit status** rather than non-empty output. On R 4.2, `R CMD config CXX23` prints its "unknown variable" error to stdout with a non-zero exit, which previously wrote a bogus `CXX23 = ccache ERROR: …` line (harmless only because RSQLite never uses `CXX23`).

## Validation

- `action.R` parses; entry generation produces the expected JSON entries (C90/C99/C17 + C++23).
- Both workflow YAML files validate.
- Ran the `compile` action's exact shell logic against RSQLite: C99/C17/C++23 install cleanly with ccache preserved and the correct `-std` in the compile line.
