title: ci: infer compiler defaults for ccache across R version matrix
description:
## Summary

The ccache setup in `.github/workflows/install/action.yml` wrapped the compilers using the recursive make trick `CC := ccache $(CC)`. This PR switches to **inferring each compiler's resolved default from `R CMD config` and prepending `ccache`**, which is more robust across the R version check matrix (`devel` + latest releases).

## Why

`R CMD config CC`/`CXX` report the fully resolved default for whichever R version is active, *including the language-standard flag R selects for that version*:

| R version | C default | C++ default |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| 4.4.x     | C17       | C++17       |
| 4.5.x     | C23 (`-std=gnu2x`) | C++17 (`-std=gnu++17`) |
| 4.6.0+    | C23       | C++20 (`-std=gnu++20`) |

By reading these resolved values and prepending `ccache`, every matrix entry keeps building with its own default standard. A plain override like `CC = ccache gcc` would drop the `-std=` flag and silently fall back to the bare compiler default (e.g. gcc 13's `gnu17`), downgrading the C standard.

## Details

- Defaults are inferred with an **empty user Makevars** (`R_MAKEVARS_USER`), so inference always reads the pristine `Makeconf` defaults and never a value written earlier in the loop.
- **Empty results are skipped**, so the loop stays correct on R versions that drop `CXX11`/`CXX14`.
- `CXX20`/`CXX23` are now covered by ccache too (previously only `CXX11`/`CXX14`/`CXX17`).

### Generated `~/.R/Makevars` (verified locally on R 4.5.3)

```make
CC = ccache gcc -std=gnu2x
CXX = ccache g++ -std=gnu++17
CXX11 = ccache g++
CXX14 = ccache g++
CXX17 = ccache g++
CXX20 = ccache g++
CXX23 = ccache g++
MAKEFLAGS = -j2
```

RSQLite does not pin a C++ standard, so it relies on R's per-version default — exactly what this preserves.

title: feat: optional HTTP/HTTPS VFS for read-only remote databases
description:
This PR adds an **experimental HTTP/HTTPS virtual file system (VFS)** that enables **read-only access to remote, immutable SQLite databases** via URI filenames (e.g. `https://host/db.sqlite?vfs=http&immutable=1`). The feature is optional and only compiled when libcurl is detected at build time.

User-facing API
- `sqlite_remote(url, immutable = TRUE, ...)`: convenience helper to open remote DBs read-only and ensure VFS registration.
- `sqliteHasHttpVFS()`: runtime capability probe (includes a lazy registration attempt).
- `sqlite_http_config(cache_size_mb, prefetch_pages, fallback_full_download)`: configure conservative process-wide behavior via env vars.
- `sqliteHttpStats()`: best-effort per-process counters (bytes fetched, range request count, full download flag).
- `sqliteHttpVfsCompiled()`: compile-time indicator of whether HTTP VFS was built in.

Implementation details
- Bundled C implementation at `http.c` with entrypoint `sqlite3_http_init` (VFS name: `"http"`).
- Read-only VFS; uses **HTTP Range requests** for on-demand page reads and an in-memory cache.
- Optional full-download fallback when Range is unsupported (configurable).
- Eager registration in `.onLoad()` is gated to only run when compiled with HTTPVFS enabled.

Build / portability
- Adds minimal `configure` / `configure.win` to detect libcurl (pkg-config / curl-config) and update `Makevars` variables idempotently (avoids repeated appends).
- Updates `deps.mk` to avoid capturing machine-specific Windows absolute include paths in .dd dependency files.

Tests
- Adds httpuv-backed tests validating:
  - basic remote read works
  - Range requests are used when available
  - open fails when Range unsupported and fallback disabled
  - compile-time indicator aligns with internal helper
  
Notes / caveats
- Experimental feature intended for **small, immutable** databases.
- Read-only; no writes/locking/truncate/etc.
- For CRAN: tests are guarded with `skip_on_cran()` and require `httpuv`.

title: chore: Remove vendored object files from the source tarball via cleanup scripts
description:
## Problem
R CMD check on current R-devel reports:

```
checking if this is a source package ... NOTE
  Found the following apparent object files/libraries:
    src/vendor/sqlite3/sqlite3.o
  Object files/libraries should not be included in a source package.
```

This is the same class of regression as the `deps.mk` issue fixed in #734.

## Root cause
`src/vendor/sqlite3/sqlite3.o` (referenced via `PKG_LIBS`) is excluded by `.Rbuildignore`. Since the R CMD build cleanup rework (PR#17549), that exclusion is applied **before** the sources are copied into the temporary build directory. Building the vignettes then triggers a temporary **installation** in that directory, which recompiles the vendored object. R CMD build's final cleanup only removes top-level `src/*.o` (the shared `clean.mk` target is empty), **not** files in the vendored subdirectory — so the object ends up in the tarball.

## Fix
Add top-level `cleanup` scripts that remove the vendored build artifacts:

- `cleanup` — Unix (Linux/macOS)
- `cleanup.win`, `cleanup.ucrt` — Windows (legacy / UCRT toolchains)

```sh
rm -f src/vendor/sqlite3/*.o src/vendor/sqlite3/*.a
```

R CMD build runs the appropriate script **unconditionally** during its final cleanup — i.e. *after* the vignette-triggered installation — so the object no longer leaks. The scripts are also run by R CMD INSTALL **only** with `--clean`/`--preclean` (i.e. after linking), so a plain `R CMD INSTALL .` is unaffected. All three are committed executable (mode `100755`), which R CMD check requires for `cleanup`.

## Verification
On a stock R-devel build exhibiting the regression (no R-side fix), using a minimal package with the identical vendored-object layout (object in `PKG_LIBS`, excluded via `.Rbuildignore`, vignette present):

- **without** the script: `vendor/<obj>.o` leaks into the tarball (reproduces the NOTE)
- **with** the script: the object is absent

For RSQLite directly: `./cleanup` removes `src/vendor/sqlite3/*.o` and `*.a` (leaving `sqlite3.c`), and `R CMD build` completes with no cleanup errors.

## Note
The underlying R CMD build behaviour (regenerated `.Rbuildignore`d files leaking into the tarball) is arguably a bug in R itself; a complementary fix that re-applies `.Rbuildignore` before tarring has been prepared against R-devel. These `cleanup` scripts make RSQLite robust on stock R-devel regardless, and are a standard, portable mechanism.

title: chore: Rename `deps.mk` to `Makevars.deps` for `R CMD check` compatibility
description:
## Summary
Rename the development-time dependency makefile fragment from `src/deps.mk` to `src/Makevars.deps` so that R CMD check no longer reports it as an "unlikely file name".

## Background
The fragment is pulled in by `include` in `src/Makevars` and exists only during development. For the tarball it is `.Rbuildignore`d, and the accompanying rule recreates an empty file when missing. Since the R CMD build cleanup rework on current R-devel (PR#17549 / r90095), that empty fragment can be **regenerated during cleanup and packed into the tarball**. R CMD check then flags it, because the source-file permit-list only accepts names matching `^Makevars` (plus a fixed set of source extensions); a `*.mk` name like `deps.mk` is not accepted.

Naming the fragment `Makevars.deps` does **not** stop it from being regenerated/packed — it ensures that *if* it is packed, the name is one the check accepts, so no WARNING is produced. (An empty `Makevars.deps` in the tarball is harmless: end-user builds simply `include` it.)

## Changes
- `git mv src/deps.mk → src/Makevars.deps` (history preserved)
- `src/Makevars`: reference `Makevars.deps` in both the rule target and the `include`, with an explanatory comment. Keep a plain, portable `include` — `-include` is a GNU make extension CRAN flags as non-portable.
- `.Rbuildignore`: `^src/deps\.mk$` → `^src/Makevars\.deps$`
- Update the stale `deps.mk` self-reference in the generated-file header comment

## Verification
Built and checked against a stock R-devel exhibiting the regression:

| fragment name | check result |
|---|---|
| `deps.mk` (before) | WARNING ("unlikely file name") |
| `Makefile.deps` | WARNING (still not an accepted name) |
| `Makevars.deps` (this PR) | clean |

`R CMD INSTALL` + `R CMD build` succeed; the produced tarball contains no `deps.mk` and no WARNING.

## Note
A complementary upstream fix (re-applying `.Rbuildignore` before tarring, so regenerated ignored files are dropped) addresses the root cause in R CMD build itself. This PR is independently sufficient because RSQLite's CI and CRAN run stock R-devel, which won't carry that fix until it is merged upstream.

title: feat: Enable the percentile extension
description:
This pull request enables the percentile extension (https://sqlite.org/percentile.html). A basic test is included to assert that the new functions are available.

The percentile extension provides four aggregate functions that compute a percentile score and/or the median value for a distribution. The extension is disabled by default and must be activated at compile-time using the -DSQLITE_ENABLE_PERCENTILE compile-time option.

title: feat: Add sqlite-lines extension
description:
This is a proposal to add the `lines_read()` function as per source code by @asg017 at https://github.com/asg017/sqlite-lines/ with MIT licence. The documentation is updated, and simple tests are included. Local `devtools::test()` completed without errors. 

As per @asg017's README, "sqlite-lines is great for line-oriented datasets, like [ndjson](https://ndjson.org/) or [JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org/), when paired with SQLite's [JSON support](https://www.sqlite.org/json1.html)." Thus, I see interesting and important use cases for this extension, providing large performance improvements over loading data using e.g. `DBI::dbAppendTable()`. Also, other DMSs have similar `SQL` functions for reading data from file, including `duckdb`. 

I acknowledge this PR pulls in source files from _outside_ the SQLite repository, thus enlarging the risk surface of `RSQLite`; please let me know about any policy and source control requirements (I am not a C/C++ developer and cannot offer source code quality review). 

Many thanks for considering!

PS. I could not get the derived `fileio_scan()` function working as available at https://github.com/nalgeon/sqlean/blob/main/docs/fileio.md

title: feat: Add uuid extension
description:
This is a proposal to add `uuid()` functions as per source code here: https://www.sqlite.org/src/file?name=ext/misc/uuid.c&ci=tip. The documentation is updated, and simple tests are included. Local `devtools::test()` completed without errors. 

I trust that users will welcome to be able to generate `UUIDs` within the database, as this is performant and can be part of `SQL` logic (such as in my use case). There do not seem to be risks or unintended consequences (e.g., footprint, performance, security aspects). 

Possibly the same could be said about other extensions in the source repository; not sure if you plan for others to be included or a generic mechanism for compiling even with sources from outside the `SQLite` repository? 

Many thanks for considering!

title: Inline BH
description:
Documentation follows. Key code chunks:

```sh
sudo apt install libboost1.71-tools-dev
# https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_75_0/tools/bcp/doc/html/index.html
mkdir -p src/vendor; bcp --boost=../../bh/inst/include --list-short src/*.cpp src/*.h
# Compiler flags: -Ivendor -MD, remove -MD later: https://stackoverflow.com/a/5835035/946850 (check out -H flag)
cd src; sed -r -i '/^[^ ]/ D; s/ \\$//g;s/(.) ([^\\])/\1\n \2/g' *.d
cat *.d | sort | uniq | grep -v '^ /' | xargs git add
# Keep unused files in separate branch, in case other compilers need it
ag -g gcc src/vendor
# Add files for other compilers
git checkout f-bh-unused -- $(ag -g gcc | xargs dirname | xargs dirname) src/vendor/boost/{predef,winapi,container_hash,integer/static_log2.hpp,detail/container_fwd.hpp,type_traits}
```

title: SQLite: build with SQLITE_USE_URI=1
description:
We have seen some problems attaching to in-memory databases from RSQLite that have been created from within C code, resulting in files being created on the filesystem such as `tests/testthat/file:name?mode=memory&vfs=some-stub`, due to RSQLite not understanding that these are URIs.

We have managed to resolve these problems with the attached patch, which essentially enables URI support at compile-time.

It may be relevant to reviewers to note that the SQLite developers [state](https://sqlite.org/uri.html) that it is safe for most applications to enable URI processing:

> Since SQLite always interprets any filename that does not begin with "file:" as an ordinary filename regardless of the URI setting, and because it is very unusual to have an actual file begin with "file:", it is safe for most applications to enable URI processing even if URI filenames are not currently being used.

CC: @jrandall

title: Implementation of RStudio Connection contract
description:
I have implemented the RStudio Connection contract (<https://rstudio.github.io/rstudio-extensions/connections-contract.html>) for RSQLite. Which makes it possible to see the contents of the SQLite database you are connecting to.

This does not introduce extra dependencies for RSQLite, but will call the functions:

- `on_connection_opened` (in `dbConnect`)
- `on_connection_closed` (in `dbDisconnect`)
- `on_connection_updated` (in `dbWriteTable` and `dbRemoveTable`)

These functions return invisible NULL in a normal R session, but will do something whenever "connectionObserver" option is set. (which is typically the case within RStudio). 

I can imagine that this PR with this specific RStudio functionality is worth a discussion, but I think it will make working with SQLite in R for a many Data Scientists a little bit more pleasant.

Best,

Edwin

title: Set `-DHAVE_USLEEP` to solve poor concurrency on Unix
description:
Without this, sqlite3 can only wait whole seconds when waiting on a locked DB, which greatly increases the chance that processes time out. @Enchufa2 found a blog post that describes the issue in detail: https://beets.io/blog/sqlite-nightmare.html

`usleep()` is not used on Windows, and it is present on every Unix system. It is actually considered to be obsolete, in favor of `nanosleep()`, but systems still have it for compatibility.

Also added the `dbSetBusyHandler()` function to expose the `sqlite3_busy_timeout()` and `sqlite3_busy_handler()` APIs.

The new test case will fail for the first commit of the PR (on Unix), this will be fixed in subsequent commits.

The main purpose of adding `dbSetBusyHandler()` is to debug concurrency issues, and to show that adding the `-DHAVE_USLEEP` compile time flag (coming in the next commit) indeed improves the concurrency of RSQLite a lot.

See #280, #56, https://github.com/r-lib/liteq/issues/28, etc.

Closes #280.

title: Autoincrement 2
description:
(Hi @krlmlr, this PR replaces #58)

Can someone confirm that this is the intended behavior?  I'd hate to be writing tests that approve an unintended effect.

When the autoincrement column isn't in the data.frame sent to the database, it's populated by SQLite.

But when it is populated before getting to the database, SQLite won't assign/update values.  And when retrieved from SQLite, the data.frame will be re-ordered (corresponding to the values in the (ignored) autoincrement column).

``` r
> ds_local
    id name score
1  126    a     1
2  125    b     2
3  124    c     3
...
24 103    x    24
25 102    y    25
26 101    z    26

> dbWriteTable(con, name = 'tbl', value = ds_local, append = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
> ds_remote <- dbReadTable(con, "tbl")

> ds_remote
    id name score
1  101    z    26
2  102    y    25
3  103    x    24
...
24 124    c     3
25 125    b     2
26 126    a     1
```

title: should mark UTF-8 on the non-ASCII colnames
description:
Without the UTF8 marking, `DBI::dbListFields()` returns garbage strings on Windows. 

Furthermore, `DBI::dbWriteTable(..., append = TRUE)` will fail, if the table fields contain non-ASCII strings, since it depends on `DBI::dbListFields()`.

https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/blob/33d3631f2809df4eb2ab01460ef3ce73788e1488/R/table.R#L115-L116

This PR will fix the issue.

### Example

``` r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite())
tbl <- data.frame("中文" = 'a')
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, name = 'test', value = tbl)
got <- DBI::dbListFields(con, 'test')
got
#> [1] "涓枃"
Encoding(got)
#> [1] "unknown"
Encoding(got) <- 'UTF-8'
got
#> [1] "中文"

title: allow dbWriteTable method for text file to work within open transaction
description:
`dbWriteTable` previously failed when run within a transaction passing a text file rather than a dataframe. (signature `conn="SQLiteConnection", name="character", value="character"`)

MRE:

```
library(RSQLite) # current dev version or below
tmp <- tempfile()
db <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname=tmp)

tmp_csv <- tempfile()
write.csv(mtcars, tmp_csv)

# fails 
dbWithTransaction(db, {
    dbWriteTable(db, 'tbl_mtcars', tmp_csv, overwrite=TRUE)
})
dbDisconnect(db)
```
returns error message
```
Error in result_create(conn@ptr, statement) : 
  cannot start a transaction within a transaction
```

This PR uses the  approach in `dbWriteTable` signature for 
`conn="SQLiteConnection", name="character", value="data.frame"` to avoid this error.

title: Only export relevant symbols to shared library.
description:
Hi, 

I have problems using RPostgres and RSQLite from the same R-process.

I get stacktraces such as these:

```
 *** caught segfault ***
address 0x1000000010, cause 'memory not mapped'

Traceback:
 1: result_release(res@ptr)
 2: dbClearResult(rs)
 3: dbClearResult(rs)
 4: dbExecute(con, "SET TIMEZONE='UTC'")
 5: dbExecute(con, "SET TIMEZONE='UTC'")
 6: .local(drv, ...)
 7: DBI::dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), dbname = "kingfisher")
 8: DBI::dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), dbname = "kingfisher")
 9: eval(expr)
10: eval(expr)
11: create_connection(production = production)
12: load_list_of_tables("ensembl", tables, production = production)
An irrecoverable exception occurred. R is aborting now ...
bin/load_ensembl.sh: line 7: 36907 Segmentation fault      (core dumped) Rscript R/load_ensembl.R
```

After wading through the code with gdb it appears that RSQLite's result_release collides with RPostgres' result_release in their respective shared libraries. The best way to fix that is probably to only export symbols from the shared library which will be needed by R.

So I suggest changing default symbol visibility to hidden, so the two libraries can coexist peacefully.

See here for more information:
https://github.com/RcppCore/Rcpp/pull/720

title: test: Declare DBItest 1.8.3.6 in the DBItest contexts
description:

title: test: Run the HTTP VFS tests for real, and make their errors fail the check
description:
The three tests in `tests/testthat/test-httpvfs.R` that start a local httpuv server have failed on every CI run, `main` included, while `R CMD check` reported `Status: OK`. The testthat summary in the logs reads `[ FAIL 3 | ... ]`, but each test's cleanup then disconnected a fixture connection that was already closed, and testthat only counts a test as errored when the error is its last result (`summarize_one_test_results()`), so the "Already disconnected" warning recorded after the error hid it from `test_check()`; #837 tracks that trap. This came up on #829, where the maintainer asked for a fix from `main` that makes such errors fail loudly. This pull request makes those errors fail the check and makes the tests run for real against the HTTP VFS on `main`. The fixes for what they found are stacked on top of it, as listed below.

**Masking.** The fixture database is built and closed in its own scope (`http_test_db()`), and the remote connection's cleanup is registered with `withr::defer()` only once the connection has opened. An error therefore stays the last result of the test. With only this change, `test_local(stop_on_failure = TRUE)` on the old tests stops with "Test failures."

**The tests themselves.** The URL now carries the `file:` prefix (via `http_vfs_uri()` or `sqliteRemote()`); without it SQLite ignores `vfs=http` and opens a local file of that name. The server runs in a separate R process started with `callr::r_bg()` (`local_http_server()` in the new `helper-httpvfs.R`): the VFS performs blocking libcurl requests on the main R thread, so an httpuv app in the same process can never answer. The child gets the test's temporary directory as its `TMPDIR`, so the session directory it leaves behind when killed is removed with it, and it logs each request it receives. The test server answers HEAD without a body; httpuv otherwise sends the body for HEAD too, which corrupts the next response on the kept-alive connection and made some runs fail with libcurl's "HTTP/0.9 not allowed" error. The Range test compares the `range_requests` and `bytes_fetched` counters of `sqliteHttpStats()` with their values before the query, because they are process-wide, checks that the server sent less than the whole file, and pads the database so that the query reads only a fraction of it. The test for a server without Range support expects the "disk I/O error" that the open actually reports. The first test passes `default.extensions = FALSE`, since the default extensions cannot load over the HTTP VFS on `main`; #840 removes that. The tests skip with "HTTP VFS not compiled in (configure did not find libcurl)" when the VFS is not built, unless `RSQLITE_TEST_HTTPVFS=true` is set, in which case they fail; they also fail if the VFS is built but cannot be registered.

**Until #842.** These tests now make real transfers, and the HTTP VFS sets no libcurl timeout until #842, so a server that accepts a connection and never answers would hang the check; the test server answered in every run so far. Merge #832 through #842 together, or at least without a release in between.

**CI coverage.** No workflow installs libcurl headers for RSQLite on purpose, and `DESCRIPTION` declares no `SystemRequirements` for it. They arrive anyway: `libcurl4-openssl-dev` is the system requirement of the `curl` package, which the suggested packages gh, gert and rvest pull in, and macOS and Windows find libcurl on their own. The custom after-install step now sets `RSQLITE_TEST_HTTPVFS=true`, so losing libcurl on a runner fails the tests instead of skipping them. On this pull request, CI runs only the Linux smoke test, since the versions matrix is built for pull requests only from forks or `cran-*` branches; the full matrix (macOS, Windows, arm64, R 4.2 to devel) ran green on all 15 jobs, with the HTTP tests on each, at fa0b2349, the last head of the earlier combined version of this pull request ([run](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/actions/runs/42873141082)).

**The stack.** As the maintainer asked, the earlier combined version is split into scoped pull requests, each based on the one before:

1. this one: the tests run for real;
2. #839: stop printing the response headers of every remote open;
3. #840: load the default extensions on HTTP VFS connections;
4. #841: `sqliteRemote()` loads the default extensions;
5. #842: time out stalled transfers;
6. #843: let an interrupt abort a transfer.

The top of the stack has the same tree as fa0b2349 merged with `main`, apart from a corrected sentence in `?sqliteHttpConfig`. The problems found along the way that none of these fix are #834, #835, #836 and #837.

**Reviews.** Three clean reviews of the combined version ([first](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/832#issuecomment-6773042612), [second](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/832#issuecomment-6774170797), [third](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/832#issuecomment-6775136216)) found no High issue, and their Medium and Low findings are fixed in the layers they concern. title: fix: Never restart a statement after an error in `dbFetch()` or `dbBind()`
description:
Found while reviewing #795, where the maintainer asked for a separate pull request from `main`: two pre-existing bugs in how a result behaves after an SQLite error. Both come from the same SQLite behavior: since 3.7.0, `sqlite3_step()` on a statement that failed resets it and runs it again from the start instead of returning `SQLITE_MISUSE`, and RSQLite stepped such a statement again on the next fetch. It is stacked on #850, which, as the maintainer asked here, keeps the rows of a fetch when the step past its last row fails and raises that error from the next fetch.

**Error in the middle of a result.** When `sqlite3_step()` failed after some rows had been returned, `dbFetch()` raised the error, but `dbHasCompleted()` stayed `FALSE` and the next `dbFetch()` restarted the query from the first row. It returned a row of `NA` followed by the first rows again, or raised the same error again, with `dbGetRowCount()` growing each time. This affected plain queries, any parameter set of a `dbBind()` with several sets, and a later parameter set that fails to bind. Now an error ends the execution: `dbHasCompleted()` returns `TRUE`, a further `dbFetch()` returns zero rows with the result's columns, and a new `dbBind()` makes the result usable again. `dbGetRowCount()` no longer counts the rows read by a fetch that fails, also not when the conversion to a data frame fails, because they are not returned. The same holds for any other error that leaves a fetch: one raised while converting values, for example an unparsable `DATE` with `extended_types = TRUE` or the mixed-type warning under `options(warn = 2)`, a handler that leaves the fetch on a warning, or an interrupt. Before, such an error either repeated on every further fetch, so a `while (!dbHasCompleted(res))` loop that caught it never ended, or skipped the rows of that fetch while the result went on. `dbFetch(n = 0)` and `dbColumnInfo()` read no row, so an error while converting the row they look at leaves the result as it is. Completing the result also ends the statement, so a result that ends with an error releases its read lock, as it does when it reaches its end. An interrupt during a fetch completes the result too: `dbHasCompleted()` returns `TRUE`, `dbGetRowCount()` does not count the rows of the interrupted fetch, and the next fetch returns zero rows, where `main` went on after the rows that were lost. An allocation failure in R's own functions still leaves a fetch without completing the result. The warning for a fetch from a statement that is not a query now passes its message as an argument rather than as a format, so its condition call is `NULL`. A handler of a warning raised during a fetch, bind or `dbColumnInfo()` can no longer clear or use that result: `dbClearResult()` and further fetches fail with #795's messages instead of reaching freed memory, which on `main` could crash R.

**Failed `dbBind()`.** When the first parameter set of a list `dbBind()` failed, either in binding or in the statement, its parameters stayed in place. The next `dbFetch()` ran them once more, raising the error again, or returned rows from a statement whose bindings were partly cleared. Now a failed `dbBind()` leaves the result unbound, as it was before the first bind: `dbFetch()` raises "Query needs to be bound before fetching", which is what a failed Arrow bind in #795 already does. `dbHasCompleted()` returns `FALSE` and `dbGetRowCount()` returns 0; `dbGetRowsAffected()` reports the changes since the failed bind, for example 2 when the third of four inserts fails, and 0 for a failed query (it stays `NA` only before the first bind).

**Why these semantics.** DBI's specification does not cover errors during a fetch. Completing the result follows from `dbHasCompleted()` returning `TRUE` "if no more rows are available for fetching" and from fetches past the end returning zero rows; #795 does the same when a later Arrow parameter set fails to bind. The rejected alternative was to keep the error and raise it again on every further `dbFetch()`: that needs extra state, because SQLite's error message is overwritten by later calls, and it turns `while (!dbHasCompleted(res))` loops that handled the error into repeated errors. A failed `dbBind()` is treated differently because the failing call is the bind itself: asking for a new bind is louder than silently returning zero rows that look like an empty result. With #850 underneath, one error is kept after all: the one from the step past the last row a fetch returns, which the next fetch raises once, so that no row is lost; after that, the result completes as described above.

**Merging into #795.** A trial merge of this stack into #795 (43db19f5) conflicts in two hunks of `src/SqliteResultImpl.h` and nine of `src/SqliteResultImpl.cpp`, and passes `test-arrow.R`, `test-dbSendQuery.R` and `test-read-ahead.R` with this resolution: in the header, keep #795's `nrows_` and `executions_` and add `bind_started_` before them, and keep both `raise_sqlite_exception(int rc)` and `raise_kept_error()`; in the `.cpp` file, keep #795's includes and Arrow constants and add `<stdexcept>` with the `step_error` class, keep both sides of the constructor (this stack's kept-error fields before #795's Arrow fields), keep #795's `bind()` and `bind_row()`, take this stack's `"%s"` warning and the `try`/`catch` loop of `fetch_rows()` (written as `nrows_ = nrows_ + n_fetched` for #795's counter), keep #795's `arrow_row_read_ = false;` in `step()` before this stack's `try`/`catch` and add it at the start of `read_ahead()`, keep #795's `raise_sqlite_exception(rc)` in `step_run()`, and keep #795's Arrow functions while adding `raise_kept_error()`. Beyond the conflicts: `raise_sqlite_exception(int rc)` throws `step_error` for both of its messages, so no R function is called on the step path; `raise_kept_error()` also completes the result; `after_set_params()` sets `bind_started_`, drops a kept error, and wraps `bind_row()` and `after_bind()` in a `try` whose `catch` resets `params_`, `ready_`, `complete_` and `nrows_` before rethrowing; `bind_row()` turns a `std::runtime_error` from the parameter source into a `step_error`, and `SqliteListParamSource::bind_parameter()` throws instead of calling `cpp11::stop()`, so that `read_ahead()` keeps a later set that fails to bind; `step_done()` no longer completes the result in its `catch`; `fetch_arrow_rows()` starts by raising a kept error, counts its rows only once the chunk is built, and should get the same `catch` as `fetch_rows()`, so that an interrupt or a conversion error completes an Arrow result too; and `ensure_arrow_columns()` reads a row only when the result is neither complete nor keeping an error. Two Arrow tests go with it: an error in the middle of an Arrow result completes it, and an error kept by a data-frame fetch comes from the next Arrow chunk. On the merged build, an interposer counted no R call off R's main thread while five error paths ran on a worker thread. The guard that keeps a running fetch from being cleared is a port of #795's, without its thread and Arrow parts, so in `src/DbResult.cpp`, `src/DbResult.h` and `src/result.cpp` the merge keeps #795's side, which gives files identical to #795's.

The tests are in `tests/testthat/test-dbSendQuery.R`, with their fixtures in helper files so that every block runs on its own after `load_all()`; the tests this pull request adds fail on `main`, among them one for the read lock after an error while converting values a `callr` test that interrupts a fetch and skips unless its session loads the RSQLite under test, and tests that a warning handler cannot clear the result of a running fetch. Four clean reviews, [first](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/830#issuecomment-6772663614), [second](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/830#issuecomment-6773298506), [third](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/830#issuecomment-6801679440) and [one of the stack with #850](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/830#issuecomment-6803299676), found no High issue; their Medium and Low findings are fixed up to aa070342, and what remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/830#issuecomment-6855249716).

Closes #838, which shows both bugs with a reprex against the current CRAN release.

title: fix: A fetch returns its rows when the step past its last row fails
description:
Asked on #830: "Accuracy is important. Do we still need to fetch one row ahead? If yes, perhaps implement a transparent one-row cache in a fresh PR against `main` and stack this PR on top?" This is that pull request; #830 is stacked on it.

**Why the fetch loop reads ahead.** Sending or binding a query steps once, which runs the statement; after that, `fetch_rows()` reads the current row and then steps, so the statement always stands on the next row to return, and the last step of a fetch of `n` rows goes one row past the rows it returns. DBI and DBItest do not require this: `has_completed_query_spec_partial` leaves `dbHasCompleted()` unspecified after fetching exactly all rows, and a version that steps lazily passes DBItest (658 tests) and RSQLite's own suite unchanged. The read-ahead still buys two things. `dbHasCompleted()` is `TRUE` right after the fetch that returns the last row, so the vignette's `while (!dbHasCompleted(rs)) dbFetch(rs, n = 10)` over 30 rows fetches 10, 10, 10 rather than 10, 10, 10, 0. More importantly, the step that reaches the end finishes the statement, which releases its read lock: without it, a reader that fetched exactly all its rows keeps the lock until the next fetch or `dbClearResult()`, and a write from another connection fails with "database is locked". So the read-ahead stays.

**What changes.** When the step past the last row of a fetch fails, that fetch now returns all its rows, and the error is kept and raised by the next fetch; until then, `dbHasCompleted()` is `FALSE`. On `main`, the fetch that held row k - 1 raised the error of row k and those rows were lost, or, with several parameter sets, the error of a later set that fails to bind or to run was raised by the fetch that held the last row of the set before. `dbFetch(n = 0)` and `dbColumnInfo()` leave a kept error alone, and a new `dbBind()` drops it. The same holds for a value in a later parameter set that SQLite refuses to bind, which completes the result since #868: when the read-ahead keeps that refusal, `dbHasCompleted()` stays `FALSE` until the next fetch raises it, and only then is the result complete (`kept_error_completes_`), with the row count of the rows returned. An error among the rows a fetch asks for is still raised by that fetch: `dbGetQuery()` sends, fetches with `n = -1` and clears, so holding that error back would silently return a result cut short. A failed step or an unbindable parameter now throws a C++ exception, `step_error`, that carries SQLite's message and result code, instead of calling `cpp11::stop()`, which signals the R error at once and so could not be held back; a kept error keeps both. The exception reaches R through cpp11's entry points, which turn it into the same R error as before, with the same message and condition call. An SQLite error message that contains `%`, such as the name of a `CHECK` constraint, is no longer read as a printf format, also when a statement fails to prepare; two warnings that quote the query still are, as on `main`. `dbGetQuery(n = 4)` over a result whose fifth row fails returns four rows, as `LIMIT 4` would, and the kept error goes with the cleared result. What happens after the kept error is raised is #830's business.

**Tests.** `tests/testthat/test-read-ahead.R`, with its fixture in `tests/testthat/helper-read-ahead.R` so that every block runs on its own after `load_all()`: an SQLite message with `%` in it, through a fetch and through a kept error; `dbGetQuery(n = )`; a kept message that survives later failing statements on the connection; fetches of 1, 2 and 4 rows with row 5 failing; several parameter sets, including a third set that fails to bind; a value SQLite refuses to bind after a fetch, kept for the next fetch; the column structure staying available while an error is kept; a new bind dropping it; the statement finishing, and releasing its lock, after the last row; and an error among the asked-for rows. Eight of the ten blocks error on `main` (53f26934); the other two pin behavior `main` already has. `devtools::test()` and `R CMD check --no-manual` pass apart from the HTTP VFS errors that #832 is about, and the read-ahead and query tests run clean under AddressSanitizer and UBSan.

**Merging into #795.** #795 already throws from `raise_sqlite_exception()` so that the fetch loop can run inside an Arrow stream callback, which this pull request now matches. The resolution of a trial merge of this stack into #795 is in #830's description.

[A clean review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/850#issuecomment-6801678942) found one Medium finding, the error path running the opposite way to #795's, and three Low ones; all are fixed in 8be7cd88 except the retry on `SQLITE_BUSY`, which #848 tracks. A [review of the fixes](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/830#issuecomment-6803299676), with #830 on top, found nothing above Low for this pull request. A clean review of the merge of `main` with #868 found one Medium issue that `main` already has, now in #838, and three Low ones: the comment on `step_error`'s result code is fixed in c029a2cd, this description now covers the merge, and `dbGetQuery(n = )` dropping a refused parameter set is up for a [question](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/850#issuecomment-6857862297). What remains is under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/850#issuecomment-6857867751).

title: feat: Check text read into a character column with `dbConnect(check_utf8 = TRUE)`
description:
As asked on #799: checks of the text read into a character column, behind a `dbConnect()` argument that defaults to the current behavior, on top of the UTF-8 infrastructure of #845. Unlike #799, which checked only blobs that turn up in a text column, this also checks text values, the more common case.

**The argument.** `dbConnect()` gains `check_utf8`, which defaults to `FALSE`, must be `TRUE` or `FALSE` (anything else stops with an error), and is kept with the connection. There is no R option: the maintainer [decided on #829](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6797414447) for an argument only.

**`check_utf8 = FALSE`, the default.** Every fetch runs the code of `main`: text with a NUL byte is cut silently, text that is not valid UTF-8 is returned marked as UTF-8, and a blob in a character column is read as text, so `X'00ff'` comes back as `""`. Three regression tests pin this, and they pass against `main` too.

**`check_utf8 = TRUE`.** A text or blob value read into a character column is read with its byte length (`sqlite3_column_text()` or `sqlite3_column_blob()`, then `sqlite3_column_bytes()`) and validated. A value that is not valid UTF-8, or holds a NUL byte, becomes `NA`, with one warning per column and fetch that counts the replaced values: "Column `x`: 2 values are not valid UTF-8 or contain NUL bytes, NA is returned". The fetch that returns a row raises the warning; a peek with `dbFetch(n = 0)` or `dbColumnInfo()` does not. A blob read with `sqlite3_column_blob()` is not transcoded in a UTF-16 database and keeps its storage class after a peek. Integer and real values in a character column, and blob columns, are read as before. The new warning passes its message as an argument, not as a printf format.

**Not changed here.** The mixed-type warning still passes the column name inside its format, its text is not marked as UTF-8, and `fetch_blob()` still hands a NULL pointer to `memcpy()` for an empty blob; all three belong to [the open question on format strings](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6771849788). `dbConnect()` on an existing connection does not carry `check_utf8` over here; #852, stacked on this pull request, makes a clone keep it, together with `extended_types` and `bigint`. The checks apply to every query on the connection, including RSQLite's own, so `dbListTables()` reports a table name that is not valid UTF-8 as `NA`. The new warning, like the mixed-type warning, is not marked as UTF-8.

**Tests.** `tests/testthat/test-check-utf8.R` covers invalid text, text with a NUL byte, invalid and valid blobs, empty text and blobs, a fetch in chunks where a later chunk holds the bad values, a peek between chunks, a UTF-16 database, and a column name containing `%s%d`; undoing each part of the change makes them fail. `R CMD check --no-manual` was rerun after dropping the option (only vignette and hidden-directory warnings of the local build tree), and the new and changed tests pass under AddressSanitizer and UBSan. Fetching 8 million strings takes as long as on `main` with the default, and 7% to 18% longer with `check_utf8 = TRUE`, depending on the data; many small fetches of wide results cost the same as on `main`.

A [clean review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/846#issuecomment-6799669749) found nothing above Low; four of its six findings are fixed, and what remains is under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/846#issuecomment-6857659565). The tests' fixtures live in helper files, so every block runs on its own after `load_all()`.

title: feat: Add a UTF-8 validator for strings read from SQLite
description:
As asked on #799, which is reimplemented from `main` as a stack: this pull request adds the UTF-8 infrastructure, and #846 builds the checks of text columns on it.

`rsqlite_is_utf8_string()`, declared in `src/utf8.h` and defined in `src/utf8.cpp`, tells whether a byte range is well-formed UTF-8 without a NUL byte, which is what an R string can hold. It follows RFC 3629, so it rejects overlong forms, surrogates and code points beyond U+10FFFF. ASCII text is checked eight bytes at a time; a word that holds a NUL or a byte above 127 is checked sequence by sequence, and the loop then returns to whole words. `text` may be NULL when `size` is 0.

Nothing calls the validator yet, so there is no user-visible change. #795 carries its own copy of the validator for the Arrow path (`src/utf8.h`, with the fast path in `src/SqliteArrowColumn.cpp`); when it switches to this one is [a question on #829](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6797414906). Defining the function in a `.cpp` file follows the recommended answer to [the question about the header](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6771483015).

The unexported `utf8_valid()` exposes the validator to the tests, whose fixtures live in `tests/testthat/helper-utf8.R`, so every block runs on its own after `load_all()`. `tests/testthat/test-utf8.R` compares it with a reference built from base R (`validUTF8()` after a check for NUL bytes) on every 1- and 2-byte string, grids of 3- and 4-byte strings, padding across the eight-byte words, a NUL at every position up to 20 bytes, and random strings. Breaking the validator in six ways, one at a time (the limits after E0, ED and F4, NUL detection in the fast path and for single bytes, accepting C0 and C1), makes the tests fail each time. `R CMD check --no-manual` reports Status OK.

A [clean review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/845#issuecomment-6798971332) found nothing above Low; its three findings about what the tests can detect are fixed in eda8143c, so the test hook now copies each input into a buffer with continuation bytes behind it and passes NULL for empty input, and what remains is under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/845#issuecomment-6855245225).

title: docs: Add an experiment record for incremental builds of vendored extensions
description:
The reproducer for #836, as an experiment record: an incremental build is not something a reprex can host. It follows the experiment convention of [cynkra/handbook-tools](https://github.com/cynkra/handbook-tools/blob/main/handbook/meta/experiments/README.md): `experiments/README.md` is the registry and names every record, and each record is a directory named for its date and topic, whose `README.md` says what it measures, when and on what, and what it supports, followed by the method, the findings and how to replicate them, with the driver and its output beside it. RSQLite has no handbook, so a record supports an issue instead of a handbook page. Nothing under `experiments/` runs on its own or gates a merge, and `.Rbuildignore` leaves the directory out of the package; `R CMD build` gives a tarball without it.

title: fix: Time out stalled HTTP VFS transfers
description:
The HTTP VFS set no libcurl limits, so a server that accepted a connection and never answered blocked R, and with it `R CMD check`, indefinitely. Every handle now gives up connecting after `RSQLITE_HTTP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` seconds (default 30) and aborts a transfer that receives less than one byte per second for `RSQLITE_HTTP_STALL_TIMEOUT` seconds (default 60). Only whole numbers of seconds of at least 1 are honored, in any notation R writes such as `1e+05`; larger values are capped at 2147483 seconds (and libcurl 8.19.0 or later caps the stall timeout at 65535 seconds itself), and anything else uses the default, as documented in `?sqliteHttpConfig`, which now also says that these settings are read each time a remote database is opened. A handle whose limits cannot be set is not used, and the open then fails with "unable to open database file", a query with "disk I/O error".

Opening used to probe the server up to four times, since the file size and the header read each sent a HEAD and a GET. A failed probe is now not repeated within one open, and a HEAD that cannot connect or times out skips the GET, so a silent server costs one timeout. A stall during the open reports "unable to open database file", during a query "disk I/O error".

The test server can now accept requests without answering them. A new test opens such a server with `RSQLITE_HTTP_STALL_TIMEOUT=1`, expects the open to fail within seconds, and checks that the server received exactly one request, the HEAD, so a refused connection cannot pass for a stall.

An interrupt still cannot abort a transfer here: Ctrl-C takes effect only once the stall timeout ends the transfer. #843 adds that, and completes the wording on aborted transfers in the documentation.

title: feat: Check dictionary indices, 64-bit lengths and self-binding of Arrow parameters
description:
Pull request 12 of the [Arrow rework plan](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193). It stacks on #866 (bind the rows of an Arrow stream to a statement), which stacks on #865, #864, #863, #862, #861, #860, #859, #857, #856, #855, #830 and #850. It picks up what #866 left to it: dictionaries, 64-bit lengths and self-binding.

## What changes

All of it is behind the internal `bind_arrow_stream()` of #866; no DBI method calls it yet, and the default `dbBind()` path is unchanged.

**Dictionaries.** A dictionary-encoded column, such as a factor of a data frame converted by nanoarrow, binds the value its index points to, for every value type that #866 binds on its own (text, blobs, integers, reals, times and so on, also their large variants), with indices of any integer type from int8 to uint64. A null index and a null value of the dictionary bind NULL; unused levels don't matter. The index is checked also for a dictionary of the null type, whose values all bind NULL. Validation of an array doesn't look at the indices, so each index is checked at its row: one that is negative or beyond the dictionary fails with "Can't bind the dictionary index 2 of parameter 1 in row 2, out of range for 2 values." (a uint64 index shows its unsigned value) before anything is read. A dictionary of values that can't be bound fails before any row runs with the type error of #866, now naming the whole dictionary type. The slicing of #866 carries over: the index array and the dictionary each add their own offset.

**Offsets and lengths.** nanoarrow's default validation, which `ArrowArrayViewSetArray()` runs on each array, checks only the first and the last offset of a string or binary array. Each value of utf8, large utf8, binary and large binary (also as dictionary values) now has its own two offsets checked before it is read: offsets that are negative, decreasing or beyond the data fail with "Invalid Arrow parameters: the offsets of parameter 1 in row 2 point outside its data." A value longer than the connection's `SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH` (by default `SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH`, which `src/Makevars` sets to 2147483647 bytes) fails with "Can't bind the value of 3000000000 bytes of parameter 2 in row 1, beyond SQLite's length limit of 2147483647 bytes." before its data is read; sizes are 64-bit throughout, so a large value isn't truncated into a small one. At the default limit only large utf8 and large binary values can exceed it, since 32-bit offsets can't; a limit lowered with `sqlite3_limit()` applies to all four types. Without the check, `sqlite3_bind_text64()` and `sqlite3_bind_blob64()` refuse it as well, but without the parameter and the row. The check per value costs two loads of offsets, a few comparisons and a call of `sqlite3_db_handle()` and `sqlite3_limit()` for the current limit, which stays within the noise of a bind; full validation through `ArrowArrayViewValidate()` would also have covered dictionary indices, but it walks every chunk's dictionary again and reports neither the parameter nor the row. Rows are counted across the arrays of the stream, from 1, null struct rows included.

**Self-binding.** Binding a result to an Arrow stream of RSQLite that reads the same result, from this execution or an earlier one, fails up front with "Can't bind a result to an Arrow stream of its own rows." A chain of results whose parameters read each other's streams, which would recurse into the busy guard or leave the results holding each other, fails with "Can't bind a result to an Arrow stream of a result whose parameters read the rows of this one." `DbResult::check_arrow_params()` follows the chain: from the stream to the result it reads (a new `arrow_stream_result()` recognizes RSQLite's streams by their `release` callback), then to the Arrow stream that result is bound to, and so on, with a set of visited results. `bind_arrow_stream()` calls it through a new `result_check_arrow_params()` before reading the schema, since the schema of a stream of RSQLite fetches the first chunk; `DbResult::bind_arrow()` calls it again. A refused stream is neither read nor taken over, and the result keeps its previous bind. Before, a result bound to its own stream failed only at the first row, through #864's check of the execution, after the schema had fetched a chunk. A stream that has ended no longer reads its result, so it doesn't count as a link: binding the first result of a chain to the stream at its end is allowed and runs once the first stream has ended, because the rows that result would read are already in the chunks the next result holds, and nothing reads the first result again. Reading the schemas along a chain fetches ahead, so a chain of five results over three rows in chunks of one row is already in that state, and the first result then reads the chain's rows without recursion.

**Test hook.** A new internal `connection_limit_length(con, n)` sets `SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH` and returns the previous limit, so that the tests use 31-byte values instead of gigabytes. SQLite doesn't go below 30 bytes.

## Deliberately left out

- A stream implemented in R, or any other wrapper, that reads a stream of RSQLite hides the chain from the check: such a cycle still fails at its first row through the busy guard or #864's check of the execution, as before.
- The C data interface carries no buffer sizes, so the last offset of a string or binary array gives the size of its data. A producer whose last offset lies beyond its data buffer is still trusted; nothing on the consumer side can check that.
- The uint64 message of #866 names the parameter but not the row; it is unchanged here.
- Requested types: pull requests 13 and 14. `dbBindArrow()` and the other DBI methods: pull request 17.

## Tests

`tests/testthat/test-arrow-bind-checks.R`, through nanoarrow, with helpers in `helper-arrow.R` that build dictionaries and string arrays by hand, without validation:

- a factor with NA and an unused level; dictionaries with every index type from int8 to uint64 over utf8, int32, binary and large utf8 values, with null indices and null values; a sliced dictionary array over a sliced dictionary
- indices out of range at the second row (too large, negative, 255 in uint8 and 2^64 − 1 in uint64), raised by the bind of an `INSERT` after the first row
- with the length limit lowered to 30 bytes, 31-byte values of utf8, large utf8, binary, large binary and a dictionary fail at their row, after the first row; with the default limit, a large binary claiming 3e9 bytes over a one-byte buffer fails before its data is read
- negative, decreasing and out-of-range middle offsets for all four string and binary types fail at their row
- a dictionary of the null type with an index out of range, which fails like the others
- a result bound to its own stream, which is left unread; a cycle of two and of three results on separate connections, after which the stream still reads all rows
- the first result of a chain of five bound to the stream at its end once the first stream has ended, which is allowed and reads the right rows

`test-arrow-bind.R` keeps its test of types that can't be bound, with a date64 column in place of the factor. Every `test_that()` block of both files passes on its own after `load_all()`. `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true` passes except the three known errors in `test-httpvfs.R` (#832, #837). valgrind (`--leak-check=full`) reports no errors and nothing lost for `test-arrow-bind-checks.R` and `test-arrow-bind.R`; an AddressSanitizer and UBSan build reports nothing from the new code (only the known `memcpy(…, NULL, 0)` in `fetch_blob()` noted on #866).

title: feat: Bind the rows of an Arrow stream to a statement
description:
Pull request 11 of the [Arrow rework plan](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193). It stacks on #865 (Arrow streams outlive `dbClearResult()` and `dbDisconnect()`), which stacks on #864, #863, #862, #861, #860, #859, #857, #856, #855, #830 and #850.

## What changes

A new internal entry point, `bind_arrow_stream(res, stream)`, binds the rows of a nanoarrow array stream of struct arrays (or of anything nanoarrow converts to one, such as a data frame) to a prepared statement, and runs the statement once per row, as `dbBind()` does with a data frame. No DBI method calls it yet; the default `dbBind()` path is unchanged.

**Parameter source.** The rows come through a new `SqliteArrowParamSource`, next to #855's list source behind `SqliteParamSource`. `SqliteResultImpl::bind()` is split so that both sources share the start of a bind (`start_bind()`) and the count check (`check_param_count()`), with the same messages as before. The source reads the stream's arrays as the statement runs, one `get_next()` whenever the rows of the current array are bound, and skips empty arrays. A null row of the struct array binds NULL to every placeholder. The offset of a sliced struct array applies to its columns, which may have offsets of their own, as Arrow's `StructArray.slice()` exports them.

**Placeholders.** Named placeholders take the columns of the same name, anonymous and numbered ones take unnamed columns by position, through #855's `is_unnamed_placeholders()` and `match_placeholders()`, which gets the schema's named `children`. The messages are those of `dbBind()`: a column without a name counts as an unnamed parameter, as in DBI's default `dbBindArrow()`, which drops names that are all empty. A stream that isn't of struct arrays fails with "Parameters must be an Arrow stream of struct arrays, with a column per placeholder."

**Types.** These bind to the storage classes that `dbBind()` uses for the matching R types:

- bool and the signed and unsigned integers of 8 to 64 bits as integers; a uint64 value beyond `INT64_MAX` fails with its value and parameter
- half float, float and double as reals
- utf8 and large utf8 as text, binary and large binary as blobs; an empty value stays an empty text or blob, not NULL
- the null type as NULL
- date32 as days since the epoch, time32 and time64 as seconds since midnight, timestamp as seconds since the epoch, and duration as seconds, all as reals and in any unit; a timestamp is an instant, whatever its time zone. These include the date32, time64[us] and timestamp[us, UTC] of the read path of #861, so a chunk read with `extended_types` binds back as it was stored. A duration binds as `dbBind()` binds a difftime in seconds, such as an hms; `dbBind()` binds a difftime in other units as its bare number, while nanoarrow converts it to a duration, which binds as seconds.

Nulls come from the validity bitmaps. Every other type, such as a dictionary (a factor of a data frame), a list, a decimal or date64, fails with "Can't bind parameter 1 of Arrow type …" before any row runs: the source checks the schema in its constructor, before the result drops its previous bind, and takes the stream over only then, so the stream stays with its owner and the previous bind goes on. The result of every `sqlite3_bind_*()` call is checked. `bind_arrow_stream()` reads the schema through nanoarrow before it calls the C++ code, so a failing `get_schema()` reports nanoarrow's message ("array_stream->get_schema(): …") rather than the source's "Can't read the schema of the Arrow parameters: …", which only a stream whose schema fails the second time would reach.

**Errors.** An error of the stream's `get_next()` ("Can't read the Arrow parameters: …") or of a value fails like a later parameter set of `dbBind()` (#830, #855): it becomes a `step_error` with `SQLITE_ERROR`, so after a full fetch it is kept for the next one, a statement without rows raises it from the bind after the earlier rows ran, and `dbGetRowsAffected()` counts those rows. The stream's callbacks may call R, as a stream of RSQLite (#864) does to warn about converted values: they run under `cpp11::unwind_protect()`, so an R error that leaves one by a jump, such as a warning made an error by `options(warn = 2)`, unwinds the C++ frames and leaves the result unbound, like any other failed bind. A stream of RSQLite protects its own callbacks with cpp11 in turn, and cpp11 protects such nested calls from 0.4.6 on, so `LinkingTo` now asks for cpp11 (>= 0.4.6). #830's busy guard covers the whole bind, so a handler of such a warning can't clear the result meanwhile. The source releases the stream from its destructor, unprotected, also from a new bind, `dbClearResult()` or a finalizer: as the Arrow C stream interface expects, a stream's `release()` must not raise an R error, which a code comment states.

## Deliberately left out

- Dictionary arrays, and with them the factor columns of a data frame, checks and tests of values beyond 32-bit lengths, and binding a result to its own stream (or two results to each other's streams): pull request 12. Dictionaries fail with the type error above; the 64-bit binds of SQLite are used and their result codes checked, but not tested with values beyond 2 GiB. A result bound to a stream of itself fails at the first row, which #864's check of the execution refuses.
- Requested types: pull requests 13 and 14.
- `dbBindArrow()`, `dbAppendTableArrow()` and the other DBI methods: pull request 17.
- Streams read on worker threads: pull request 15. The source calls the stream on R's main thread, inside the bind or fetch that needs the next row.

## Tests

`tests/testthat/test-arrow-bind.R`, through nanoarrow:

- a round trip of a data frame of integer, real, text, blob, Date, hms and POSIXct columns with nulls into a table with `extended_types`, read back with `dbGetQuery()`, and of its chunk from the Arrow read path into a second table, read back both ways
- every integer width, signed and unsigned, booleans, half floats, floats, doubles and the null type, with their storage classes
- large utf8 and binary, time32 in milliseconds, a timestamp in seconds with a time zone, a duration in milliseconds, and a null row of the struct array
- a sliced struct array of integer, text, boolean and binary columns, with and without a validity bitmap of its own, and one whose columns are sliced as well; the boolean values and the validity bitmaps start at a bit offset
- a stream of several arrays with an empty one in between, fetched in two steps, and a stream without arrays, for a query and a statement
- named, `$`, `@`, anonymous and numbered placeholders
- the messages of mismatched parameters, compared with those of `dbBind()`, and a stream that isn't of struct arrays
- dictionary and list columns, which fail before any row runs, leave the stream readable and the previous bind fetching

title: feat: Let Arrow streams outlive `dbClearResult()` and `dbDisconnect()`
description:
Pull request 10 of the [Arrow rework plan](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193). It stacks on #864 (a result read as a lazy Arrow array stream), which stacks on #863, #862, #861, #860, #859, #857, #856, #855, #830 and #850.

## What changes

A stream of the internal `read_arrow_stream()` now keeps working after `dbClearResult()` and `dbDisconnect()`, where #864 failed its next callback. These are the semantics that DBI's `dbGetQueryArrow()` needs, since it clears the result before the stream is consumed.

**After `dbClearResult()`.** The stream already holds a share of the result (#856, #864). `dbClearResult()` now only drops R's share, rather than freeing the statement under the stream: the statement lives as long as a stream shares the result, and is finalized when the last stream that reads it ends or is released, by `release()` or by R's garbage collector. A result without a stream is destroyed at once, as before. The stream keeps reading lazily, one chunk per `get_next()`, also while other statements run on the connection.

**After `dbDisconnect()`.** The connection counts the streams that read from it. While one does, `dbDisconnect()` marks the connection closed for R (`dbIsValid()` is `FALSE`, every later use fails as before) but leaves the SQLite handle open, with its busy handler; the last stream to end or be released then closes it with `sqlite3_close_v2()`, which completes once the statements are finalized. Without a stream, `dbDisconnect()` closes the handle at once, as before. Deferring the close, rather than reading through the zombie handle that `sqlite3_close_v2()` leaves, keeps the connection fully usable for the stream: its errors keep SQLite's message (the old stack had to fall back to `sqlite3_errstr()`), its virtual tables stay connected, and its R busy handler stays registered and is called as before. A result whose connection is already closed can't start a stream ("Can't read a result as an Arrow stream after its connection has been closed."), so a stream never reads through a zombie handle. `read_arrow_stream()` checks this before it claims the result for Arrow, so a failed call leaves `dbFetch()` usable.

**The busy handler of a closed connection.** Before every close, immediate or deferred, an R busy handler is now unregistered from SQLite (`sqlite3_busy_handler(conn, NULL, NULL)`) and only then released. An uncleared result can still step its statement through the zombie handle, with `dbFetch()` or `dbBind()`; until now SQLite could then call the released R closure ("attempt to apply non-function", or a crash), on #864 and on `main` after a plain `dbDisconnect()` with an open result as well. Such a step now fails at once with "database is locked". A busy timeout, set by `sqliteSetBusyHandler()` with an integer or by `PRAGMA busy_timeout`, calls no R code and stays, so such a step still waits for it, as on `main`.

**Errors through a closed handle.** `sqlite3_errmsg()` of a zombie handle only reports API misuse, so an error of a statement stepped after its connection was closed read "bad parameter or other API misuse" (also on `main`). Once the handle is closed, the error now carries SQLite's message for the step's result code (`sqlite3_errstr()`), such as "database is locked". While a stream keeps the handle open after `dbDisconnect()`, errors keep SQLite's full message.

**Unchanged.** `dbIsValid()` of the result and the connection, the warnings and errors of `dbClearResult()`, `dbFetch()` and `dbDisconnect()` on the default path, and #830's busy guard, which still makes `dbClearResult()` refuse while a fetch runs, also from a handler of a stream's own warning. The warning of `dbDisconnect()` about results in use counts them as before: a result cleared while a stream still reads it doesn't count (#864 got this by dropping the connection in `clear()`; now the connection counts such results). A result that R's garbage collector frees while a stream reads it doesn't count either, unlike on #864: the finalizer of the result's external pointer now marks it as `dbClearResult()` does. A stream still fails after `dbBind()`, whose types may differ from its schema. The release during a callback, the final failures and the mixed-fetch claim of #864 are untouched.

**Lazy, not buffered.** A stream reads its rows lazily after the clear, because buffering would hold the whole rest of the result in memory, which defeats a stream, and would have to read it eagerly inside `dbClearResult()`, where errors and coercion warnings would surface at the wrong call. The price: until the stream has ended or is released, it keeps its statement open, and with it a read transaction and the database file, also after `dbDisconnect()`. Meanwhile, on the same connection, `DROP TABLE` on a table it reads fails with "database table is locked", and on a file database another connection's writes fail with "database is locked"; a transaction left open at `dbDisconnect()` is rolled back only when the connection finally closes. This is what a pending statement means in SQLite, and the old stack documented the same.

## Deliberately left out

- Reading streams on worker threads: pull request 15. The last `release()` still destroys the result, and now possibly closes the connection, on the thread where it runs, which must be R's main thread.
- `dbSendQueryArrow()`, `dbFetchArrow()`, `dbFetchArrowChunk()` and `dbGetQueryArrow()` through the stream, and user documentation of the lifetime: pull request 16.

## Tests

`tests/testthat/test-arrow-stream-lifetime.R`, through nanoarrow:

- clear then read, chunk by chunk, with another query on the connection between chunks; clear before any fetch
- disconnect then read, with an open result (the warning as before) and with a cleared one (no warning)
- a result of a closed connection can't start a stream, and stays usable with `dbFetch()`
- `rm()` and `gc()` of the result and the connection while a stream lives, also of a connection never disconnected
- a result freed by `gc()` while a stream reads it doesn't count as in use
- a busy handler kept across `dbDisconnect()` while a stream lives and called through the deferred handle, then not called once the stream's release closed it; and not called after a plain `dbDisconnect()` with an open result, where the result fails with "database is locked" (on #865's first commit this test aborts R)
- an integer busy timeout still applies to a result of a closed connection
- `options(warn = 2)` and a release from a handler of the stream's own warning, after clear and disconnect
- on a file database with a write transaction open at `dbDisconnect()`: three streams of one connection, one released before its end, one read to its end and then released, one freed by `gc()`; another connection stays locked out until the last of them, and then sees the transaction rolled back, so the connection was closed exactly then
- a stream that ends lets the connection close before it is released
- two streams of one connection, read interleaved, one released early

The two tests of `test-arrow-stream.R` that expected the failures are gone. Every new block fails on #864 and passes on its own after `load_all()`. `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true` passes except the three known errors in `test-httpvfs.R` (#832, #837). A script of default-path behavior (fetch after disconnect, clearing twice, disconnecting twice, results freed) prints the same on #864 and here; the only intended changes on the default path are the busy handler and the error message through a closed handle above.

valgrind (`--leak-check=full`): no errors and nothing definitely lost for `test-arrow-stream-lifetime.R`, `test-arrow-stream.R` and `test-dbClearResult.R`, nor for the review's reproducers (busy handlers, lifetimes in every order of `rm()` and `gc()`, the claim, the default path), nor for reproducers that release a stream of a cleared result of a disconnected connection, with a custom busy handler, from a handler of its own warning during `get_next()` and `convert_array_stream()`, that leave a stream by `options(warn = 2)` and free it by `gc()`, and that release ten streams of one connection in random order, before and after their end.

title: feat: Read a result as a lazy Arrow array stream
description:
Pull request 9 of the [Arrow rework plan](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193). It stacks on #863 (Arrow chunks end before string and binary offsets overflow), which stacks on #862, #861, #860, #859, #857, #856, #855, #830 and #850.

## What changes

A new internal entry point, `read_arrow_stream(res, n = 65536L)`, returns a `nanoarrow_array_stream` over an open result. Each `get_next()` fetches the next chunk of at most `n` rows (all of them for `-1`) with the chunk machinery of #859 to #863: the same column types, the coercion warning once per chunk, and the byte limit that ends a chunk before its string or binary offsets overflow. Nothing is fetched when the stream is created. `get_schema()` reads the first chunk, which decides the column types as for `result_fetch_arrow_chunk()`, and keeps it for the first `get_next()`, so no row is handed out before the schema and the schema always matches the chunks. The schema is cached in the stream once read. A result without rows ends the stream without a chunk, with the types of the declared columns. No DBI method calls the stream yet, and the default `dbFetch()` path is unchanged except for the check below.

**Lifetime.** The stream holds a share of the result (the `DbResultPtr` from #856), so the result lives through every callback, also if R's garbage collector frees the R result object meanwhile. `dbClearResult()` now calls `DbResult::clear()`, which frees the statement and drops the connection even while a stream holds a share. The next `get_schema()` or `get_next()` then fails with "Can't read an Arrow stream after its result has been cleared." It likewise fails after `dbDisconnect()` ("…after its connection has been closed.") and after `dbBind()` starts a new execution, whose types may differ from the stream's schema ("…after its result has been bound to new parameters."). The stream never touches the freed statement: it checks these conditions before each fetch, and its `release()` only drops its share. A stream that reaches its end drops its share at once.

**Errors.** C++ errors, among them SQLite's, become the stream's `EIO` with the message in `get_last_error()`. The fetch loop is the same as for `result_fetch_arrow_chunk()`, so #830's semantics hold: an error at the step that reads ahead after a full chunk is kept for the next `get_next()`, any error completes the result, and the busy guard stops a warning handler from clearing the result during a fetch. An interrupt, or a coercion warning made an error by `options(warn = 2)`, arrives as a `cpp11::unwind_exception`. Its jump continues once the callback's C++ objects are destroyed, as at cpp11's entry points, and the chunk kept by #862 comes with the next `get_next()`. Any other failure of a callback is final: later `get_next()` calls, and `get_schema()` calls until a schema is cached, fail again with its message, rather than end the stream as if its rows were complete, so a consumer that goes on after an error or an interrupt can't take a truncated result for a complete one. The flag is never cleared once set.

**Release during a callback.** A handler of a warning raised inside the stream's own `get_schema()` or `get_next()` may call the stream's `release()`. The stream counts its running callbacks: such a release only marks the state released and detaches it from the C struct, and the callback deletes the state, with its share of the result, once its body returns and before it continues an R jump. Without this, the callback would write into the freed state, or into a freed result when R had dropped its object. A consumer that doesn't check `release` between chunks, such as nanoarrow's `convert_array_stream()`, may call the released stream again: its `get_schema()` and `get_next()` then return `EINVAL` without touching any state, and `get_last_error()` returns "The Arrow stream has been released." Each callback body runs under `R_ExecWithCleanup()`, so the count of running callbacks stays right even if an R error leaves the body by a jump that bypasses cpp11.

**Mixed fetches.** This applies the recommended answer of the [mixed-fetch question](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830183898), which nobody has decided yet. Once a stream has been created for a result, `dbFetch()` on it fails with an error of class `RSQLite_error_fetch_kind`. Once `dbFetch()` has been called on a result, with any `n`, creating a stream fails likewise. The claim holds for the result's lifetime, also across `dbBind()`. The rule lives in one place, `claim_fetch_kind()` in `R/arrow-stream.R`: dropping its error allows mixing, which the internal fetches already support. `result_fetch_arrow_chunk()` is not part of the rule, so the tests of #859 that alternate the two kinds of fetch keep working.

## Deliberately left out

- Reading a stream after `dbClearResult()` or `dbDisconnect()`: pull request 10.
- Reading a stream on a worker thread, as arrow's scanner and Acero do: pull request 15. The callbacks call R and must run on R's main thread, and a `release()` that drops the last share destroys the result where it runs.
- `dbSendQueryArrow()`, `dbFetchArrow()` and `dbFetchArrowChunk()` through the stream: pull request 16.
- The old stack's buffered stream and its rethrow of R jumps for C++ consumers in this package belong to those later pull requests.

## Error message

The error uses `rlang::abort()` rather than `cli::cli_abort()`. cli is only in Suggests, and `dbFetch()` can raise this error.

## Tests

`tests/testthat/test-arrow-stream.R`, run through nanoarrow (`$get_schema()`, `$get_next()`, `convert_array_stream()`):

- chunk lengths and `dbGetRowCount()` as the stream advances, and agreement with `dbGetQuery()`
- the schema before any row is handed out, decided by the first chunk
- a result without rows
- the coercion warning once per chunk, and a warning made an error under `options(warn = 2)`, after which the stream goes on with the kept chunk
- the errors after `dbClearResult()`, `dbDisconnect()` and `dbBind()`
- a stream that keeps reading after R frees its result object
- an SQLite error at the read-ahead step and inside a chunk, after which `get_next()` keeps failing, and an SQLite error while the schema is read, after which three `convert_array_stream()` calls all fail
- a `release()` from a handler of the stream's own warning, with the R result object kept and with it freed, and from a handler during `convert_array_stream()` (also run under valgrind, with the reviews' reproducers)
- the mixed-fetch rule in both directions, with snapshots of the messages
- the checks of `n`

Every `test_that()` block runs on its own after `load_all()`. `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true` passes except the three known errors in `test-httpvfs.R` (#832, #837), and `R CMD check --no-manual` passes.
