title: feat: End Arrow chunks before string and binary offsets overflow
description:
Eighth step of the Arrow rework (plan: https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193): an Arrow chunk now ends before a row whose text or blobs would take a `utf8` or `binary` column beyond the 2^31 - 1 bytes that the 32-bit offsets of these types address, and the next chunk starts with that row. Before, such a chunk failed with "Can't append to Arrow array", and the error completed the result (#860). The entry point `result_fetch_arrow_chunk()` stays internal, so nothing changes for users.

What changes:

- `result_fetch_arrow_chunk(res, n)` returns fewer than `n` rows, also for `n = -1`, when the next row doesn't fit, and never fails for the size of a chunk alone. A chunk takes at least one row: a value beyond the limit on its own fails the chunk that it would start, after the chunk before it has come out, with "Column `s`: a value of 11 bytes exceeds the 10 bytes that an Arrow utf8 or binary array can hold." As any error of a fetch since #830, it completes the result. With the real limit, no value gets there: SQLite holds at most 2^31 - 1 bytes per value (`SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH` in `Makevars`), so the error only guards the lowered limits of the tests.
- The check counts what the append adds: the bytes of text and blobs, the text that SQLite renders for a number in a `utf8` or `binary` column, and nothing for `NULL` and for text and blobs that are `NULL` in a `utf8` column as not valid UTF-8. A column still undecided in the first chunk counts its value for the type that the value would give it. Each column has its own limit; the first one that a row would overflow ends the chunk.
- `fetch_loop()` asks `takes_row()` before each row: `ArrowChunk` checks the bytes there, `SqliteDataFrame` takes every row. A row that the chunk doesn't take stays the current row of the statement, as the row read ahead past a full chunk does (#850), and no step happens. So `dbHasCompleted()` is `FALSE` and `dbGetRowCount()` counts the rows handed out. A step error after the held-back row comes with the fetch that steps past it: it fails that fetch, or is kept for the next one if that fetch is full and only reads ahead.
- Each value is read once for the check and the append: `SqliteArrowColumn::read_type()` reads its storage class before anything converts it, `read_bytes()` reads the bytes of a `utf8` or `binary` value and checks its UTF-8, and `append_row()` uses both. A held-back row keeps its storage classes for the next chunk until the next step clears them, since reading the row as a data frame meanwhile, with `dbColumnInfo()` or `dbFetch(n = 0)`, converts a blob in a character column to text. Its bytes are read again by the next chunk, as such a read can move them.
- Conversions are logged when a value is appended, never by the check, so the conversions of a held-back row are reported by the chunk that returns it, with its row number in the result (#862).
- A `dbFetch()` after a held-back row returns it first, reading its storage classes itself. The check has rendered a number in a `utf8` or `binary` column as text, after which SQLite documents `sqlite3_column_type()` as undefined; the bundled SQLite keeps the class of a number next to its text, which `dbColumnInfo()` followed by `dbFetch()` already relies on, and a test pins it. The check doesn't convert text or blobs: a blob in a `utf8` column keeps its bytes (#860).
- `dbBind()` starts a new execution with its own first row, and keeps the limit of the result.
- The internal `result_set_arrow_max_bytes()` lowers the limit of one result, so that the tests need little memory. It refuses a limit that isn't a whole number between 0 and 2^31 - 1.

The row read ahead past a full fetch (#850) now keeps its storage classes as well, in a commit of its own (fix: Keep the storage classes of an Arrow row read ahead). On #862, the next Arrow chunk read them only when it took the row, so a `dbColumnInfo()` or `dbFetch(n = 0)` in between, which reads the row as a data frame and converts a blob in a character column to text, made the chunk take the blob for text and leave it out of the warning. Now `read_ahead()` has the Arrow columns read the storage classes of the row at once, after an Arrow chunk and after a data-frame fetch between Arrow chunks, and the next chunk keeps them until the next step, as for a held-back row. Before the first Arrow chunk of an execution there are no Arrow columns yet: a data-frame fetch and a `dbColumnInfo()` before it still leave that chunk to read the converted classes, as on #862.

The design comes from #795: 569fe5d7 (end the chunk before the row), 943b178e (read each value once), c0891bf5 (keep the storage classes of a held-back row), 3f988e8a (the limit of one result instead of a global hook) and 1449720a (the hook for the large test in GitHub Actions). Where it differs:

- #795 also ended a chunk after the row at which a column reached 1 GiB. That is a choice of chunk size, not a limit of the format, and is left out here; streams (pull request 9) can bring it if their batches want it.
- #795 took a value beyond the limit into an empty chunk; here it fails, so that no column of a chunk holds more than the limit.
- #795 refused `dbFetch()` while a row was held back, because its check read blobs in a `utf8` column as text, which changes their storage class; here the check reads them as bytes, and `dbFetch()` returns the row.
- #795 counted the bytes of text that isn't valid UTF-8, which is `NULL` in the chunk; here it counts nothing.

Deliberately left out:

- `large_utf8` and `large_binary`, whose 64-bit offsets need no limit (43fdcaaa), come with the requested types in pull request 14.
- Lazy strings (c2b41f72 and its follow-ups 7fdae79f and 63f16ca7) are pull request 23.
- The 64-bit row count is #858, from `main`.

Tested:

- New `tests/testthat/test-arrow-chunks.R`, with the limit lowered to 6 to 150 bytes: chunks end exactly before the row that would overflow, with the first row of a chunk at the limit, a value of no bytes in a full column, and `n` ending a chunk before or after the limit, for text and for blobs, with no row lost or repeated; several text and blob columns with numbers and `NULL`, where each column ends a chunk, a number counts the bytes of its text and text that isn't valid UTF-8 counts nothing; the read-ahead boundary, with a step error after the rows: a chunk ended by the limit before it, the next one full and keeping the error, or asking for more rows and failing, and the row stepped past a full chunk reading its own storage classes; conversions of a held-back row reported with the chunk that returns it, with their row numbers after a `dbFetch()`, and a blob held back across a `dbColumnInfo()` that converts it to text still reported as a blob; a value beyond the limit on its own, failing after the rows before it and in the first row of a result, with the result completed; `dbFetch()` after a held-back row and `dbBind()` starting anew. `dbHasCompleted()` and `dbGetRowCount()` are checked after each chunk. A last test fetches blobs of 1e9, 1.2e9 and 1 bytes with the real limit, in chunks of 1 and 2 rows; it needs about 2.5 GB of memory (2.49 GB peak measured, 5 s) and runs only with `RSQLITE_TEST_LARGE_ARROW=true`, after `skip_on_cran()`.
- `.github/workflows/custom/after-install/action.yml` sets `RSQLITE_TEST_LARGE_ARROW=true` where it is unset, as 1449720a did, so every hosted job that calls the hook runs the 2.5 GB test: in `R-CMD-check.yaml`, `rcc-smoke` with its coverage run, each entry of the `rcc-full` matrix of operating systems and R versions, its coverage entries included, and each entry of `rcc-suggests`; and in `R-CMD-check-dev.yaml`, the daily `rcc dev` base job and each job per dev dependency. R-hub's containers call no custom action and skip it, as do CRAN and users. Reviewers may weigh that cost against the coverage; dropping the hook keeps the test off everywhere unless the variable is set.
- `tests/testthat/helper-arrow.R`: `write_sized_table()`, `local_limited_result()`, `fetch_arrow_chunks()` and `chunk_lengths()`.
- New test of the read-ahead fix: a blob read ahead after an Arrow chunk and after a data-frame fetch, converted to text by `dbColumnInfo()`, is still reported as a converted blob by the next chunk. It fails without the fix.
- Each `test_that()` block of the five Arrow test files (`test-arrow-chunks.R`, `test-arrow-coercion.R`, `test-arrow-columns.R`, `test-arrow-text.R` and `test-arrow-dates.R`) passes on its own in a fresh session right after `pkgload::load_all()`: 57 blocks pass, and three skip there, the large test and the two out-of-memory blocks whose `callr` sessions need an installed build.
- Mutations, each caught by the new tests: `<` for `<=` at the limit, numbers counting nothing, invalid UTF-8 counting its bytes, failing a value beyond the limit also after other rows, reading the storage classes anew for a held-back row, not clearing them at a step, and no check at all.
- Against an installed build, the five Arrow test files, `test-read-ahead.R` and `test-extendedTypes.R` pass, the large test and the out-of-memory blocks included.
- Under AddressSanitizer (gcc, `-O1`), after the merge and the read-ahead fix, `test-arrow-chunks.R` with the large test, `test-arrow-coercion.R`, `test-arrow-columns.R`, `test-arrow-text.R`, `test-arrow-dates.R`, `test-read-ahead.R`, `test-dbSendQuery.R`, `test-dbClearResult.R`, `test-error.R`, `test-dbBind.R` and `test-extendedTypes.R` pass without a report, and so does a script of 300 random tables of text, numbers, blobs and `NULL` with random limits and chunk sizes and `dbColumnInfo()` between chunks, 2820 chunks in all, which checks that no chunk holds more than the limit in a column and that no row is lost.
- `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true`: no failures beyond the three errors in `test-httpvfs.R` that also happen on `main` (#832, #837).

Cost of the check, measured before the merge and the read-ahead fix, which only moves the reading of one row's storage classes per full fetch to the read-ahead: one million rows from a file database in one chunk, `-O2`, median of 11 runs, seven rounds alternating between #862 and this branch. One text column of about 20 bytes: 0.114 to 0.126 s on both. Three text columns: 0.264 to 0.276 s on #862, 0.275 to 0.285 s here, about 4 %. One blob column: 0.113 to 0.122 and 0.114 to 0.123 s. An integer, a text, a real and a blob column: 0.288 to 0.311 and 0.309 to 0.319 s, about 4 %. The three text columns in chunks of 100 rows: 0.417 to 0.468 and 0.435 to 0.475 s, about 3 %. #795 measured about 6 %. The check moves the reads of the append rather than adding any, and a variant that reads the storage classes and the bytes in one pass over the columns measured the same.

After the [clean review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/863#issuecomment-6835992976), f61447cc restores the `src/*.dd` files that CI's auto-update filled with absolute paths (#836, fixed by #853), and 975e379b answers two of its Lows: the CI hook's comment names `rcc dev`, and the setter refuses a fractional limit.

Sits on #862 at ea9f8364 (merged into this branch, with #862's review fixes), which is on #861, #860, #859, #857, #856, #855, #830 and #850, and merges #845. The merge resolves two conflicts: a `binary` value is read before its conversion is logged on both sides, here in `read_bytes()`, and the comment of `fetch_arrow_chunk()` keeps both the kept chunk and the byte limit.

## Size

About 190 hand-written lines of C++: 80 in `SqliteArrowColumn.cpp` and `.h`, 90 in `SqliteResultImpl.cpp` and `.h` with the read-ahead fix, and 20 in `SqliteResult`, `SqliteDataFrame.h` and `result.cpp`; 335 lines of tests, 280 in `test-arrow-chunks.R` and 55 in `helper-arrow.R`; and 12 lines of the CI hook. That is about 540 in all, within the plan's 600. No `.dd` file changes, since no file includes a new header.

title: test: Declare DBItest 1.8.3.6 in the DBItest context
description:
DBItest gates its newest specs behind the `dbitest_version` tweak, with a counter of its own (1.8.0.1 to 1.8.0.50, then 1.8.3.1 to 1.8.3.6). r-dbi/DBItest#571 gated six specs for requested Arrow schemas at 1.8.3.1 to 1.8.3.6: `arrow_fetch_arrow_schema`, `arrow_get_query_arrow_schema`, `arrow_get_query_arrow_schema_zero_rows`, `arrow_fetch_arrow_chunk_schema`, `arrow_read_table_arrow_64_bit` and `arrow_send_query_schema_stable`. This PR declares `dbitest_version = "1.8.3.6"` in `tests/testthat/helper-DBItest.R`, the highest gate RSQLite has been run against, so that the six specs run and a spec DBItest gates later stays off until RSQLite has been checked against it. It is the `main` counterpart of the declaration in #831, which sits on the old Arrow stack and also changes a second, Arrow-specific context that `main` does not have; only the default-context line is brought over.

The six specs need a DBItest newer than the CRAN release 1.8.3, which gates nothing above 1.8.0.50, so with the released version nothing changes. They are in the development version, 1.8.3.9013 on r-universe (`https://r-dbi.r-universe.dev`) and GitHub `r-dbi/DBItest`. The declared value is deliberately 1.8.3.6 and not the development version number, because the gates are compared with `as.package_version()` and a declaration of 1.8.3.9013 would also switch on every spec gated at 1.8.3.7 or later before RSQLite has run it. `DESCRIPTION` keeps `DBItest (>= 1.8.0)`: declaring a version above the installed one is harmless. No `Remotes:` or `Config/Needs` entry is needed, because the development DBItest is only installed by the `rcc dev` job (nightly on `main`), which installs it from r-universe itself, and `R-CMD-check` keeps installing CRAN's.

Tested by running `tests/testthat/test-DBItest.R` (the default context) after `pkgload::load_all()`, with DBItest 1.8.3 from CRAN and with 1.8.3.9013 installed from r-universe into a separate library, on `main` and on this branch:

- With DBItest 1.8.3, both give 658 tests and 9677 expectations, 59 skipped, no failures or errors (9678 and 58 when RSQLite is installed, since the `reexport` spec then runs).
- With DBItest 1.8.3.9013 on `main`, 664 tests and 9684 expectations, 64 skipped, no failures, and the six specs skipped.
- With DBItest 1.8.3.9013 on this branch, 664 tests and 9787 expectations, 58 skipped, no failures or errors, and all six specs run and pass: `arrow_send_query_schema_stable` (61 expectations), `arrow_fetch_arrow_chunk_schema` (18), `arrow_fetch_arrow_schema`, `arrow_get_query_arrow_schema` and `arrow_get_query_arrow_schema_zero_rows` (9 each) and `arrow_read_table_arrow_64_bit` (3). DBI's default Arrow methods are enough for them, as #831 reported.

The specs do not run in this PR's checks, since `R-CMD-check` installs DBItest from CRAN. They run in the `rcc dev` job (nightly on `main`, and on `cran-*` pushes, `v*` tags and manual dispatch) and in DBItest's own `backends` job, which clones RSQLite's default branch. The copies of this helper in DBItest and DBI still declare 1.8.1 until they are regenerated.

The [plan to rework the Arrow stack](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193) splits this out as a separate pull request from `main`, since nothing else depends on it.

Reviewed in a [clean review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/854#issuecomment-6830801884), which found nothing above Low; see the [accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/854#issuecomment-6835593142). Squash-merge, so that the first commit, which carries a regenerated `src/cpp11.dd`, does not reach `main`.

title: feat: Report values converted to an Arrow column's type once per chunk, with their rows
description:
Seventh step of the Arrow rework (plan: https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193): the internal Arrow engine of #859, #860 and #861 now reports the values it converts to the type of their column, or makes `NULL`, with one warning per chunk. The entry point `result_fetch_arrow_chunk()` stays internal, so nothing changes for users.

What changes:

- `SqliteArrowColumn` logs every value that #859, #860 and #861 convert silently, in a new `CoercionLog` per column: grouped by storage class and what happened, with the count and the first five row numbers. Row numbers count from 1 across the whole result, as `dbGetRowCount()` counts rows, so a chunk after a data-frame fetch goes on from the rows of that fetch. Logging calls no R API. The groups:
  - converted, as SQLite converts: a real truncated in an `int64` column fixed by the first chunk, text and blobs read as numbers, numbers rendered as text, text in a `binary` column, and a blob of valid UTF-8 in a `utf8` column. This includes values of another storage class within the first chunk, after the first value has decided the type. Text and blobs that an open `int64` column reads as beyond its range take their reading as reals when a real widens the column later in the chunk (#860), and the log then counts them as converted.
  - out of range, `NULL` instead: a real, or the leading integer of text or a blob, beyond `int64`; a count of days beyond `date32`; seconds beyond `int64` microseconds, or an infinity; a time outside the day, as a number or as text.
  - not valid UTF-8 or with a NUL byte, `NULL` instead: text and blobs in a `utf8` column.
  - not parsable, `NULL` instead: text that isn't a date or time, and any blob, in a date or time column.
  - dropped by the null type: any value in a column of the null type.

  Not reported, since `dbFetch()` reads them the same way without a warning: integers in a `double` column, integers widened to `double` within the first chunk, and numbers within the range of a date or time column.
- Once the chunk is complete, `SqliteResultImpl::fetch_arrow_chunk()` hands the logs to `warn_coercion()` in the new `R/warn-coercion.R`, which raises one warning of class `RSQLite_warning_coercion` with a line per column, and carries the logs in its `coercions` field:

  ``` Warning: Values converted to the Arrow type of 4 columns:
  * Column `i` (int64): 2 text values converted (rows 3 and 5); 1 real value converted (row 4)
  * Column `s` (utf8): 1 blob value not valid UTF-8 or with a NUL byte, NULL instead (row 3); 2 integer values converted (rows 4 and 5)
  * Column `b` (binary): 1 text value converted (row 3); 1 integer value converted (row 5)
  * Column `n` (null): 1 integer value dropped by the null type (row 3); 1 text value dropped by the null type (row 4) ```

  The groups of a column come in the order of their first rows. More than five rows end in `...` after the first five; row numbers are printed in full, `100000` and not `1e+05`. The condition is built and signalled with base R's `warning()`, not `rlang::warn()`, which made each warning cost about 0.4 ms instead of 0.05 ms.
- The warning is raised after `fetch_loop()` has returned and the struct array is assembled, never while values are read: no R code runs while a chunk is half-built, and an error made of the warning doesn't pass the handler of the fetch loop, which ends the result. It is raised while the busy guard of #830 still holds the result: a handler can read `dbGetRowCount()` and `dbHasCompleted()`, while fetching from, binding or clearing the result fails with the guard's error, such as "Can't clear a result while one of its fetches or binds is running, as from a handler of a warning that it raised." Raising it from R after the entry point has returned would let a handler clear the result between building the chunk and handing it out.
- The chunk stays in the result until it is handed out. When the warning exits instead of returning, because `options(warn = 2)` turns it into an error ("(converted from warning) Values converted to the Arrow type of 1 column: ..."), a handler signals an error (the guard's included) or an exiting handler catches it, the error reaches the caller and the chunk is kept. The next `result_fetch_arrow_chunk()` hands it out without warning again, whole, whatever its `n`: after a fetch of 100 rows whose warning failed, a fetch of 1 row returns those 100 rows. The fetches after it go on with the next rows, so no row is lost. Until then its rows don't count: `dbGetRowCount()` leaves them out and `dbHasCompleted()` is `FALSE`, so a loop until `dbHasCompleted()` gets them. `dbFetch()` refuses with "Can't fetch a data frame before the Arrow chunk that was kept when the warning about its values exited.", since its rows would come out before the earlier rows of the kept chunk, and `dbBind()` drops the kept chunk with the rest of the execution. The same counting holds while a handler runs.
- Each chunk starts with empty logs, so a fetch that fails after converting values (a step error, an interrupt) doesn't report them with the next fetch. A value that runs out of memory while it is read is an error that fails its chunk (#860, #861), not a conversion: the log notes a value only after reading it, and goes with the failed chunk.
- The simpler alternative, for the maintainers to choose: raise the warning inside the `try` of the fetch loop, so that a warning that exits ends the execution, as an error of `dbFetch()` does, with its warning turned into an error by `options(warn = 2)`. That drops `KeptArrowChunk` and its special cases in `complete()`, `n_rows_fetched()`, `fetch()` and `bind()`, about 50 lines with their tests, and the `n` of a fetch would always hold. The cost: the rows of the chunk are lost, and so are the remaining rows of the result, so that with `options(warn = 2)` the first chunk with a conversion ends the read. The open question of mixing data-frame and Arrow fetches on one result may settle it too.
- `SqliteResultImpl.h` keeps nanoarrow out, as #859 has it: the kept chunk lives behind the forward-declared `KeptArrowChunk`, defined in `SqliteResultImpl.cpp`.

The design comes from #800 (ef68461a: `CoercionLog`, `R/warn-coercion.R`), with its refinements 7f6a01e2 (the log of a failed fetch is discarded), 1fcf5a44 (row numbers in full), 4a4e5804 (values of the null type reported as dropped) and a5f157ab (`rlang::warn()` without `call`), applied to the Arrow path only. Where it differs:

- #800 warned inside the fetch, before handing out the chunk, so that an error made of the warning released the chunk with its rows; here the chunk is kept, and the warning comes after the fetch loop.
- #800 kept the first 20 and the last two row numbers per group and formatted them with cli when installed, through `rlang::warn()`; here the first five and `...`, with `*` bullets, joined and signalled with base R.
- The messages say `NULL`, as the Arrow arrays hold it, where #800 said `NA`, and "text" for the storage class #800 called "string". #800's text for worker threads (`coercions_text()`) is left out.

The data-frame path is unchanged: `dbFetch()` keeps its "mixed type" and date warnings exactly as they are, raised while it reads. Extending the per-fetch report to `dbFetch()` would be a separate, user-visible change, also for the data frames that pull requests 19 and 20 build through Arrow, for which #800 warned once per `dbFetch()`.

Deliberately left out:

- Byte limits are pull request 8, requested types pull requests 13 and 14.
- Streams are pull request 9, which has to raise the warning outside the C frames that call a stream's `get_next()`.
- Worker threads are pull request 15, which needs the text of the warning without calling R, as #800 has it in c7327bec.
- Row numbers beyond 2^31 are not tested end to end: the base counts rows in a 32-bit `int` and has no hook to set the count (#858 adds both). The logs take row numbers as `int64_t`, computed in 64 bits from the count, and R formats them as doubles; the test formats numbers beyond 2^31 directly.

Tested:

- New `tests/testthat/test-arrow-coercion.R` with a snapshot of the message (`_snaps/arrow-coercion.md`): several columns with several groups at once, and the `coercions` field; one block per kind of conversion: reals truncated and values beyond `int64`, text beyond `int64` that a later real in the chunk turns into a converted real, the null type, text, blobs and numbers converted between `utf8`, `binary` and `double` with invalid UTF-8 and a NUL byte, and unparsable and out-of-range dates, times and timestamps; 30 values (the list shortened) and rows 100000 and 123456 in full, with numbers beyond 2^31 formatted directly; row numbers in later chunks and after a `dbFetch()` in between; `options(warn = 2)`: the error, `dbGetRowCount()`, `dbHasCompleted()` and `dbFetch()` meanwhile, the kept chunk handed out by the next fetch and the rest after it; a calling handler that muffles, which gets the chunk and sees the result busy; a handler that clears the result, refused by the guard, with the chunk kept; a new bind dropping a kept chunk; a step error after a converted value, not reported by the next fetch; and no warning when nothing is converted: widening within a chunk, integers in a `double` column, `NULL`, all-`NULL` columns and dates as numbers and text, in one chunk and in chunks of one row.
- `tests/testthat/helper-arrow.R`: `fetch_arrow_chunk()` and `fetch_arrow_all()` take `converted = TRUE` to expect the warning, and `expect_same_chunks()` lets it through where it already allows `dbFetch()`'s warnings (`mixed = TRUE`, `unparsable = TRUE`); `warnings_of()` and `expect_coercions()` collect and check the warnings. The fetches in `test-arrow-columns.R`, `test-arrow-text.R` and `test-arrow-dates.R` that convert values now expect the warning; their values are unchanged.

title: feat: Build Arrow date, time and timestamp arrays with `extended_types`
description:
Sixth step of the Arrow rework (plan: https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193): with `extended_types = TRUE`, the internal Arrow engine of #860 builds `date32`, `time64` and `timestamp` arrays from columns declared as DATE, TIME, DATETIME or TIMESTAMP. The entry point `result_fetch_arrow_chunk()` stays internal, so nothing changes for users.

Commits:

1. **refactor: Split the date and time parsers from their warnings.** `SqliteColumnDataSource` gets the static `parse_date()`, `parse_time()` and `parse_datetime_local()`, which parse the text of these columns into whole days or microseconds and return whether they could, instead of warning. `fetch_date()`, `fetch_time()` and `fetch_datetime_local()` call them, scale the result as before (`static_cast<double>(days)` and `micros * 1e-6`) and raise the same warnings for text they can't parse and for blobs. #800 (ef68461a) split the same functions into members that read the current value and return seconds; parsing text into integers instead lets the Arrow path keep every microsecond, so it needs no second copy of the boost calls, as the old stack's `parse_micros()` had (2e62edec in #801).
2. **feat: Build Arrow date, time and timestamp arrays with `extended_types`.** The Arrow handling of #795 (43db19f5) with its refinements up to 34363581, read from the type rules at the top of `34363581:src/SqliteArrowColumn.h`.
3. Merges of #860 at 3ac16c66 and at 32dea06a, whose conflicts were adjacent additions; a merge of the CI's auto-update (2e3606eb), keeping its formatting of `src/SqliteResultImpl.cpp`, and a commit that restores the `.dd` files it filled with absolute paths (#836).
4. **fix: Fail date and time chunks on out of memory, and round seconds exactly**, from the review of 229c74a8.
5. **fix: Round real seconds to the nearest microsecond of their double**, from the review of cfba409c.

What changes:

- With `extended_types = TRUE`, a column declared as DATE, TIME, DATETIME or TIMESTAMP is `date32`, `time64[us]` or `timestamp[us, UTC]` from the start, whatever its values, as the data-frame path reads it as `Date`, `hms` or `POSIXct` in UTC. The declared types match through `datatype_from_decltype()` of the data-frame path, made public for this, so both paths agree on names such as `datetime` (they match the whole name, case-insensitive: `DATETIME(6)` is not one). A column of only `NULL` takes these types too, also in a result of no rows. Expressions and other declared types follow the value-based rules of #860.
- Values are read as the data-frame path reads them:
  - Text goes through the parsers of the first commit, read as UTF-8 with #860's `value_text()`: a conversion that runs out of memory fails the chunk at once, as for the other columns, instead of becoming `NULL`.
  - A number in a DATE column is a count of days since 1970-01-01, truncated toward zero; in a TIME or TIMESTAMP column it is seconds, since midnight or since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, rounded to the nearest microsecond. A Julian day is such a count too, as for `dbFetch()`.
  - A real number of seconds becomes the microsecond nearest to what its double holds, which `dbFetch()` keeps, as CPython's `datetime.fromtimestamp()` rounds it: `std::modf()` splits it into whole seconds and their fraction, both exact, and only the fraction is rounded, with `std::nearbyint()`, halves to even in the default rounding mode, which R keeps. Rounding the seconds times 1e6 rounds twice, since the product is rounded to a double first, a multiple of 1/4 µs for present-day timestamps: #795's `std::floor(x * 1e6 + 0.5)` and `std::nearbyint(x * 1e6)` (cfba409c) missed the nearest microsecond of about one present-day timestamp in eight (`1759618878.0778434` gave …844 where the double holds …843.43), and the former also rounded an odd count between 2^52 and 2^53 one up (`5000000000.000001` gave …002). `std::llround()` would round halves away from zero, and is unspecified for an infinity or a value beyond 64 bits. The whole seconds are range-checked before their cast, and the sum stays within the int64 microseconds but their smallest value, which bit64 reads as `NA`, as for an integer: a real of -9223372036854.775808 s gave exactly -2^63 µs at cfba409c. The tests pin three present-day timestamps that the product missed, the 2^52 example and its negative, the exact halves 0.0078125 s and 0.0234375 s (7812 and 23438 µs), and the double nearest to -2^63 µs (…775391 µs) with the next one down (`NULL`).
  - An integer number of seconds is scaled exactly, and text keeps all its microseconds, also beyond the 2^53 that a double holds (2e62edec).
- `NULL` takes the place of a blob and of text that can't be parsed, where `dbFetch()` warns and returns `NA`, and of values beyond the range of the Arrow type:
  - a count of days beyond 32 bits, which `dbFetch()` reads with `sqlite3_column_int()` and wraps; here it is read in full (b99d1104);
  - a huge or infinite real in a DATE column, which `sqlite3_column_int()` saturates at 64 bits before keeping the low 32: `dbFetch()` reads `1e300` and `9e999` as 1969-12-31 and `-9e999` as 1970-01-01, without a warning;
  - a number of seconds beyond the range of int64 microseconds, -2^63 µs included, or an infinity (fc0d6d86);
  - a time outside `[00:00:00, 24:00:00)`, such as `86400`, `-1` or `'25:00:00'`, which `time64` can't hold and Arrow's full validation rejects; `dbFetch()` keeps such durations as `hms`. Rounding a number just below midnight stops at the last microsecond of the day (ca06a58a).
- None of these conversions is reported yet, as #859 and #860 keep theirs silent until pull request 7.
- Without `extended_types`, these columns follow the value-based rules as before: text is `utf8`, numbers `int64` or `double`, and a column of only `NULL` takes the `double` of NUMERIC affinity.

The data-frame path is unchanged. New tests in `test-extendedTypes.R` pin its exact values, the order and text of its warnings, and that a warning made an error completes the result; they pass on #860 and after each commit. Two of the pinned values, the time and the timestamp of the last row, differ between `micros * 1e-6` and `micros / 1e6`, so the pin catches a change of the formula (checked by mutation).

The shared parser has quirks that this pull request keeps on both paths, and the tests pin them, since the Arrow arrays must read what `dbFetch()` reads: it knows no `T` between date and time, no `Z`, no `+02:00` and no ` UTC` (all `NA` or `NULL`); a timestamp needs a time; a date ignores anything after a space that follows the day; years run from 1400 to 9999. It also misreads a negative UTC offset, without a warning, on `main` today and so on both paths here: boost's tokenizer splits on `-` and takes the fields after the seconds for the fraction of a second. `'2024-01-02 12:00:00-02:00'` reads as 12:00:00.02 (`-05:30` and `-0500` as .05 s), `'2024-01-02 12:00-02:00'` as 12:00:02, and after a fraction (`'2024-01-02 12:00:00.5-02:00'`) the offset is dropped; TIME columns read `'12:00:00-02:00'` the same way. The instant is off by the whole offset. The tests pin the first shape in both `test-extendedTypes.R` and `test-arrow-dates.R` as behavior shared with `dbFetch()`; fixing the shared parser, for both paths at once, is left to a separate pull request.

Deliberately left out:

- Reporting converted and `NULL` values once per chunk with their rows is pull request 7.
- Requested types, such as `date64`, `time32` or other units and time zones, are pull requests 13 and 14.
- The Arrow data-frame path, which builds times and timestamps as doubles in seconds to keep the default path's precision and range, is pull request 19.
- Byte limits are pull request 8, the DBI methods pull request 16.

Tested:

- New `tests/testthat/test-arrow-dates.R`: each declared type with ISO text, month names, numbers (days, Unix seconds, reals, Julian days), fractional seconds from one to nine digits, time zones and offsets in timestamps under a session time zone that is not UTC, dates and timestamps from 1400 to 9999 with 1969, 1900 and 2038 around them, values beyond the range of each Arrow type and infinities, blobs and text that can't be parsed (invalid month and day, empty text, a year before 1400, a timestamp without a time), `NULL` and all-`NULL` columns, a result of no rows, text, numbers, blobs and `NULL` mixed in one column fetched in chunks of all rows, of 1 row up to one past the end, and of 2, 3 and 4 rows, a rebound statement, declared names in other cases and with a size, aliases and expressions, a UTF-16 database, and `extended_types = FALSE`. Where the rules agree, each chunk is compared with `dbFetch()` on the same connection in the same chunk sizes, with the values converted to the same instants, and with `dbHasCompleted()` and `dbGetRowCount()` after each chunk; exact microseconds are compared as `integer64`.
- A callr test runs out of memory while the text of a DATE, TIME and TIMESTAMP column is converted to UTF-8 (generated columns whose 20 million characters are computed as they are read, in a UTF-16 database) and expects the chunk to fail at once, as #860's test does for the other columns; `fetch_arrow_chunk_out_of_memory()` takes setup statements and `extended_types` for it. It passes against an installed build and fails without `value_text()`; under `load_all()` it skips, as #860's does, since the callr session loads another RSQLite.
- `tests/testthat/helper-arrow.R`: `arrow_values()` converts `date32`, `time64` and `timestamp` to `Date`, `hms` and `POSIXct` in UTC, `expect_same_chunks()` takes `unparsable = TRUE` where `dbFetch()` warns of values it can't convert, and the new `arrow_micros()` and `fetch_arrow_all()` read exact microseconds and fetch a whole result. Every chunk passes `expect_valid_chunk()`, nanoarrow's full validation.
- By hand, arrow 26.0.1's `ValidateFull()` accepts all 29 chunks that `test-arrow-dates.R` builds under `load_all()`, and all 124 chunks of the three Arrow test files (arrow is not a test dependency here). It rejects a `time64` of 24:00:00, which nanoarrow's validation accepts, so the range of `time64` is checked explicitly in the tests.
- Mutations: without the range check of `time64`, without the stop at the last microsecond of the day, with either former rounding, or reading days with `sqlite3_column_int()`, one or two blocks fail; without `extended_types` reaching the Arrow column, all blocks but the one with `extended_types = FALSE` and the callr one fail.
- Each `test_that()` block of `test-arrow-dates.R`, `test-arrow-columns.R`, `test-arrow-text.R` and `test-extendedTypes.R` passes on its own in a fresh session right after `pkgload::load_all()`.
- At 229c74a8, `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true`: no failures beyond the three errors in `test-httpvfs.R` that also happen on `main` (#832, #837).
- At 229c74a8, under AddressSanitizer (gcc, `-O1`), `test-arrow-dates.R`, `test-extendedTypes.R`, `test-arrow-columns.R`, `test-arrow-text.R`, `test-read-ahead.R`, `test-dbSendQuery.R`, `test-dbClearResult.R`, `test-error.R` and `test-dbBind.R` pass without a report, and so does a script with chunks of several sizes over dates, times and timestamps from text, numbers, blobs, infinities and values out of range, rebinding, and arrays converted after their result was cleared and the connection closed, also under `gctorture(TRUE)`.
- At 229c74a8, `R CMD check --no-manual --no-tests --ignore-vignettes` on a built tarball: `Status: OK`. `src/SqliteArrowColumn.dd` gains the three package headers it now includes, written by hand, since the build adds absolute system paths to it (#836).

Timing at 229c74a8, one million rows in one chunk from a file database, median of nine runs, three rounds with the same result, on an `-O2` build:

- Timestamps as text (`2023-11-14 22:13:57.123`): 0.70 s for the Arrow chunk, 0.94 s for `dbFetch()`.
- Timestamps as reals: 0.09 s for the Arrow chunk, 0.30 s for `dbFetch()`.
- Dates as text: 0.35 s against 0.59 s; times as text with six fractional digits: 0.44 s against 0.74 s.
- `dbFetch()` takes the same time as on #860 within 1 to 3 %, which is the spread between rounds. The Arrow chunk of text takes 0.11 s on #860, where it stays `utf8`: the boost parser is most of the cost on both paths.

Sits on #860, which is on #859, #857, #856, #855, #830 and #850, and merges #845.

title: feat: Build Arrow arrays from text and blob columns
description:
Fifth step of the Arrow rework (plan: https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193): the internal Arrow engine of #859 now builds arrays from text and blob columns. The entry point `result_fetch_arrow_chunk()` stays internal, so nothing changes for users.

This branch merges `claude/utf8-infra` (#845) with a merge commit, for its validator `rsqlite_is_utf8_string()`. Until #845 lands, its changes show in this diff: `src/utf8.cpp`, `src/utf8.h`, `src/utf8.dd`, the registration of `utf8_valid()`, `tests/testthat/helper-utf8.R` and `tests/testthat/test-utf8.R`. The change of this pull request is in the three commits that aren't merges: the feature, and the fixes of its two reviews. A second merge commit brings in the current head of #859.

What changes:

- `SqliteArrowColumn` types a column whose first value that is not `NULL` is text as `utf8`, and one whose first such value is a blob as `binary`. A column whose values in the first chunk are all `NULL` takes the type of its declared affinity, now also `utf8` for TEXT (`TEXT`, `CHAR(n)`, `CLOB`, ...) and `binary` for BLOB, as the data-frame path maps them. This replaces the error "Arrow arrays of text and blobs are not supported yet." of #859, and its test.
- Values that don't fit the type of their column follow #795 at 43db19f5 with its refinements up to 34363581 (e273dfbf, 2521ae0c, b85c0e72, 22c4927b):
  - Numbers in a `utf8` or `binary` column are the text SQLite renders, as the data-frame path reads them.
  - Text in a `binary` column is its UTF-8 bytes, also in a UTF-16 database, as the data-frame path reads it.
  - A blob in a `utf8` column keeps its bytes, which must be valid UTF-8. `sqlite3_column_text()` would take them for text in the encoding of the database and transcode them in a UTF-16 one.
  - Text and blobs in an `int64` or `double` column are read as SQLite reads them: the leading integer, or the leading real. Where SQLite would saturate the leading integer of text or a blob, the value is `NULL`, as #859 already does for a real beyond the range of int64 (22c4927b). To tell a saturated integer from 2^63 - 1, the column reads the digits as SQLite does, as text in the encoding of the database: unlike #795, which read the raw bytes of a blob, this sees the digits of a blob in a UTF-16 database, where SQLite reads them as UTF-16.
  - In the chunk that decides the types, text and blobs that an `int64` column has read as integers take the readings as reals they would have in a `double` column when a real widens the column later in that chunk, so `1, '2.5', 3.5` gives `1, 2.5, 3.5` in any order of the rows. #795 kept the integer reading (`2`), and `NULL` for a saturating integer, so the values depended on the order of the rows. Once the first chunk has fixed the type, text in an `int64` column keeps its integer reading. While the type is open, the column keeps the reading as a real of each such value that differs from its integer reading, 16 bytes each, and releases them once the first chunk fixes the type. For one integer followed by 5 million text values in one chunk, words such as `'abc1'` keep nothing (peak +40 MB, as without this rule) and values such as `'1.5'` keep 80 MB (peak +164 MB). Reading every such value as a real also takes time: for 2 million words, the chunk takes 0.21 s instead of 0.15 s.
  - Text and blobs in a `utf8` column that are not valid UTF-8 are `NULL`: SQLite doesn't enforce UTF-8 for text, and a blob keeps any bytes. Arrow requires valid UTF-8 in `utf8` arrays, and its full validation rejects a chunk that holds anything else.
  - Any value in a column of the null type stays `NULL`, as in #859.
- A value whose conversion runs out of memory fails the fetch at once, which completes the result like any other error. SQLite reports such a conversion as a `NULL` pointer from `sqlite3_column_text()` or `sqlite3_column_blob()` and fails only the next step, but after a full chunk that step only reads ahead, and keeps its error for the next fetch: the chunk would come back with an empty string, a `NULL` or a zero in place of the value. The size of a blob is read before `sqlite3_column_blob()`, which tells a `zeroblob()` that can't expand from a blob of no bytes, and text read into a `double` column is read as UTF-8 text first, so that `sqlite3_column_double()` has nothing left to allocate. A blob read into a `double` or open `int64` column is read with `sqlite3_column_double()` alone, so that a `zeroblob()` isn't expanded just to read 0; SQLite reports running out of memory while copying a blob for that reading only through the error code of the connection, which is compared with its value before the call, as a code left from an earlier call can't be told apart (the next step then fails, as before).
- Text is checked with #845's `rsqlite_is_utf8_string()` itself. #795's `is_utf8_text()` wrapper is not carried over, since the validator has its own ASCII fast path.
- Text with an embedded NUL byte is `NULL` in a `utf8` column, and keeps all its bytes in a `binary` column. This is #795's rule, and it is what the validator implements, so the two don't conflict. Arrow itself allows NUL in `utf8`, but R strings can't hold it: nanoarrow fails when a converted string with a NUL is used, and arrow refuses to convert it unless `arrow.skip_nul` is set. Ending the text at the first NUL, as the data-frame path does, would change the value without a trace, while `NULL` treats a NUL like the other bytes that are not text.

None of these conversions is reported yet. The task left the choice between #795's simpler warning and saying what I chose: I kept them silent, as #859 keeps its own conversions (a real in a fixed int64 column, a value in a column of the null type) silent until pull request 7. One rule then holds for every conversion of a column, and pull request 7 adds the report for all of them at once instead of replacing a warning that only some of them raise. #795's warning is raised once per column from inside the fetch loop, where its handlers run while the busy guard holds the result; it is about 30 lines if reviewers prefer it in the meantime.

Where the values differ from `dbFetch()`:

- Text that is not valid UTF-8 is `NULL`, where `dbFetch()` passes it through; the tests pin both.
- Text with a NUL byte is `NULL`, where `dbFetch()` ends it at the first NUL; the tests pin both.
- In a UTF-16 database, a blob in a text column is its bytes, where `dbFetch()` transcodes them from UTF-16 on this base. The tests pin only the Arrow value, since #799 reads such blobs as bytes on the data-frame path too.
- Later chunks keep the types of the first chunk, as in #859, where `dbFetch()` types each fetch anew.
- Text read into a column of integers: `dbFetch()` keeps the integer reading after a real widens the column (`'2.5'` gives `2`), and gives `-1` or `0` for a saturating integer in a 32-bit column.

Deliberately left out:

- Reporting conversions once per chunk with their rows is pull request 7.
- Byte limits for the 32-bit offsets of `utf8` and `binary` arrays are pull request 8. Until then, a chunk whose values in one column exceed 2^31 - 1 bytes fails with "Can't append to Arrow array", which completes the result like any other error of a fetch.
- Dates, times and timestamps are pull request 6, requested types such as `large_utf8` are pull requests 13 and 14, and the DBI methods are pull request 16.
- The data-frame path is unchanged.

Tested:

- New `tests/testthat/test-arrow-text.R`: text and blob columns with empty strings, empty blobs and `NULL` among them; numbers and blobs in a `utf8` column and text and numbers in a `binary` one; text and blobs in `int64` and `double` columns, with the saturating cases; mixed types within the first chunk and converted in a later chunk, also into columns typed by TEXT and BLOB affinity and into the null type; text that is not valid UTF-8 (cast from blobs: a stray continuation byte, a truncated sequence, an overlong form, a surrogate, beyond U+10FFFF, an invalid byte between runs of 20 ASCII bytes, and a sequence truncated after them), in `utf8` and in `binary` columns; embedded NUL bytes at the start, middle and end; values up to 2 MB; chunks of 1, 2, 3 + 4 and all rows up to one past the end, with the read-ahead row starting the next chunk; a UTF-16 database with non-ASCII text, a blob in a text column, a lone surrogate at the end of the text, which makes it `NULL`, and one before another character, which SQLite merges into one code point (`x'780000d86100'` becomes `"x\U00010061"`, the same in `dbFetch()`), and a NUL character; the digits of blobs in a UTF-16 database read into an `int64` column, in the chunk that decides the type and in a later one; whitespace and a sign before saturating integers; text in an `int64` column that a real widens, in three orders of the rows; and values that run out of memory as the last row of a full chunk, in `utf8`, `int64`, `double` and `binary` columns and as a blob in a `double` column, and a `zeroblob()` in a `double` column that reads as 0 under a heap limit below its size. Where the rules agree, each chunk is compared with `dbFetch()` in the same chunk sizes, with `dbHasCompleted()` and `dbGetRowCount()` after each chunk.

title: build: Vendor the nanoarrow C library
description:
Third step of the Arrow rework (plan: https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193): vendor the nanoarrow C library and compile it into the package, with nothing calling it yet. Landing the build change alone is meant to prove that the C sources compile and link on every CI platform before any code depends on them; the full CI matrix (Windows and macOS included) will be run on this branch before merging.

What changes:

- `src/vendor/nanoarrow/` holds `nanoarrow.c`, `nanoarrow.h` and `nanoarrow.hpp` of nanoarrow 0.9.0 (the current CRAN release), plus `LICENSE.txt`, `NOTICE.txt` and a `README.md` that records the origin, the delta and how to update. The three sources are byte-identical to `src/` of the nanoarrow 0.9.0 CRAN tarball except for one line, `#define NANOARROW_NAMESPACE RSQLite` (upstream `RPkg`), which prefixes every exported symbol so that it cannot collide with the nanoarrow package's own copy or the one in arrow. `LICENSE.txt` and `NOTICE.txt` match the release tag `apache-arrow-nanoarrow-0.9.0`.
- `src/Makevars` defines `NANOARROW_DLL` empty so that the symbols are not exported from the shared object, makes the object depend on `nanoarrow.h`, and links `vendor/nanoarrow/nanoarrow.o` next to `vendor/sqlite3/sqlite3.o`, the same way (there is no `src/Makevars.win`, so Windows uses the same file).
- `cleanup`, `cleanup.ucrt`, `cleanup.win` and `.Rbuildignore` also remove and ignore the nanoarrow object file, so that it does not end up in the source tarball.
- `inst/COPYRIGHTS` and `inst/licenses/` install the Apache-2.0 licence and the NOTICE with the package (so that binaries carry them) and list the terms of the other bundled code as far as the sources state them; `DESCRIPTION` has `Copyright: See file COPYRIGHTS.`, and lists the Apache Software Foundation as copyright holder (`cph`) for the included nanoarrow sources.

Deliberately left out:

- nanoarrow is not added to `Imports` or `LinkingTo`: nothing uses its R-side helpers (`nanoarrow/r.h`) yet, and those come in with the first code that needs them.
- A new `.covrignore` keeps `src/vendor/nanoarrow/` out of the coverage report, so that the unused library does not lower the project number on Codecov; the bundled SQLite is left as it was.
- No `.dd` file for the vendored object: `src/Makevars.deps` only includes the `.dd` files of the package's own objects, and the existing `src/vendor/sqlite3/sqlite3.dd` is not read by anything.

Tested:

title: feat: Build Arrow arrays from the integer, real and NULL columns of a result
description:
Fourth step of the Arrow rework (plan: https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193), and the first piece of the internal Arrow engine: fetch up to `n` rows of a result into a nanoarrow struct array, for columns whose values are integers, reals or `NULL`. The entry point is internal; no DBI method calls it until pull request 16 of the plan, so nothing changes for users.

What changes:

- `result_fetch_arrow_chunk(res, n)`, registered through cpp11 and not exported, returns a `nanoarrow_array` of a struct type, with its schema in the tag of the external pointer as the nanoarrow package expects. It holds at most `n` rows, or all remaining rows for `n = -1`. Other values are refused: a chunk of no rows would have to fix the column types without seeing a value. The fetch runs under the busy guard of #830, like `dbFetch()`, and fails like it for an inactive or unbound result.
- The first commit is a refactor without change of behavior: the loop of `fetch_rows()` moves into the member template `fetch_loop()`, which takes the rows to fill and a function that completes them. Data-frame fetches and Arrow fetches both run through it, so the Arrow fetch has #850's one-row read-ahead (the row stepped past the last row of a full chunk is the first row of the next chunk, and a chunk that returns the last row completes the result and releases its read lock), #830's error semantics (an error of that step is kept and raised by the next fetch, and any error that leaves the fetch, including one from building the arrays, completes the result), and `dbGetRowCount()` counting rows once they are returned.
- `SqliteArrowColumn` builds the child array of one column. The type comes from the first value that is not `NULL`: int64 for an integer, double for a real. An int64 column widens to double when a real arrives later in the same chunk, as the default path widens integers. A column whose values in the first chunk are all `NULL` takes the type of its declared affinity: int64 for `INTEGER`, double for `REAL` and `NUMERIC` (which includes unknown declared types), and the null type without a declared type, as for an expression. The first chunk of an execution fixes the types for its later chunks: there, a real in an int64 column is truncated toward zero, or `NULL` beyond the range of int64 where SQLite would saturate, and a value in a column of the null type is `NULL`. A new `dbBind()` starts a new execution, whose first chunk decides again.
- `DbArrow.h` holds `check_arrow()`, which turns a nanoarrow error code into a C++ exception, so that the arrays under construction are released on every error. `SqliteResultImpl.h` only declares the Arrow types, so that the nanoarrow headers are compiled only where arrays are built (`SqliteArrowColumn.cpp`, `SqliteResultImpl.cpp`, `result.cpp`).
- `DESCRIPTION` adds `nanoarrow (>= 0.4.0)` to `LinkingTo`, for the header-only helpers of `nanoarrow/r.h` that create the external pointers with the class and the finalizer the nanoarrow package expects, and to `Suggests`, for the tests. 0.4.0 is the first version that ships `r.h`; 0.3.0.1 has only `r_nanoarrow.h`. Nothing more is needed from it: looking into the returned array from R needs the nanoarrow package loaded, which the tests do through `nanoarrow::`. Through `LinkingTo`, nanoarrow is now needed to build the package.

`DbArrow.h` and `SqliteArrowColumn.*` come from #795 at 43db19f5 with its refinements up to 34363581, cut down to int64, double and the null type. The data-frame mode, `ArrowTarget`, `CoercionLog`, the byte limits, `ProgressValue` and the `SqliteColumnDataSource` member are left out, and so is the split of `read_row()` from `append_row()` that only the byte limits need. The truncation of a real in a fixed int64 column follows `integer_value()` of 34363581. The struct array is assembled in the shared fetch loop instead of a loop of its own.

Mixing data-frame and Arrow fetches on one result stays undecided (https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830183898), and the entry point neither refuses nor supports it on purpose. What happens today: each fetch continues at the next row of the result, whichever kind came before, so no row is lost or read twice, and `dbHasCompleted()` and `dbGetRowCount()` follow both. Each path types its columns on its own: the first Arrow chunk of an execution fixes the Arrow types, `dbFetch()` keeps its types as before, and neither sees the other's. Nothing is handed from one path to the other, because nothing reads ahead by more than the one row that both share; the question becomes concrete with the byte cut (pull request 8) and the schema read-ahead of streams (pull request 9).

Where the values differ from `dbFetch()`: integers are int64, which nanoarrow converts to double unless asked for `integer64`; a column without declared type and only `NULL` values is of the null type rather than logical; later chunks keep the types of the first one, where `dbFetch()` widens integers again in a later fetch; and an int64 column that holds a value beyond 2^31 widens to double when a real arrives, where `dbFetch()` keeps `integer64` and truncates the real with a warning. The tests pin each of these.

Deliberately left out:

- Text and blobs come in pull request 5. Until then, a text or blob value fails the fetch with "Column `x`: Arrow arrays of text and blobs are not supported yet.", which completes the result like any other error. So does a column of `NULL` values declared as `TEXT` or `BLOB`, which would otherwise need a type that pull request 5 changes.
- `extended_types` is not consulted until pull request 6: a `DATE`, `TIME` or `TIMESTAMP` column comes through as the numbers it stores, as double if it holds only `NULL` (by its `NUMERIC` affinity), and text dates fail as text.
- The conversions in later chunks are silent until pull request 7 reports them once per chunk with their rows.
- Byte limits (pull request 8), streams (pull request 9), requested types (pull requests 13 and 14) and the DBI methods (pull request 16) come later. The row count stays 32-bit, as on `main`; counting in 64 bits is a separate pull request.

Tested:

- New `tests/testthat/test-arrow-columns.R` with fixtures in `tests/testthat/helper-arrow.R`: integer, real and `NULL` columns; the first-value rule; widening within a chunk, also from beyond 2^53; the types fixed by the first chunk; the affinity of all-`NULL` columns (`INTEGER`, `REAL`, `NUMERIC`, none, and an expression); int64 values beyond 2^53 and up to 2^63 - 1 kept exactly; chunks of 1, k and all rows up to past the end, and a chunk ending on the last row releasing the read lock for a writer on another connection; an empty result and a statement without columns; a step error (`json()` on invalid JSON, as in #850's tests) after the rows of a chunk and among them; a busy handler that runs during the step past the last row of a chunk and can neither clear the result nor fetch from it; text and blob values and declared types failing the fetch and completing the result; a new execution deciding its types again; an unbound query and invalid `n`. Where the rules agree, a helper fetches the same query with `dbFetch()` in the same chunk sizes and compares the values, `dbHasCompleted()` and `dbGetRowCount()` after each chunk.
- Each `test_that()` block passes on its own in a fresh session right after `pkgload::load_all()`.
- `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true`: no failures beyond the three errors in `test-httpvfs.R` that also happen on `main` (#832, #837). The refactor commit alone passes `test-read-ahead.R`, `test-dbSendQuery.R`, `test-dbClearResult.R`, `test-error.R`, `test-dbBind.R` and `test-basic-types.R`.
- Under AddressSanitizer (gcc, `-O1`), the new tests and `test-read-ahead.R`, `test-dbSendQuery.R`, `test-dbClearResult.R`, `test-error.R` and `test-dbBind.R` pass without a report, and so does a script with chunks of several sizes, widening, a text error, rebinding, and arrays converted after their result was cleared and the connection closed, also under `gctorture(TRUE)`.
- The code compiles against the `r.h` of nanoarrow 0.4.0, and the Arrow tests pass with nanoarrow 0.4.0 installed as well as with 0.9.0.
- arrow 26.0.1's `ValidateFull()` accepts chunks with int64, double and null columns (checked by hand; arrow is not a test dependency here).
- `R CMD check --no-manual`: Status OK.

title: refactor: Own results through a shared pointer, as connections are
description:
This is the second pull request of the reworked Arrow stack, as planned in https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193. The external pointer of a result now owns a `DbResultPtr`, a `boost::shared_ptr<DbResult>`, the way the external pointer of a connection owns a `DbConnectionPtr`. This lets a later pull request give an Arrow stream a share of the result, so that the stream can outlive `dbClearResult()`. Nothing changes in behavior or messages.

## What changes

- `DbResult.h` declares `DbResultPtr` next to `DbConnectionPtr`, and makes `~DbResult()` virtual. The shared pointer is built from the `DbResult*` that `create_and_send_query()` returns, so it deletes the `SqliteResult` through a pointer to its base, as cpp11's deleter did before. That was undefined behavior on the base too, harmless only because `SqliteResult` has no members of its own. A virtual destructor is the smallest fix (one line), and it covers any later owner of a `DbResultPtr`, such as the Arrow stream, not just `result_create()`. Its cost is one vtable pointer per result.
- `result_create()` wraps the new result in a `DbResultPtr` and returns an external pointer to it, as `connection_connect()` does with a `DbConnectionPtr`. `result_release()`, behind `dbClearResult()`, and cpp11's finalizer delete that `DbResultPtr`, which drops R's share of the result.
- The `as_cpp()` specialisations for `DbResult*` and `SqliteResult*` in `RSQLite_types.h` read the `DbResultPtr` and return the result it points to. So the entry points that take a `DbResult*` or a `SqliteResult*` are unchanged. `result_valid()` and `result_release()`, including #830's busy guard, look through the shared pointer.
- `src/cpp11.cpp` is regenerated for the new types of the three entry points.

## What a reviewer may want to check

- **When a result is freed.** R's share is the only one, so the result, with its statement and its share of the connection, is freed at the same moments as before: by `dbClearResult()`, or by the finalizer of a result that was never cleared. The finalizer of a cleared result finds the external pointer cleared and does nothing, as before. The "results in use" warning of `dbDisconnect()` counts the shares of the connection, and each result still holds one.
- **Empty shared pointers.** `as_cpp()`, `result_valid()` and `result_release()` also check that the shared pointer is not empty, as #795 does. It never is, because `create_and_send_query()` throws instead of returning `NULL`, so these checks change nothing today.
- **The reference.** This takes only the ownership change from #795 (43db19f5): its `RSQLite_types.h`, and its `result_create()`, `result_release()` and `result_valid()` without the Arrow calls around them. #795 keeps the non-virtual destructor.

## Left out

The second owner of a result, an Arrow stream that keeps it after `dbClearResult()` and `dbDisconnect()`, comes in pull request 10 of the plan. The thread-aware busy mark and the deferred release of results let go on other threads, which #795 adds for streams read by arrow's scanner, come in pull request 15. Everything else Arrow comes later too.

## Tests

Six new tests in `test-dbClearResult.R` cover `dbIsValid()` before and after `dbClearResult()` and a second `dbClearResult()` with its warning. They pin the exact error of every use of a cleared result, through both `as_cpp()` specialisations. They also cover a result cleared when the next query is sent, a result collected by `gc()` without being cleared (the connection still runs queries and disconnects without the "results in use" warning), and the exact warning of `dbDisconnect()` with results in use, after which the result still fetches and clears. In that test, the last result holds a read lock on a database file after the disconnect, and a write from a second connection fails until `gc()` collects the result, so the test fails if the finalizer doesn't free a result after `dbDisconnect()`. The last test has a handler that catches the busy guard's error, after which the result is cleared normally. The tests pass on #855 (7387832e and c352631f) and on this branch, and each `test_that()` block passes on its own after `pkgload::load_all()`. `devtools::test()` passes except for the three errors in `test-httpvfs.R` that `main` has as well (#832, #837).

title: fix: Count rows in 64 bits, so that `dbGetRowCount()` and `dbGetRowsAffected()` stay right beyond `INT_MAX`
description:
`dbGetRowCount()` counted the rows fetched from a result in an `int`, incremented once per row. A result read in chunks, such as `dbFetch(res, n = 1e6)` in a loop, can pass `INT_MAX` rows in total, for example a recursive CTE that generates its rows without storing them. The signed increment then overflowed, which is undefined behavior; in practice `dbGetRowCount()` returned `NA` at 2^31 rows and negative counts after that.

`dbGetRowsAffected()`, and with it `dbExecute()`, had the same problem: it subtracted two values of `sqlite3_total_changes()`, which SQLite truncates to an `int`, so that the count turned negative once the changes since one `dbBind()` or `dbExecute()`, summed over all its parameter rows, passed `INT_MAX`. Where a connection's total of changes passes `INT_MAX`, the subtraction itself also overflowed, even for a statement that changes a few rows, although in practice the wrapped result came out right there.

Both counts are now `int64_t`, and the changes come from `sqlite3_total_changes64()`, which the bundled SQLite 3.54.1 has. `dbGetRowCount()` and `dbGetRowsAffected()` return an integer while the count fits, as before, and a double beyond `INT_MAX`, the only R type without bit64 that holds the count exactly up to 2^53. `dbGetRowsAffected()` still returns an integer `NA` before `dbBind()`.

The fix of the fetched rows is the one the old Arrow stack carries in 1914d202 (#795), without the Arrow parts around it, and it moves out of item 8 of the [plan to rework the Arrow stack](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193), which keeps the end of Arrow chunks before string offsets overflow. The fix of the changed rows is new: the old stack keeps the `int` there.

### Tests

`tests/testthat/test-row-count.R`, with every `test_that()` block self-contained:

- Two tests set the counts just below `INT_MAX` through two unexported entry points for the tests, `result_set_rows_fetched()` and `result_set_rows_affected()`, then fetch real rows across the limit and check the exact values on both sides: an integer up to `INT_MAX`, a double beyond. The changed rows go across the limit for real through an `INSERT ... RETURNING`, whose changes SQLite counts once its last row is fetched. The hook moves the start of the count, not SQLite's total of changes, so that only the gated test below catches a return to the 32-bit `sqlite3_total_changes()`. Both hooks stop with an error unless the count is a whole number from 0 to 2^53. On `main`, both fail, as the entry points do not exist there.
- Two tests reach the limit for real and are skipped unless `RSQLITE_TEST_INT_MAX_ROWS=true`, with the variable's name in the skip message. One fetches 2^31 + 1 rows of a recursive CTE in chunks of 10^6 rows, which took 608 s here on a machine busy with other jobs (a run of 10^7 rows suggests about six minutes when idle); on `main`, `dbGetRowCount()` returns `NA` at 2^31 rows and -2147483647 one row later. The other runs `UPDATE` on a table of 2^20 rows with 2^11 + 1 parameter rows, 2^31 + 2^20 changes in one `dbExecute()`, which took 107 s here; on `main`, `dbExecute()` returns -2146435072.

`devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true` passes, apart from the three errors in `test-httpvfs.R` that `main` has as well (#832, #837) and "interrupt in busy handler" in `test-dbConnect.R`, whose callr session found no installed RSQLite after `pkgload::load_all()`; #830 skips it in that case, and it passes against the installed build.

### Speed of the default path

A fetch of 5 million rows of an integer and a real column, as a whole and in chunks of 10^5 rows, median user CPU time of seven runs, three alternating runs per build: 1.16 s as a whole and 1.14 to 1.24 s in chunks on `main`, 1.15 to 1.16 s and 1.10 to 1.17 s with this pull request. The difference is within the noise.

### Where this sits

This is a separate pull request from `main`. The new Arrow stack, on #830 and #850, picks it up by merging `main` once this lands. `git merge-tree --write-tree origin/claude/fix-error-mid-result HEAD` reports conflicts in four files, in five small hunks: in each, #830 adds a line next to a declaration or a `sqlite3_total_changes()` call that this pull request changes (`busy()` next to `n_rows_fetched()` in `DbResult.cpp` and `DbResult.h`, `bind_started_` next to the counts in `SqliteResultImpl.h`, in `n_rows_affected()` and in `bind()`). Keeping both sides resolves all of them. The fetch loop that #850 and #830 rewrite merges without a conflict, as this pull request leaves the line that counts the rows alone: #830 adds an `int` count of the rows of one fetch to `nrows_`, which is now an `int64_t`. #850 alone merges without any conflict. A trial merge into #830 with these resolutions builds, and `test-row-count.R`, `test-dbSendQuery.R`, `test-read-ahead.R` and `test-dbClearResult.R` pass on it.

### For the reviewer

- The R type: `dbGetRowCount()`, `dbGetRowsAffected()` and `dbExecute()` return a double instead of an integer beyond `INT_MAX`, where they returned `NA` or a negative integer before. DBI's specification allows either type: "a scalar number (integer or numeric)". Code that checks for an integer with `is.integer()` sees the change only beyond `INT_MAX`.
- Windows, where `long` is 32 bits: the counts use `int64_t` and SQLite's `sqlite3_int64`, never `long`, and reach R through a cast to `int` or `double`, never through a format string.
- The speed of the default path, measured above: the per-row increment is now on an `int64_t`.

Reviewed in a [clean review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/858#issuecomment-6831905326), which found nothing above Low; its points are fixed in 7ca358da or listed in the [accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/858#issuecomment-6831943570).

title: fix: `dbConnect()` on a connection keeps `bigint`, `extended_types` and `check_utf8`
description:
Calling `dbConnect()` on an existing `SQLiteConnection` clones it, but the clone passed on only the database, the VFS, the flags and `loadable.extensions`, and ignored every argument given to `dbConnect(con, ...)`. It dropped `bigint` and `extended_types`, so a clone of a connection opened with `bigint = "character", extended_types = TRUE` fell back to `integer64` and to untyped dates and times. It also dropped `check_utf8`, added in #846, so a clone of a connection that checks text for valid UTF-8 did not check it.

Reproduced on `main` with a connection opened with `bigint = "character", extended_types = TRUE` on a table with a `DATE` column and the value 1099511627776:

- the original returns `d` as `Date` and `big` as `chr "1099511627776"`;
- the clone returns `d` as `chr "2020-01-02"` and `big` as `integer64`, and `clone@bigint` is `"integer64"` and `clone@extended_types` is `FALSE`.

`dbConnect_SQLiteConnection()` now has explicit formals that mirror those of `dbConnect_SQLiteDriver()`, with the connection's `dbname`, `loadable.extensions`, `flags`, `vfs`, `bigint`, `extended_types` and `check_utf8` slots as defaults, and passes every argument on to the driver method. So arguments to `dbConnect(con, ...)` are matched by name and by position as `dbConnect(SQLite(), ...)` would match them: `dbConnect(con, bigint = "integer64")`, `dbConnect(con, extended_types = FALSE)` and `dbConnect(con, check_utf8 = FALSE)` return what is asked, and `dbConnect(con, other_path)` opens `other_path`. The formals also show up in completion and in `args()`. A connection object saved by an older RSQLite, before the `bigint`, `extended_types` or `check_utf8` slots existed, lacks those slots; for it, they fall back to the driver's defaults (`"integer64"`, `FALSE`, `FALSE`) instead of failing with `no slot of name`. An argument that is `NULL` stays `NULL`, as in the driver: `synchronous = NULL` skips the pragma and `dbname = NULL` fails with the driver's error, `length(dbname) == 1 is not TRUE` (before this change, on `main`, a `NULL` `dbname` on a connection was not an error but opened a new temporary database). The error for cloning a temporary database remains, unless another `dbname` is given, and a misspelled `dbname` does not count as one. The documentation of `drv, conn` says what a clone keeps, and that a connection to a temporary database is only a template for another `dbname`: its settings carry over, its data does not. The note under `check_utf8` that a clone does not keep it is removed.

Effects beyond reads, now consistent with the parent:

- Writes: through a clone of an `extended_types = TRUE` parent, a `Date` column is created as `DATE` instead of `REAL`.
- A clone of a `bigint = "integer"` parent now returns `NA` for values beyond 32 bits, like the parent, instead of `integer64`.
- A clone of a `check_utf8 = TRUE` parent warns and returns `NA` for text that is not valid UTF-8, like the parent.

Accepted limitations, not changed here: `default.extensions`, `synchronous` and `cache_size` are not carried over (a parent opened with `synchronous = "full"` clones with `"off"`, `cache_size = 1234` becomes SQLite's default of -2000). `flags`, `vfs` and `loadable.extensions` were already kept. A wrapper that passes on a missing `dbname` now gets the driver's error.

Tests, in `tests/testthat/test-dbConnect.R`, each self-contained, thirteen new: a clone keeps `bigint` and `extended_types` and reads and types data accordingly; a clone keeps `check_utf8` unless overridden; a clone of a default connection has the defaults; `bigint` and `extended_types` arguments override the parent; a second positional argument is the database; a connection to a temporary database can be used as a template for another `dbname`; `NULL` arguments are kept (`synchronous = NULL`, and `dbname = NULL` fails with the driver's message); a misspelled `dbname` does not clone a temporary database; a temporary database cannot be cloned otherwise; the formals match those of the driver method, with the same defaults except for the ones taken from the connection; with the driver method mocked, each formal and any extra argument reaches it unchanged; and each default comes from the matching slot of the connection (`default.extensions` from `loadable.extensions`); and a connection object without the `bigint`, `extended_types` and `check_utf8` slots, as an old saved one looks, clones with the driver's defaults. Run against the base, ten of the thirteen fail and three pass (defaults, misspelled `dbname`, temporary cannot be cloned). Leaving `check_utf8` out of the forwarding call, or taking the `flags` default from elsewhere, makes the mocked tests fail. `test-dbConnect.R` passes in full (24 tests, 85 expectations, with the package installed for the `callr` test). `devtools::test()` passes except the three known errors in `test-httpvfs.R` (#832, #837) and, without an installed build, the one test that starts a `callr` session.

The pull request sits on #846, which adds `check_utf8`. `NEWS.md` is maintained by fledge, so it is not edited. The fix comes from the old Arrow stack (01946d80 in #795); the [plan to rework that stack](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193) splits it out as a separate pull request. Three review rounds ([first](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/852#issuecomment-6830616443), [second](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/852#issuecomment-6831025568), [third](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/852#issuecomment-6831551399)) led to ff7fc0b8, 43dd7e77 and 5ac4a575. The explicit formals, asked for after those rounds, had a clean review of their own at 68f541a9 that found nothing above Low; its fixes are d66dfddd (tests that every argument reaches the driver and every default comes from the connection) and 48ef91f8 (the fallback for missing slots); see the [accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/852#issuecomment-6857797320).
