title: refactor: Bind list parameters through a parameter source
description:
This is the first pull request of the reworked Arrow stack, as planned in https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193. It moves the binding of list parameters out of the result into a parameter source, so that a later pull request can add an Arrow parameter source next to it. No behavior and no message changes.

## What changes

`SqliteResultImpl` bound list parameters itself: `bind_row()` reset the statement and bound one parameter set through `bind_parameter_pos()`, while `group_` and `groups_` counted the sets. That code moves, unchanged apart from names and the type of exception it throws, into `SqliteListParamSource`, behind a small abstract `SqliteParamSource` whose one method, `bind_next_row()`, resets the statement, binds the next set, and returns whether there was one. The result keeps the source of its latest bind in a `boost::scoped_ptr` and calls it from `bind_row()`, which is all that is left of the binding in `SqliteResultImpl`. The comment of the interface says that a source must not leave by the longjmp of an R error, which would leave the result ready on a statement that was reset and only partly bound; the list source reads its vectors with R's API directly, as the result did before, which fails only for an ALTREP vector whose data pointer can't be taken.

On the R side, `db_bind()` gets `is_unnamed_placeholders()` and `match_placeholders()` from #795, for the Arrow bind to share later. Unlike #795's version, `match_placeholders()` takes the parameters rather than their names, and counts the unused ones with `seq_along(params)` as `db_bind()` did. #795 counted them with `seq_along(param_names)`, which turned "Named parameters not used in query: " into "Query does not require parameters." for an unnamed list bound to a query without placeholders. So `match_placeholders()` takes any object whose names are matched, and the Arrow bind of pull request 11 will pass, for example, the schema's named `children` rather than a vector of column names.

## What a reviewer may want to check

- **Lifetime of the R vectors.** The source holds the `cpp11::list`, which protects the vectors across the fetches that bind the later sets, as the `params_` member of the result did. A new bind, or a first set that fails, destroys the source and releases the list, as before. Values are bound with `SQLITE_TRANSIENT`, so the statement never points into R memory. A new test binds vectors that only the result refers to and calls `gc()` between fetches; the same bind also passed under `gctorture()`.
- **Errors of later sets.** The source throws a `std::runtime_error` for a value it can't bind, and `bind_row()` turns it into a `step_error` with `SQLITE_ERROR`, which is what #850's `bind_parameter_pos()` threw. So `read_ahead()` still keeps the error of a later set for the next fetch, and the fetch returns its rows. #795's list source called `cpp11::stop()` there, which bypassed `read_ahead()`. `step_error` stays private to `SqliteResultImpl.cpp`, and the interface does not depend on it.
- **The busy guard.** Only `bind()` replaces the source, and only `bind()` and the fetches use it, all under #830's guard, so a handler can't replace the source while a fetch or a bind uses it. A new test pins that a `dbBind()` from a warning handler of a fetch is refused.
- **Speed of the default path.** The virtual call happens once per parameter set, not once per value. Binding 100k rows of five columns (integer, double, character, logical and integer64) takes the same time before and after, within a millisecond, through an `INSERT` (40 ms), an `UPDATE` that changes no row (30 ms) and a `SELECT` per set that returns the rows (70 ms); 1M rows through the `UPDATE` take 0.29 to 0.30 s at best on both builds.

## Left out

The Arrow parameter source and its R entry point (pull request 11 of the plan), `executions()`, the `holds_r_objects()` method that #795's interface has for reading streams on other threads (pull request 15), and everything else Arrow.

## Tests

The first commit adds `test-dbBind.R`, which pins the messages for named, unnamed and missing parameters, including an unnamed list bound to a query without placeholders, the messages for values that can't be bound, parameter sets that return several rows, none, or that are empty, a later set that fails to bind after earlier sets wrote to the database, rebinding, bound vectors across fetches, and the refused bind from a handler. A later set that fails to bind in a fetch, which returns the earlier rows and raises from the next fetch, was already pinned in `test-read-ahead.R` and `test-dbSendQuery.R`. The new tests pass on #830's head (aa070342) as well as on this branch, and each `test_that()` block passes on its own after `pkgload::load_all()`. `devtools::test()` passes except for the three errors in `test-httpvfs.R` that `main` has as well (#832, #837). `R CMD check --no-manual` passes its tests, with one NOTE for the `.git` file that a git worktree puts in the built tarball.

## Stack

Based on #830 (`claude/fix-error-mid-result`), which is based on #850. Next in the new stack: owning results through a shared pointer, and vendoring nanoarrow.

## Review

The [clean review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/855#issuecomment-6831505878) found nothing above Low; its two points are answered by comments in c352631f. See the [accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/855#issuecomment-6855257850).

title: build: Keep system headers out of the generated `.dd` files on gcc's continuation lines
description:
The filter that turns the compiler's dependency output into the checked-in `src/*.dd` files drops system headers only from lines indented by two spaces, which is how clang writes continuation lines. gcc indents them by one space, so a build with gcc kept absolute system header paths (and `vendor/` and `..` paths) in every regenerated `.dd` file, and the CI step "Auto-update from GitHub Actions" then committed that bloat. The rule in `src/Makevars.deps` now first joins continuation lines of any indentation into one line, and the existing splitting and filtering run on the result, so both compilers give the same files. It is the same fix as commit 95de00be of the old Arrow stack, without the regenerated `.dd` files, because on `main` the checked-in files are already clean.

This fixes only part of #836, so it does not close it. The issue also asks to keep `vendor/extensions/` dependencies in the `.dd` files so that an incremental build notices edits to the bundled extensions, and the filter still drops every `vendor` path by design. That needs a decision on which `vendor` paths to keep and a regeneration of the `.dd` files, and is left for a separate pull request. This one is the second checkbox of the issue.

Tested at `main` (3b7bea34) with gcc 13.3.0: touching all `src/*.c` and `src/*.cpp` files and running `pkgbuild::compile_dll()` regenerates the `.dd` files. Without the change, `git status` shows 26 modified `.dd` files, with about 13,500 added lines, 4,606 of them absolute `/usr` or `/opt` paths. With the change, the same rebuild leaves no `.dd` file modified. With clang (`CC=clang`, `CXX=clang++`) the same rebuild also leaves the `.dd` files unchanged. `R CMD check --no-manual` (without vignettes) passes with one NOTE about a hidden `.git` entry, which comes from building in a git worktree.

A second commit changes `LOCALE=C sort` in the same rule to `LC_ALL=C sort`, because `sort` ignores `LOCALE`, so under a locale such as `en_US.UTF-8` a rebuild reordered the entries of 19 `.dd` files (39 lines); with it, rebuilds under `en_US.UTF-8`, `de_CH.UTF-8` and `C.UTF-8` all leave the `.dd` files unchanged.

A third commit, asked for by the maintainer, makes the rule resilient against CRLF line endings. A `.d` file with CRLF endings, as a compiler on Windows may write, left a `\r` before each line end, so the continuation-line join did not fire, the filter kept system headers, and stray `\r` bytes ended up in the generated `.dd` file. The rule now pipes the `.d` file through `tr -d '\r'` before the `sed` calls; `\r` is a POSIX escape for `tr`, so this works with GNU, BSD/macOS and Rtools' `tr` alike, whereas `\r` in a `sed` regular expression is a GNU extension that BSD `sed` reads as a literal `r`. Tested by running the rule (`make` on a wrapper Makefile including `src/Makevars.deps`) on hand-written gcc-style (one-space continuation lines) and clang-style (two-space) `.d` files with absolute system headers, `vendor` and `..` paths, each with LF and with CRLF endings: with the change, CRLF and LF give byte-identical `.dd` files with LF endings, no `\r` and no absolute paths, and the LF output is byte-identical to that of the previous rule; before it, the CRLF output differed, carried `\r` bytes and kept a `/usr` path. A full `R CMD INSTALL` with gcc after touching all sources regenerated all 27 `.dd` files and left none modified.

The full CI matrix, dispatched by hand for 71d9fb81 ([run 43414159767](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/actions/runs/43414159767)), passes on every job: Ubuntu x86 and ARM with R 4.2 to devel, macOS with R 4.5 and 4.6, and Windows x86 and ARM with R 4.5, 4.6 and devel. A dispatched run fails when the build changes a tracked file, so this also shows that no `.dd` file changes on any of these platforms.

The fix comes from the old Arrow stack (95de00be in #795); the [plan to rework that stack](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6830171193) splits it out as a separate pull request from `main`, since nothing else depends on it. title: fix: `dbFetch()` raises "out of memory" instead of crashing when SQLite cannot convert a text value
description:
When SQLite runs out of memory while it converts a column value, for instance while transcoding a large text value from a UTF-16 database under a heap limit, `sqlite3_column_text()` and `sqlite3_column_blob()` return `NULL` and set `SQLITE_NOMEM` on the connection. With `check_utf8 = FALSE` (the default, and the only behavior of RSQLite 3.53.3 from CRAN), `fetch_string()` passed that `NULL` to `Rf_mkCharCE()` and R crashed. With `check_utf8 = TRUE`, `fetch_checked_string()` returned `""` and relied on the next `sqlite3_step()` failing in the same fetch; with the read-ahead of #850, that step runs ahead and keeps its error, so the `""` would reach the caller. The `extended_types` date, datetime and time readers passed the `NULL` on to their parsers.

## What changes

- `SqliteColumnDataSource` gets `check_out_of_memory()`, which raises `Cannot read column <j>: out of memory` (SQLite's own message) when a text or blob pointer is `NULL` and `sqlite3_errcode()` is `SQLITE_NOMEM`, as the SQLite documentation describes for these functions. A `NULL` for a NULL value, or a `NULL` blob with `sqlite3_column_bytes() == 0` (an empty blob), is never an error: the connection can still hold `SQLITE_NOMEM` from an earlier read of the same row, and such a value reads as `""`, as before.
- `fetch_text()` wraps `sqlite3_column_text()` with that check; `fetch_string()` (with `check_utf8 = FALSE`), `fetch_date()`, `fetch_datetime_local()` and `fetch_time()` use it. `fetch_checked_string()` runs the check on both its text and its blob pointer, so it no longer depends on the following step, and its comment no longer claims that the `""` never reaches the caller.
- `fetch_blob()` already raised an error for a `NULL` blob with a nonzero size and is unchanged.
- Two internal, unexported entry points in `src/rsqlite.cpp`, `sqlite_heap_limits()` and `sqlite_memory_used()`, let the tests cap SQLite's heap and lift the cap afterwards. `PRAGMA hard_heap_limit` can only lower the limit, and lowering the hard limit also lowers the soft limit for the whole process; leaving the soft limit behind made `test-transactions.R` fail with "database is locked" in an earlier draft, so the helper restores both.

## Left out

Other SQLite accessors that return `NULL` on out of memory, such as `sqlite3_column_name()` and `sqlite3_column_decltype()`, are not part of this change; `sqlite3_column_decltype()` returning `NULL` is already handled as "no declared type".

## Tests

`tests/testthat/test-out-of-memory.R`, with fixtures in `helper-heap-limit.R`, caps the heap at 16 MB above SQLite's current use and reads a 4-million-character value from an in-memory UTF-16 database: both `check_utf8` settings and a `DATE` column with `extended_types = TRUE` now raise "Cannot read column 2: out of memory". Measured on Linux, the error appears for headroom from about 8.5 MB (below that the step itself fails with "out of memory") up to 24 MB, and the value reads in full from 26 MB on, so 16 MB sits in the middle; because the sizes depend on SQLite's allocator, these two blocks are skipped on CRAN. A third block reads the same row again after the error and expects the step's "out of memory", not an error blamed on an empty blob in an earlier column. Two further blocks, which also pass on `main`, read the value in full without a cap and read empty text, `X''` and `zeroblob(0)` as `""` in a UTF-16 database with both `check_utf8` settings.

`devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true`: no failures besides the three in `test-httpvfs.R` that `main` shows too (#832, #837), and `test-dbConnect.R`'s busy-handler test, which needs an installed RSQLite in its `callr` child and has none in this environment.

The review's reproducer (heap limit of 16 MB, 4 MB text in a UTF-16 file database) under valgrind 3.22.0: on `main` with `check_utf8 = FALSE`, "Invalid read of size 1" and a segfault; on `main` with `check_utf8 = TRUE`, "out of memory" from the next step; on this branch, "Cannot read column 2: out of memory" for both settings and 0 valgrind errors. The new test file under valgrind also reports 0 errors and no definite leaks. RSQLite 3.53.3 from CRAN segfaults on the same experiment at limits of 10 to 24 MB.

## Place in the stack

Based on `main` (3f746a07) and independent of the open stack. Once #850 lands on top, `check_utf8 = TRUE` raises the error in the fetch that reads the value rather than returning `""` and deferring the error to the next fetch.

Review and accepted limitations: [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/890#issuecomment-6864044689); the pre-existing `sqliteCopyDatabase()` crash found in review is #891.

Closes #889.

title: fix: `dbFetch()` applies a UTC offset in TIMESTAMP and TIME columns as SQLite does
description:
With `extended_types = TRUE`, `dbFetch()` misread text in TIMESTAMP, DATETIME and TIME columns that ends in a negative UTC offset, and gave no warning. Boost's tokenizer splits on `-`, so it read the offset as a fraction of a second: `'2024-01-02 12:00:00-05:00'` came back as 12:00:00.05 UTC. Python's `sqlite3` module writes aware timestamps in this form, so a timestamp written anywhere west of UTC came back hours off. SQLite's own `datetime()` reads the same text as 17:00:00.

The parser now splits a trailing offset off before boost reads the text, then applies the offset. It accepts the forms SQLite's date and time functions accept: `Z`, or `[+-]HH:MM` with hours up to 14, with optional whitespace around it. This covers negative and positive offsets, offsets after a fraction, and offsets after a time without seconds. Positive offsets and `Z` used to give `NA` with a warning, and now give the instant SQLite reads. A TIME with an offset becomes a time of day in UTC and wraps around midnight, as `time()` does: `'23:00:00-02:00'` reads as 01:00:00. The time before the offset must be one that `time()` accepts: `HH:MM[:SS[.SSS]]`, with hours up to 24 (hour 24 only as 24:00:00). Durations such as `'25:00:00-02:00'` or `'-01:00:00+00:00'` therefore give `NA` with a warning, and `'24:00:00+00:00'` reads as 00:00:00, as in `time()`. Without an offset, a TIME is still a duration, so `'24:00:00'` stays 24 hours. The Extended Types section of `?SQLite` now describes the offset. If anything else after the time starts with a sign or `Z`, such as `-0500` or `-15:00`, the value is `NA` with the usual warning, which matches SQLite returning `NULL` for it. Text without an offset parses exactly as before. The offset is applied as SQLite applies it, but the time before it is still read by boost, which accepts some text that SQLite rejects, such as `12:00:60` (#887, already on `main`).

Out of scope: DATE columns, a `T` between date and time, and a trailing ` UTC`. These still give `NA` with a warning, as before. #394 would replace the boost parser altogether.

Tests: four new `test_that()` blocks in `tests/testthat/test-extendedTypes.R`. They read offsets in DATETIME and TIME columns, compare the result with SQLite's `datetime()` and `time()` on the same rows, and check that the offsets and TIME values SQLite rejects give `NA` with a warning. All four fail on `main` and pass with this change. `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true` gives no new failures. The `test-httpvfs.R` errors happen on `main` as well (#832, #837). `R CMD check --no-manual` reports only a NOTE about the worktree's `.git` file.

Where it sits: this is based on `main`, outside the Arrow stack. The Arrow arrays of #861 share this parser and pin today's misreadings in their tests. Once this is merged up, #861 needs its expectations updated, and the parsing helpers it adds need the same offset handling.

Review and limitations: [review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/885#issuecomment-6861593786), [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/885#issuecomment-6863321125).

Closes #877.

title: fix: `dbConnect()` closes the SQLite handle when the database fails to open
description:
When `sqlite3_open_v2()` fails, for example because the file's directory does not exist, it usually still allocates a connection handle, and SQLite's documentation asks for that handle to be passed to `sqlite3_close()`. `DbConnection`'s constructor raised the error without closing it, and its destructor does not run when the constructor throws, so each failed `dbConnect()` leaked about 800 bytes. valgrind reports this as "definitely lost" against any package whose tests open a missing file. The constructor now reads the error message from the handle, closes the handle with `sqlite3_close_v2()`, and raises the same error as before. This is the fix proposed in the issue.

The user-visible error is unchanged. A new test in `test-dbConnect.R` pins the message for a missing directory, checks that it stays the same over repeated failed opens, and that a connection opened afterwards works. The leak itself is not observable from R, so that test also passes on `main`; the leak was checked with valgrind instead: ten failed `dbConnect()` calls lose 8,368 bytes in 16 blocks on `main` and 0 bytes with this change. `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true` passes apart from the three known `test-httpvfs.R` errors (#832, #837).

This pull request is based on `main`, ahead of the Arrow stack. Its hunk merges cleanly into `claude/fetch-row-ahead` (#850) and `claude/arrow-param-checks`, next to #865's change to the same constructor.

title: fix: `dbFetch()` no longer leaks column storage when a column spills over twice or a warning handler errors
description:
When `dbFetch()` meets a value that a column's current storage cannot hold, `DbColumnStorage::append_data_to_new()` allocates a spill-over storage and converts the value into it before `DbColumn::set_col_value()` takes ownership. This pull request closes two leaks in that function.

- **A warning turned into an error (#879).** If converting the value raises a warning that a handler turns into an error, for example under `options(warn = 2)` or `withCallingHandlers(warning = function(w) stop(...))`, the error unwinds past the raw pointer and 40 bytes leak per call. The spill-over storage is now held in a `std::unique_ptr` until `append_data()` returns. `cpp11::warning()` turns R's unwind into a C++ exception, so the destructor runs.
- **A nested spill-over, on the default path with no handler.** A full integer storage that meets a real or 64-bit value spills over twice: the new integer storage at once spills over into a real one and returns that. The caller owns only the storage returned, so the empty storage in between was dropped without an owner, leaking 40 bytes and keeping its R vector, twice the previous capacity, preserved for good. With 1,638,300 integers followed by one real, 10 fetches kept 62.5 MB of R heap. The function now releases the storage only when it is the one returned, and deletes the empty one otherwise. `main` and the CRAN release have this leak too; the review of this pull request found it ([review](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/883#issuecomment-6861552025)).

Nothing else changes: the ownership hand-off to `DbColumn`, the storage layout and the results stay as they are. A sibling leak of the same kind, `Rf_warning()` in `SqliteResultImpl::fetch_rows()` under `options(warn = 2)`, is out of scope and now tracked in #886.

Testing: under valgrind, the issue's reproducer loses 120 bytes in 3 blocks on `main` and 0 bytes here; a 101-row column of 100 integers followed by `1.5` and by `5000000000` loses 200 bytes in 5 blocks on `main` and 0 bytes here; the `warn = 2`, `tryCatch(warning = )` and `n = 5` variants lose 160 bytes in 4 blocks on `main` and 0 bytes here. Valgrind reports no memory errors with the change. The heap measurement above keeps 0 MB with the change. Neither leak is visible from R, so the new tests pin the behavior around the fix and pass on `main` as well; only a valgrind or sanitizer run catches a regression. The test in `test-extendedTypes.R` checks that the handler's error reaches the caller and that the result can be cleared and queried again. The test in `test-basic-types.R` checks that the 101-row column comes back whole as double and as `integer64`. `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true` passes apart from the known `test-httpvfs.R` errors (#832, #837).

Review rounds: two. The first confirmed the fix for #879 and found the nested spill-over, which this pull request now fixes as well; the second found nothing above Low. What remains is listed under [Accepted limitations](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/883#issuecomment-6861731909).

This pull request is based on `main`, independently of the Arrow stack (#850, #830 and up), which does not touch `DbColumnStorage.cpp`. It merges cleanly into #850; against the top of the stack the only conflict it adds is the new test appended at the end of `test-extendedTypes.R`, which the stack also extends.

Closes #879.

title: fix: `dbBind()` fails when SQLite refuses to bind a value
description:
Decided in https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6840238222.

On `main`, the data-frame path of `dbBind()` ignores the return codes of `sqlite3_bind_text()`, `sqlite3_bind_blob()` and the other `sqlite3_bind_*()` calls in `SqliteResultImpl::bind_parameter_pos()`. A text or blob value over SQLite's length limit (`SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH`, 2147483647 bytes by default, lower if a connection sets it) is therefore bound as NULL without an error, and the row is written with NULL in its place. With RSQLite's build settings, the default limit (`SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH=2147483647`) equals R's maximum string length, so a value from R cannot exceed it; the check guards connections that lower the limit, and allocation failures (`SQLITE_NOMEM`).

This pull request checks the return code of every `sqlite3_bind_*()` call of that path. A refused value fails with SQLite's message, naming the parameter by position, by name for a named placeholder, and the row of the parameters, for example `Can't bind parameter 2 (:x) in row 2: string or blob too big.` The message is passed through a fixed format string. `dbBind()` now treats the result as unbound and completed until its first row is bound, so when the first row fails, a following `dbFetch()` errors as for an unbound result instead of returning zero rows, and `dbGetRowCount()` no longer reports the previous binding's count. When a later row of the parameters fails, the result is marked complete, so no fetch reads the reset statement; the rows before it have already been executed, and rows already fetched in the same `dbFetch()` call are discarded with the error, as for an error from `sqlite3_step()` in a later row on `main`. In both cases a following `dbBind()` with valid values binds afresh, and `dbClearResult()` works as before.

#866 and #867 do the same on the Arrow path of `dbBindArrow()`, with similar wording.

For the tests, a new unexported entry point `connection_limit_length()` sets `SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH` on a connection and returns the previous limit; it has the same signature as the one in the Arrow stack, so the two converge. SQLite does not go below 30 bytes, so the tests use that limit.

Left out: `raise_sqlite_exception()` still passes `sqlite3_errmsg()` as the format string of `cpp11::stop()`; that is fixed separately rather than here, to keep this change to the bind path. The other errors raised by `bind_parameter_pos()` (an unsupported parameter type) keep their message; in the first row they now leave the same completed, unbound result as a refused value, while in a later row they still do not mark the result complete.

Tested with the new `tests/testthat/test-dbBind.R`: text and blob values one byte over the limit fail, values at the limit bind and round-trip, a named parameter in a later row is named in the message, the result is complete after the failure and can be re-bound, a query bound and fetched before errors on `dbFetch()` after a failed re-bind, reports a row count of 0, `dbHasCompleted()` TRUE and `dbGetRowsAffected()` NA, a statement reports `dbGetRowsAffected()` NA after a failed re-bind, an unsupported parameter type leaves a completed, unbound result, `dbClearResult()` succeeds after a failed bind, and `dbExecute()` with an over-long value fails and inserts nothing. `devtools::test()` with `NOT_CRAN=true`, DBItest included, passes except the three known `test-httpvfs.R` errors (#832, #837); the busy-handler test in `test-dbConnect.R` runs against an installed build.

title: fix: Never use query text or SQLite messages as a `printf()` format, and guard `fetch_blob()` against `NULL`
description:
Decided in https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/pull/829#issuecomment-6771849788: a small separate pull request from `main`, independent of the Arrow stack.

## What changes and why

`cpp11::warning()` and `cpp11::stop()` treat their first argument as a `printf()` format unless `CPP11_USE_FMT` is defined. Three calls passed user-controlled text there, so a `%n` in a query, a table name or a column name aborted R with `*** %n in writable segment detected ***`, and other conversions such as `%d%d` printed garbage:

- `SqliteResultImpl::prepare()`: the "Ignoring remaining part of query: " warning appended the rest of a multi-statement query (`dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT 1; SELECT '%n'")`).
- `SqliteResultImpl::raise_sqlite_exception()`: passed `sqlite3_errmsg()`, which quotes table and column names (`dbGetQuery(con, 'SELECT * FROM "x%n"')`).
- `DbColumn::warn_type_conflicts()`: the mixed-type warning includes the column name. This is the column-name variant found in the review of #799; that reimplementation no longer carries the fix, so it lands here.

All three now pass a fixed `"%s"`-style format with the text as an argument. A remaining query that merely contains a literal `%`, such as `SELECT 1; SELECT 'café 100%'`, gave an empty warning on `main` (confirmed by the review); the warning now shows the remaining query as written. The "Query requires %i params; %i supplied." error passed `params.size()`, an `R_xlen_t`, for `%i`; it is now cast to `int`. Every other `cpp11::stop()`, `cpp11::warning()`, `Rf_error()` and `Rf_warning()` call in `src/` (outside the vendored SQLite) already uses a literal format.

`SqliteColumnDataSource::fetch_blob()` passed the pointer from `sqlite3_column_blob()` to `memcpy()` unchecked. For an empty blob (`SELECT X'' AS x`) that pointer is `NULL`, which is undefined behavior even for zero bytes (UBSan reports "null pointer passed as argument 2"). An empty blob now returns `raw(0)` without `memcpy()`, and a `NULL` pointer with a nonzero size, which means SQLite ran out of memory, raises an error instead of crashing. A comment notes that `sqlite3_column_bytes()` must stay before `sqlite3_column_blob()`, since that check relies on the order.
